Every person well acquainted with the
English Statute Book must be aware that
while every Parliamentary session adds enor-
mouply to its bulk, there are also comprised
amongst its contents many laws and acts
which, however necessary when adopted, have,
from the lapse of time and altered circum-
stances, become obs64e, although still un-
repealed. In like maLner, the Dictionaries of
the English language, in every fresh edition
published, while they embrace large additions
to the number of words of Which our
language is composed, also contains words
formerly in constant and general use, but
which now, referring only to things of the
past, fall meaningless upon the ears of us
moderns. In the course of some late researches
into this lexicographical phenomena, I acci-
dentally stumbled over two words, with which
I was familiar in my youthful days,. but to
which my ears have of late been a stranger—
Radical—Reform. As working men of the pre-
sent day are evidently not too familiar with
these words, a brief explanation of them may
not be unnecessary. The word "Radical "-is
derived from the word "radix," or root; and
thus, any person desirous of removing an evil,
by finding out and destroying its root, was
described as a "Radical," or one desiring a
radical cure. The word "Reform," in the
limited sense it is now used, when used at all,
has generally a tail attached to it; thus,
when a home for the "social evil," or young
street vagabond, is established, it has bestowed
upon it the name of "Reformatory." For-
merly, it was generally used and best under-
stood as having a political signification. Thus,
a man desiring a complete removal of any of
the abuses foolishly, as it would now appear,
supposed to exist in connection with our
Government, or "glorious constitution," was
called a "Radical Reformer." There are still
many now living, amongst the working classes
especially, who have a lively recollection of
both seeing and hearing such persons; indeed
the breed is not yet quite extinct, but, like
the Indian race of America, it is fast dying
out. In the early portion of the present
century there were numerous healthy speci-
mens of the "Radical Reformer" existing in
this country, whose soil at that day was highly
favourable to the growth of the article.
Amongst the most prominent were—Sir
• FRANCIS BURDETT, Sir CHARLES WOLSELEY,
JOHN CAM 110BHOUSE, MAJOR CARTWRIGHT,
JEREMY BENTHAM, TTENRY HUNT, WILLTAM
COBBETT, &C., &c.; but as they died out the stock
became deteriorated, until there is now little
left to remind one of the former high and
thorough-bred "Radical Reformer."
If any argument was wanting to prove the
disuse into which the word " Reform " has
fallen, I can find it in the speeches delivered
within the last few days by the members (called,
by some demented people, the Radical mem-
bers) for the populous metropolitan boroughs of
Lambeth and Southwark. Messrs. William
Williams, Frederick Doulton, and John Locke,
have met their constituents, for the purpose of
telling them what they had done, and hearing
from them what they were wished to do. Mr.
Williams spoke for upwards of an hour
but he never allowed the word " Reform "
to escape his lips. So with Mr. Doulton ; so
with Mr. Locke. But what is still more re-
markable, not one Of the. "free and indepen-
dent electors" present at either of these
meetings seemed to retain a sufficient recollec-
tion of the word to put any question upon the
subject to their " worthy representatives."
Could anything be more convincing that the
word " Reform" is becoming fast obliterated
from the English language? The time was, and
not far distant, when the omission of this word
from the speech of one of these borough mem-
bers, would have called forth such a shout of
indignation as would have made the walls of
the building in which the meeting was as-
sembled tremble with the sound. But - times
are changed. 'Tis true, a meteoric flash, in the
shape of a "Reform Conference," passed over
London in May last, but it faded away
Like the baseless fabric of a dream,
Leaving not a wreck behind!

Pondering-. over these lost words, I, for the
moment, jumped to the conclusion that the end
sought by Radical Reformers had been obtained.
I thought that man was at last in possession
of the suffrage instead of bricks and mortar;
that the working classes had 'obtained the once-
coveted franchise, protected by the ballot;
that the House of Commons had become in
reality a representation of all classes of the
community; that extravagant public expendi-
ture had given way to retrenchment and eco-
nomy; that the bnrdens pressing upon in-
dustry had been removed, and placed upon the
shoulders of those more capable of bearing
them; that jobbery in public departments was
Unknown; that property had become alive to
the fact of its having duties as well as rights;
that the working man was prosperous, well
'midi and happy; in short, that G-overnment
now existed, not for the purposes and interests
of the few, but for the advancement of the
"greatest possible happiness of the greatest
possible number." I thought all this must
be so, or the words, "Radical Reform,"
could not have become so universally
ignored.
Further examination, however, showed me
how much I had been deceived, mid I awoke
from my pleasing illusion. I found that the
working man was still, politically, a slave;
that those 'who !possessed the franchise were
still, for want of the ballot, driven to the
hustings like cattle, ,or corrupted by filthy
lucre; that the House of Commons was still
a "sham ;" that it was still as rotten, unprin-
cipled and selfish, and as ignorant and un-
mindful of working class interests, as in the
most palmy days of boroughmongering Cor-
ruption; that it was still ready to sanction
all extravagant public expenditure, and uphold
jobbery in all its enormity; that the efforts
of the working classes to improve their con-
dition by reducing their hours of labour,
was still vehemently opposed and thwarted;
that the endeavours of trades' unions to
advance the social position of their members
were, depriyed. of political power, as fertile as
ever; tharlarge masses of my fellow-workmen
were suffering unheard of privations as the
result. of bad and class legislation; and that
Government was still carried on in the interests
of the few; and not in those of the many.
In my despair my
eye caught a flag waving
over a bright spot in the vast political desert,
on which inscribed was "Trades' Societies
PoliticaVrnion." Here, I said aloud, I shall
find the words Radical Reform" still remem-
bered and cherished; and was hastening
towards it, when the voice of the Editor
whispered in my ear, "Whatever you find
there, must be told at a future time; at present
you , have filled your allotted space." I
indignantly threw down my pen, mentally
anUtheinising all editors, and, vowing to myself
that I would at another time have my say, felt
strongly inclined to resent the interruption by
applying the SCOURGE,

DISTRESS IN LA.NC.ASIIIRE.

THE LONDON WORKING MEN'S CENTRAL

COMMITTEE

The third weekly meeting of the delegates forming
this committee was held on Wednesday evening at the
office, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, when the fol-
lowing were present :—Messrs. Jarvis .(carpenter),
Murray (boot-closer), Charles (carpenter), Odgers
(shoemaker), Cremer (carpenter), Martin (cigar
maker), Walker (bookbinder), Burns (brickmalKer),
Amos (carpenter), Howell (bricklayer) ; Messrs. Nieass
and Page, from the workmen of rotting-hill, and Mr.
Potter, treasurer, and Mr. Hornsfiy, hon. secretary.
Mr. Murray took the chair, and said: The Rev. Mr.
Verity was in attendance as a deputation from the East
Lancashire Central Operatives Committee, and, after
the delegates sent to Lancashire had made their
report, the rev, gentleman would address the meeting.
Letters were then read from' Manchester, Preston,
Blackburn, and Padiham, acknowledging the receipt of
the monies voted last week.
Mr. Cremer, one of the Committee's delegates to
Lancashire, then made their report at great length.
[As this report, which is of a highly interesting cha-
racter, will be carefully prepared, with 'names, dates,
and circumstances,' in time for our next publication.
we shall then be able to publish it in e:rtenso.]
He stated they had found the Central Operatives' Com-
mittee sitting at Padiham, as the Executive of East
Lancashire, and to whom all contributions acknow-
ledged in the - BEEHIVE up to last week had been
sent, to be perfectly trustworthy, and possess-
ing the full confidence of all classes. The ex-
ecutive committee, of which- the Rev, Mr. Verity
was the president, was composed of three repre-
sentatives from each local committee in those towns
where the funds were distributed. In conjunction
with his brother delegate he had visited Pa3iham,
Habergham, Blackburn, Burnley, Bacup, Great Har-
wood, and other places, and wherever they went they
found that co-operatives who while they held even a
shilling share in a store or mill could not by law
claim any relief from the poor-law guardians, were
universally refused relief by the local rolief com-
mittees, who were nearly all composed of professional
men and manufacturer:4 working men not being
allowed to sit on them, although they were quite
willing to receive the subscriptions of working men sent
through the Mansion-house er Mancheister Central Com-
mittees, so long as working men were foolish enough to
send their money through those channels in preference
to the London Working Men's Committee. The men
of London could form no conception of The number of
co-operators who had thus been refused relief. He
was prepared to give a number of cases which he had
personally visited, with names and all particulars, and
all these should be given in the written report he was
preparing to submit at their next meeting. In the mean-
time they might feel assured that the statements of the

Rev. Mr Veilty on this subject were rather under than
over the mark. They could not bring the cases of
unionists so clearly before them, as relief was not
denied for being a unionist; but it was most remarkable
that numbers of those operatives, of unimpeachable
characters, who had been active in trade disputes,.
had been refused relief by the committees upon
the most slender grounds, while others had been re-
lieved unquestioned. These men were repeatedly
twitted by manufacturers, members of these relief
committees, when met in the street, Well, you will
not be so ready in future to stand up for your price
lists, you have something else to think about now.'
I can furnish the names of men who have been thus
spoken to. We have waited on Mr.. Maclure, the
secretary of the Manchester Central Committee, and
spoken to him about the refusal of relief to co-operators
and holders of cottage property. He acknowledged
its impolicy, and said the subject had been mooted on
the committee, and would be considered. The distress
was not confined to the cotton operatives; all trades
were alike suffering. -
51
Mr. Burns, the other delegate, generally corrobo-
rated Mr. Cremer. He would mention one instance
of the way in which these middle class relief
committees dispose of the monies—much of it
contributed by the working classes of London and
elsewhere—entrusted to them. On the East Lanca-
shire Railway there are -two stations, Rosegrove and
Apton, the latter being one mile nearer to Padihana
than the former, but, a hill intervening, it costa the
manufacturers is. 6d. per ton more for goods brought
to the latter than to the former station. To obviate
this inconvenience a body of the unemployed opera-
tives have been employed in levelling this hill. Of
that no one could complain, providing the men were
paid out of the poor rate of the district, as the
improvement was a local one, affecting only local
interests. . But no, this labour was paid for by the
relief committee out of the public subscriptions
entrusted to them, although it was bestowed on a
local improvement,,and by which the manufacturers
Would be alone benefited.

The reports of" the delegates having been received,

The Rev. Mr. Verity s—aid he attended as a deputa-
tion from the East Lancashire Central Operative Com-
mittee, to explain the exact position in which that
committee stood. It was highly desirable that the
London Working Men's Committee and the committee
he represented should act together, one as a collecting
the other as a distributing body. The committee be
represented had the full confidence of the operatives
of East Lancashire, and so soon as sufficient funds
were placed at their command they would extend their
relief. Their operations had been at present confined
to Padiham, Burnley, and Habergham ; but they were
now going to take in Great Harwood and Bacup, and
would follow with Colne, Clitheroe,
,Darwen, Black-
burn, Accrington, and other places. In granting
relief they have laid down three principles for
their guidanc.e., lot, the relief of the co-ope-
rators, who hi:a been refused relief by the local
committees; 2nd, the relief of unionists who had
been similarly treated ; and 3rdly, to supplement the
relief given from poor law guardians to all persons with-
out distinction of sect, party, or opinions. He would
advise the London Committee to send their money
direct to the East Lancashire Executive Committee, who,
being well acquainted with the localities and their
wants, would be able to distribute the funds more
advantageously and with less likelihood of imposition.
The committee would always be happy to attend to
any wish or suggestion made by the London Com-
mittee, or to any special grants they might desire
to be made. Their accounts would be regularly
forwarded to the London Committee, and no
information withheld. He was prepared to substan-
tiate all that he had said with regard to the refusal
of relief to co-operators and unionists. He thought
the London Committee had done well in sending a
deputation into Lancashire, though they ought to have
been there a fortnight instead of a week. He con-
cluded a very earnest appeal amidst much applause.
_ Messrs. Challis, Potter, Howell, and Hornsby,
entirely coincided with the views expressed by Mr.
Verity.
Mr. Walker moved 'That the funds collected'

through this committee be sent to the East Lancashire
Central Operatives Committee for distribution by
them through their local committees.'
Mr. Amos seconded the motion, whicli was unani-
mously agreed to.
The Rev. Mr. Verity having stated it to be his in-
tention to wait upon the Mansion House Committee
to solicit a special grant, it was resolved that Messrs.

Creme; Potter, and Burns, should accompany the Rev.
gentleman as a deputation from the London Work-
men's Committee.

The treasurer was then instructed to transmit imme-
diately the sum of £4O to the East Lancashire Com-
mittee at • Padiham. The committee then adjourned
until Tuesday evening next at six o'clock.

THE CABMEN'S DELEGATE
MEETING.

The delegate meeting of the cab-drivers of the
metropolis was held at the BEEHIVE Officz., Bouverie-
street, Fleet- street, on Tuesday evening last; Mr.
Wise, of Westminster, in the chair.
Mr. Bennett, who had been hitherto acting as
secretary to the delegates, stated he was compelled,
from private reasons, to relinquish his office, but would
still continue to give the movement his best advice and
assistance.

Mr. Smith, Secretary of the South London Cabmen's
Club, having agreed to take the office of Secretary, was
unanimously elected. _ _

The Secraary reported the resolutions agreed to by
the late aggregate meeting, and stated he had waited
upon Mr. Arthur Kinnaird, M.P., who was willing to
present the petition praying for a Parliamentary Com-
mittee of Inquiry, but was not at present prepared to
undertake the charge of the bill it was desired to in-
troduce iuto Parliament.

Considerable discussion ensued, and various sug-
gestions were made, as to the best mode of carrying on
the agitation. •
Mr. Powell proposed, an Mr. Wellman seconded,
a resolution That a circular, with a copy of the minutes
of the delegates, be printed and sent to every Member
of Parliament.'

The motion on a division was negatived, it being
thought premature.

fovell then moved, and Mr. Good seconded,
a resolution 'That; the Secretary be instructed to write
to each of the Hackney Carriage Proprietors' Associ-
ation, inviting them to send an equal number of
delegates from their bodies to co-operate with the
delegates of the drivers in carrying out, the objects
agreed to at the aggregate meeting.'
.The motion, after some discussion, was agreed to.
- Some conversation then took place as to the raising
of the necessary funds for the prosecution of the
movement, but it was eventually agreed that all ques-
tions should stand over to see whether the proprietors
were willing to co-operate with the drivers.
It was then resolved that the meeting should stand
adjourned until Tuesday evening, the 30th inst., when
.it was expected that the delegates from the proprietors
would be able to attend.

articles.title: DEPUTATION TO THE MANSION HOUSE.
articles.text:
DEPUTATION TO THE MANSION HOUSE.

The deputation appointed at the above meeting,
with Mr. Verity, waited upon the Rev. Mr. Gibbs, one
of the secretaries of the Mansion House Committee,
on Thursday morning, for the purpose of bringing
under his notice the treatment of the co-operators by
the Local Relief Committees, and the claims of the
East Lancashire Committee to a special grant. The
Rev. Mr. Verity and the members of the deputation
baying laid before Mr. Gibbs the statements made at
the committee on the previous evening, offering to
verify them, by 'names, dates, and circumstances,'
who listened to them with the greatest attention, he
said, if the deputation would place their statement in
writing, and leave it with him in the course of the
dity, it should be laid before the General Committge, at
their meeting on Friday, and a reply sent. The
deputation then retired.
In the afternoon, Mr. Gibbs was supplied with
written copies of the statement, both from Mr. Verity,
and the deputation from the London Workmen's Com-
mittee.

EAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL OPERATIVES'

RELIEF FU-D.

The weekly meeting of the Executive took place on
Monday, Dec. 15th, at the Committee-rooms, Speak-
buildings, ; present the Rev. E. A. Verity,
8.D., president, Mr. James Denbigh, vice-president,
Messrs. Pinder, Crompton, Shackleton, Heap, White-
head, Hargreaves' Haworth, Wilkinson and Peacock.
(hon. secretary.) The minutes of the previous meeting
were read and confirmed.

The Secretary gave in his report, which was highly
satisfactory, and indicated favourable progress of the
charity. Two letters were read from Mr. George
Potter, one enclosing £3, and announcing the termina-
tion Of his individual labours, as collector for the
East Lancashire Central; the other enclosing
as a donation from the London Working Men's
Central.

Thanks were cordially voted to Mr. Potter, who had
generously given his services gratis, and ,to the
directors of the BEEHIVE for opening their columns and
collecting £llB 55. 2d., thus enabling tho East Lanca-
shire Central to relieve 1,584 families, consisting of
6,082 persons; also to the brethren in London for their
kind donation.

A long discussion took place respecting the propriety
of sending a deputation to London-to explain the pre-
sent position of the East Lancashire Central, after
which it was resolved that such a deputation be
appointed to wait on the London brethren when they
met on Wednesday next. The President was unani-
mously chosen.
Letters were read from Anglesea, Edinbro', Liver.
pool, Preston, and other places, evincing a hearty
desire to supplement the inadequate aid afforded the
suffering operatives.

It was proposed by Mr. James Denbigh, and seconded
by Mr. Wilkinson, tint Great Harwood be admitted
into the Central. The proposition was carried unani-
mously, and the officials from that place admitted.
Grants were then given to Burnley, Habergham,
and Padiham, and promises of aid to Bacup, Great
Harwood, and Ramsbottom. This terminated the
business, and the meeting separated.

articles.text:
THE TVO_RSBOROUGH COLLIERY

CALAMITY.

(LATEST PARTICULARS.)
The engineers met to consult as to reopening the
pit to recover the dead. A few minutes after they had
decided not to enter the pit at present another terrific
explosion occurred. It was afterwards determined to
partially fill up the cupola shaft and seal the mouths
of the other two shafts and flood the entire pit with
water. The recovery of the bodies is delayed for
months, and more lives are lost.

THE LVP.ERIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.

The tenth annual meeting of this flourishing society
was held a few days since, when the directors' report
and cash account were submitted and adopted. The
report contains a very lucid and satisfactory statement
of the objects, condition, and prospects of the society,
and shows very clearly how much good can be done
by a building society which is well managed and carried
On, as this society obviously is, for the equal benefit of
the investing and the borrowing members. The
directors state in their report, that During the past ten
years the society has conferred very great benefits on.
the two classes of members composing it. To investing
members it has given a safe, easy, and profitable means
of investing their money in large or small sums, for
long or short periods, with unusual facilities for depo-
siting and withdrawing their money. To borrowing
members it has givensfacilities for becoming the owners
of the houses in which they reside, on easy terms;
in many cases it has enabled such members to become
the absolute owners of their dwellings in a few years,
by paying sums equal to, and in most cases less than,
their rent to the society instead of to their landlords.
In other cases it has enabled owners of property to
increase the value of their property by additional
buildings, and it has also lent valuable assistance to
members in erecting houses, workshops, and even
factories and gas works. The directors in deciding to
extend their business, say, The extension of business
will be quite as much to the advantage of old share-
holders as it will be to the advantage of new members,
because every addition to the capital employed
reduces the per centage of management expenses, and,
therefore, increases the profits of old members, while
those who now join the society for the first time will do
so at a period when all the cost of establishing the
institution has been paid off, and when all new busi-
ness brings with it the maximum of profit.'

Mn. COBDEN ON THE DISTEESS.—Mr. Cobden, at the
request of the inhabitants of Midhurst, delivered an
address to them on Tuesday on the Lancashire distress.
He spoke of the distress as having been caused by the
national policy of recognising blockades in time of
war, and argued therefrom that its relief was a national
duty. The extent of the distress he illustrated by
saying that it was equal to what would be produced
if the whole of the agricultural labourers in eight
southern counties were suddenly thrown out of employ-
ment, and the income of the farmers stopped. He
showed that the mamteacturers were doing their duty,
and said his only fear was that the sacrifices they were
now making would cripple them when they should
begin work again.

MR. COMM AND THE CABMEN'S SECRETART.—A case
in which two cabmen were concerned came on the
other day before Mr. Combe, at the Southwark Police-
court. Mr. Smith, the respected secretary of the Cab-
men's Club, attended on behalf of the defendant in the
case, but not being a member of the legal profession,
felt doubtful whether the magistrate would allow him
to speak. He therefore wrote his name and occu-
pation on a piece of paper, with a request that he
might be permitted to speak, and sent it up to' the
judicial dignitary. Mr. Combe on looking at it, with
a look of virtuous indignation, tore it in pieces, and ex-
pressed his surprise at Mr. Smith's audacity in daring
to write to a magistrate. Now, this display of indig-
nation on the part of Mr. Combo would have been in
place, had Mr. Smith written anything with the view
of influencing his judgment; but as it was simply
what we above stated, Mr. Combo was guilty of gross
impertinence towards Mr. Smith, and can only be
excused on the supposition that, like Shakspeare's Dog-
bery, we may write him down an ass.'

TRE CABrdEN AND TIIE GAROTTERS.—A silly letter
appeared in the Daily Telegraph, one day this week,
respecting a boy who was sent to hire a cab for his
father, discovering a garotter waiting inside the cab;
and on the cabman being asked for his ticket he drove
off. This was, doubtless, 'sensation' letter concocted
in the Daily Telegraph Office; if not, the editor must
have had his credulity imposed upon by his correspon-
dent. We do not believe there is one word of truth
in the statement, which was both foolish and dis-
creditable.

articles.title: WORKING MEN'S CLUB AND _USTI-
articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S CLUB AND _USTI-

TUTE UIVION.

A special general meeting of this society was held
on Tuesday evening, at their rooms,so, Strand, for the
purpose of considering a proposal to substitute in the
prospectus (which states the society's objects and
principles) a strong recommendation to working men's
clubs to exclude from their premises intoxicating
drinks, instead of the stipulation that no club should
be received into membership of the unicn, unless that
exclusion were enforced. Russell Scott, Esq., was
called to the chair. The proposal was made the subject
of a lengthened and general discussion. While the
feeling was all but unanimous among both the
moderate drinking and the total abstinence parties,
gentlemen and working men, that the introduction of
intoxicating drinks into clubs and institutes for the
industrial classes would be an injurious and uncalled
for proceeding, Mr. Godfrey Lushington, M.A., Mr.
Hastings (Social Science Association), Mr. Chas. Crit-
chett, B.A. (Society of Arts), and the Rev. J. Baldwin
Brown, B.A , strongly represented that the toleration
or exclusion should be decided entirely by the local
societies. It was further urged by Mr. Neill and Mr.
Hugh Owen (chairman of the National Temperance
League Committee) that the Union would be able to
exercise a wider influence by recommending the exclu-
sion of these drinks than by making that exclusion a
condition of membership and assistance. The Rev. H.
Solly (secretary of the union) drew attention to the
fact that the adoption of the proposed alteration would'
in no way conflict with the object for which the society
was formed. The present was a question simply of the best
way of carrying that object into effect, and he agreed
with other speakers that if working men allowed these
drinks in any club or ins.itute the society was far more
likely to get them excluded by moral suasion than by
peremptorily refusing the admission of such a club to
the union. He also mentioned that they would secure
much valuable support by the proposed alteration, espe-
cially that of the adult education societies, and the
unions of mechanics' institutes, the supporters of which
while strongly objecting, for the most part, to the
introduction of intoxicating liquors into these insti-
tutes, were equally decided against the use of a stipu-
lation which savoured of dictation or coercion. It was
finally resolved, by a considerable majority, to amend
the paragraph in tho prospectus as follows :---‘ In
reference to the use of intoxicating drinks in working
men's clubs, the council are strongly of opinion that
their introduction would be dangerous to the interests
of those societies, and earnestly recommend their ex-
clusion. They make this recommendation on pru-
dential grounds, the reasonableness of which it is
believed the working classes will be the first to acknow-
ledge.'

ABANDONMENT OP THE PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION OF
PR/XES AT THE EXHIBITION.—,It seems that there is to
be no public distribution of the Exhibition prize medals
by the Prince of Wales. The Commissioners have
addressed a letter to his Royal Highness, in which,
while thanking him for consenting to distribute the
prizes, they intimate that it would be practically ho-.
possible for a single occasion, to, light and warm the
building. The distribution could not be postponed
beyond the end of January, an,d therefore the Commis-

On Tuesday evening Mr. Locke, M.P., for South-
wark, addressed a meeting of his constituents at the
Bridge-house Hotel, London-bridge. Mr. Locke was
received with loud cheers. After referring to some
local topics, the hon. member proceeded to take a gen -
ral review of the proceedings of the last session and the
part he had taken in them. He had, he said, supported
the Abolition of Whipping Bill for juvenile offenders,
although he should not object to support a bill for the
whipping of garotters. (A laugh.) The country
might, he remarked, congratulate itself upon the results
of the French treaty, of which he had been a strong
supporter. He considered the foreign policy of the
government during the last session worthy of all com-
mendation. There was a strong party in the House of
Commons in favour of intervention in American
affAirs, but the government had refused to intervene,
and be believed it had done right. (Loud cheers.)
He confessed himself confused on American subjects,
but one thing was clear to him, that one inevitable
result of the present struggle would be the complete
and total abolition of slavery. (Cheers.) He approved
of the conduct of he government on the subject of the
fortifications, but he believed a considerable reduction
of expenditure woull be proposed in the next session
of parliament, which should have his earnest support.
Several questions having been asked, and satisfactorily
answered, a vote of confidence and thanks to the hon.
gentleman for his constant advocacy of every liberal
measure and unvarying watchfulness of the local
interests of the borough was unanimously adopted.

MR. DOULTON AT LAMBETH.

Mr. Doulton, the junior M.P. for Lambeth, met his
constituents on Monday evening, at the Horns Tavern,
Kennington, on his own invitation, to address them as
to the present state of public affairs, and his conduct
and votes in Parliament since his election. Mr.
Doulton, who was warmly welcomed by a very crowded
room, in the course of his address observed: He
thought the time had arrived when the question should
be seriously considered by the English Government
and the English people whether Italy was to remain
permanently a French province. (Hear.) The American
civil war was deeply to be deplored, and he regretted
that no break yet appeared in the dark cloud that
overshadowed the American continent. It was strange,
however, that in this land of liberty, which had made
such sacrifices to abolish slavery, sympathy should be
anywhere expressed in favour of the Southern con-
federacy—the confederacy of slaveowners. (Cheers.)
Slavery had more to do with the civil war than many
people imagined. But while the South openly avowed
that the black man was an inferior being, and must be
kept in bondage, unfortunately the North was not
sound upon the question. Would to God they were,
and had placed their cause on principle rather than
expediency. (Cheers.) Of this, however, there could
be no question, that if the South succeeded slavery
would be strengthened and perpetuated. (Hear, hear.)
He deprecated any interference on the part of this
country in the fratricidal quarrel, remarking that in-
terference meant intervention, and intervention war.
The hon. member touched on some other less im•
portant subjects. At the conclusion of his address a
resolution of confidence was proposed and carried by
acclamation.

THE GREEK ELECTION.

The general voting of all Greek citizens in
London for the election of the King of Greece
commenced at the office of the Consul-General in
Gracechurch-street at one o'clock on Thursday, and
will last for ten days consecutively. On Sunday and
on Christmas Day the voting will take place at the
vestry-room of the Greek Church in London-wall. It
is apparently expected that all will vote for Prince
Alfred.

LIVERHOOL, Thursday Afternoon.
The voting of the Liverpool Greeks for the election
of their future king is completed. The result is unani-
mous. The vote of every Greek in this town is for
Prince Alfred.

IN KERRY.

ULTRAMONTANE INGRATITUDE.

A county meeting of the inhabitants of Kerry has
been held to consider the distress prevailing in Lanca-
shire and to assist in its relief. The Right Hon. Col.
Herbert, M.P., high sheriff of the county was in the
chair. A resolution to raise funds by subscription in
the county for the unemployed was moved, and was
seconded by Dr. Moriarty, the Roman catholic bishop.
An amendment was, however, proposed by The
O'Donoghue to the effect that pressing distress at
home had prior claims on the meeting. The chairman
refused to put the amendment, but on putting the
original resolution
,to the meeting it was lost by an
overwhelming majority. The high sheriff then dis-
solved the meeting and left the chair, accompanied by
his friends and the convenors of the meeting. Tho
supporters of The O'Donoghue, however, kept their
places and reformed the meeting; the amendment was
then put as a substantive resolution and carried by
•acclamation.

THE COVENTRY RIBBON WEAVERS.—A county meet-
ing, presided over by Lord Leigh, the lord lieutenant
of Warwickshire, was held at Leamington, on Wednes-
day, for the purpose of bringing before the public the
distress amongst the ribbou weavers of Coventry, and
taking steps for obtaining for them increased support.
Mr. C. N. Newdegate, M.P., and the Rev. W. L.
Clay attended as a deputation from Coventry. After
some discussion, it was determined to take steps to
secure £4,000 for the weavers for the next three
months.

STRANGE DEATH FROM INTOXICATION.—An inquiry
was held before Mr. Walthew, at the Robin Hood
Tavern, Poplar, on Wednesday night, respecting the
death of Mrs. Martha Davies. The deceased, a woman
54 years of age, had recently been married to a man
considerably her junior. Last Thursday evening, she
discovered him speaking to a friend, and she became
immediately greatly excited, and a violent quarrel
ensued. Deceased returned horte, and though she had
been a tetotaller for some years, she broke the pledge,
and took to drinking neat rum almost continually until
Saturday morning, when she died. She had been in
perfect health up to that time. The marriage, quarrel,
and death took place in less than a month. The jury
returned a verdict of' Death from intoxication.'

(The following appeared in the Devenport Independent).
SHIPWRIGHTS AND BOILER-MAKERS'
DISPUTE.
Srn,—My attention has been drawn to a letter which
appeared in your issue signed A. J., and another by
the same writer, evidently a shipwright. Residing as
I am at a distance from the Government Dockyards,
and not being personally cognisant of the circum-
stances referred to in these letters, I cannot speak
thereon, but merely beg permission to make a few
remarks on the statements contained in these letters.
The dispute between the Shipwrights and Boiler-
makers is one, the treatment of which requires no
eloquence, no finely expressed phrases, nor any super-
fluity of words,—but plain common-sense facts, that
may come within the perception of the most common
observer.
In the first place, Mr. Editor, I had considered this
dispute long since settled, seeing that such uncontra-
dictable facts had been brought forward on the part of
the boiler-makers to substantiate their position, capa-
bility and right to build iron ships. A. J. endeavours
to advocate a system which has long been fraught with
the very worst consequences, namely, Shipwrights
attempting to build iron ships. Attempting, I expressly
pronounce it, for of all the ships turned out by them,
not a single one was what a ship ought to be. A. J.
speaks very boastfully of his class as being superior
iron ship builders to those whose profession it is to
work plate and angle iron. And that is the ques-
tion. Is it probable that men whose faculties have
been called into activity in the manipulation of
wood can form or fit iron plates and bars equal to
those whose abilities, physical and mental, have
been exercised on iron for a number of years? A.
J. seems to infer that boiler-makers have no right
to build iron ships. Ire the name of justice who would
ever think of employing a mason or bricklayer to
build an iron house or iron bridge? and yet it belongs
to masons and bricklayers to build houses, and they
never dispute each others right to build houses so long
as the one sticks to his bricks and the other to his
stones. Hatters never dispute the right that straw hat
makers have to make hats of straw. To whom belongs.
the right to make steel pens ? not to quill dressers I
should think. A. J. may think he has a right to make
anything; yes, if he can; bat the very fact that on the
workmanship of our ships depends so much that is of
the most vital importance, takes away the right of a
green hand' to meddle with them. And then he
speaks as if all those who profess Boiler-making
and iron ship building were merely Boiler-makers,
when the fact is that for every one trained to
Boiler-making there have been twenty trained to
iron ship building alone. The iron ship yards of
the Clyde have within the last twenty years turned
out thousands, the great majority having serVed
regular apprenticeships to iron ship building; hun-
dreds of them never worked upon a boiler, but the pro-
cess being the same, boiler makers and iron ship
builders being workers of plate and angle iron, they not
• onlyprofess to build boilers and ships, but tanks, bridges,
gas holders, gas purifiers, pontoons, water wheel buckets,
and all or everything composed of plate and angle
iron; and if I may give A. J. a hint without aiming to
hurt his feelings, I know of no class of tradesmen so
jealous of any one encroaching upon their trade as the
shipwrights are and ever have been. The fact is still
fresh in the memory of many how the shipwrights used
the joiners who once attempted to do a portion of the
wood work which shipwrights considered belonged to
them, and yet there is not such a great difference
between the work of the shipwright and the joiner as
there is between the shipwright and the iron ship
builder—indeed there is no comparison.
A. J. may dispute his right, or the right of ship-
wrights, and their fitness to build iron ships: he may
boast of the superiority of his class over boilermakers,
but he never can convince, even the greatest ignoramus,
far less men of experience, that men used to work on
wood can build an iron ship equal to men used to work
on iron. it is not probable, and if the shipwright
wants ocular demonstration as to the total failure of
the system he propounds, I would refer him to those
ships turned out by his class not fifty miles from Dum-
barton. Aye, and if shipwrights are doing such won-
derful things in the government service at Devonport
or elsewhere; how does it become that they are offering
Bs. per day for platers in Chatham dockyard, and
shipwrights (according to A. J.'s account) can do the
work as well, and for a little more than half the wages
offered to boilermakers? Who are considered, then,
the most qualified? this speaks for itself! With regard
to what he says about his class and labourers levelling
plates, I would just remark, and most particularly
too, that plate levelling is one of the most critical and
nice branches belonging to 'the plate working, and I
have seen tinsmiths, who are generaly allowed to be
the most proficient hands at levelling thin plates, very
much puzzled with some plates;. there is a particular
cut in it which no one can accomplish without having
had a good deal of experience in levelling plates. I
have invariably observed that whenever a boilermaker's
assistant, or any other, lent the boilermaker a hand,
they brought the face of the hammer down upon the
plate in such a manner as to cut and indent the plate,
and if left alone to themselves to level it, would make
it a hundred degrees worse than it was originally; for,
as simple a job as A. J. thinks it to be, I have seen both
shipwrights and smiths (allowed to be very qualified
men in their own departments) discharged for spoiling
plates they attempted to level. His statement of labourers
doing it is a very bad admission on his part; but pre-
judice blinds men's reason, and makes them do and say
such things as stamps them with the name of fools.
If experienced labourers they might make, what would
seem to the judgment of green hands,' a very good
attempt at levelling plates, but if they could level'
plates equal to boilermakers, they stand very much
in their own light, as there is always a demand for
good plate levellers, at far higher wages than either
shipwrights or labourers receive. Then, I would re-
mind A. J., that boilermakers have never refused to
admit old and experienced assistants among them as
being entitled to the privilege of working at the trade
from having been years helping and sustaining a good.
character; not like his class, the shipwrights, who
would persecute to the death any man who dared to lift
an axe or an adze. Again, he says the machine broke
down three times in punching the holes; just so, quite
a natural result, but one he ought to have avoided
making mention of, as it proves, among other things,
the old adage, that it is dangerous to meddle with
things one knows nothing of. During my experience
as a boilermaker and iron shipbuilder I have wit-
nessed many serious break downs in punching machines,
resulting from their being used by inexperienced
hands. This is a common occurrence in all iron ship-
building yards when any presumptuous or careless
individual tries his hand. In many yards there are
notices posted upon the machines prohibiting any
one from using them save an experienced workman,
because it endangers life and limb, incurs expenses,
throws men idle, and keeps the work back. In my
travels I have seen a small steamer made of gutta
percha, another entirely of wire work, and barges made
of reeds. A. J.' better lay claim to the right and qua-
lification of building such vessels: in the estimation
of common sense men, it would not be so ridiculous as
to presume to build iron ones. In the beginning or
his first letter he speaks about the free and unfet-
tered ventilation of any subject of national impor-
tance as being the birthright of every Englishman.
Amen, I say, and of all men in the world. But it
rather looks like inconsistency on his part to make
use of such sentiments, seeing that he would rob hi
fellow man of that civil right which, in virtue of his
talents and practice, society has conferred upon hitn„
via., the right to live by the trade to. which he was
trained. Moreover, this effort on the part of the ship-
wrights to outdo iron ship builders is, if I may -13
allowed to use the expression, very un-English, if we
are to associate the name of Englishman with the
virtue of manhood. Alas! for the principle or man-
hood of that man who would creep in by toadyism or
stealth, and filch from his fellow man the means by
which he lives. But lam not in the least astonished,
at the boastful spirit of A. J.'s letters Men who can,
unblushingly attempt and presume to do that which
they have neither the right nor the aualification to.
do, are just the very sort of men who easily become
the tools of unprincipled capitaliats to trample on
their fellow men, to sow the seeds of dissension among
their brother producers, and keep divided those busy-
toiling bees, who sacrifice their talents, life, and health,
ire producing that wealth on which is based the great-
ness of the British Empire, and instead of aiding pro-
gress rather retard it, knowing that on the union of the
working classes, with a good kindly feeling existing
amongst them, depend the advancement of their order,
and the emancipation of the toiling millicas. A. J., in
speaking of Stephenson,. Watt, and other mechanical
celebrities, is entirely out of place; they were precocious
with all their gifts, sacrificed
ind ivid uals—geniu ses,. awl)
much to accomplish their ends. Surely he does not
lay claim to being possessed of their talents; if so let
him come out.. Ships, need improvement, there is a field
open for him,. and if he makes an iron or a wooden ship
capable of contending against all the elements of nature,
and the war instruments of man, we will very
cordially
admit higi amongst us as a brother.
I remain, yours, &c.,
J. McLniair.

articles.title: PBESIDENT' S MESSAGE.
articles.text:
THE PBESIDENT' S MESSAGE.

NEW Yon, Dec. 2. —Congress assembled at Washing-
ton yesterday. The Message delivered by President
Lincoln is moderate in tone towards the South, but firm
for the maintenance of the Union. On foreign rela-
tions he says :
If the condition of foreign relations is less gratifying
than at former periods, it is certainly more satisfactory
than a nation so unhappily distracted might have appre-
hended. In June last there were some grounds to
expect that the maritime Powers, which at the com-
mencement of American difficulties so unwisely and
'unnecessarily recognised the insurgents as belligerents,
would soon recede from that position, which has proved
only less injurious to themselves than to America. But
temporary reverses which afterwards befel the Federal
arms, and which were exaggerated by disloyal
citizens abroad, have hitherto delayed that act of
simple justice. Civil war has disturbed the
social condition and deeply affected the prosperity of
the nations with which America has carried on an in-
creasing commerce during half a century. It has at the
same time excited political ambitions and apprehensions,.
which have produced profound agitation throughout the
civilised world. In this unusual agitation America has
forborne from taking part in any controversy between
foreign States, and between parties or factions in such
States. America has attempted no propagandism and
acknowledged no revolution but has left to every nation
the exclusive Conduct and management of its own
affairs. Foreign nations have, of course, contemplated
the American struggle less with reference to its own
merits than to its suppo•,ed and often exaggerated effects,
and the consequences resulting to those nations them-
selves. Nevertheless, complaint on the part of the
Federal Government, even if it were just, would cer-
tainly be unwise.'
President Lincoln acknowledges with special pleasure
that the execution of the Slave Trade Treaty by the
British Government has been marked with a jealous
respect for the authority of the United States and the
right of their moral and loyal citizens.
The blockade of 3,000 miles of sea coast could not,'
he says, 'be established and vigorously enforced in a
season of great commercial activity like the present
without committing occasional. mistakes and inflicting
unintentional injuries upon foreign nations and their
subjects. Civil war in a country where foreigners
reside and carry on trade under treaty stipulations, is
necessarily fruitful of complaints of violations of
neutral rights. All such collisions tend to excite mis-
apprehension and, possibly, to produce mutual recrimi-
nations between nations which have a common interest
in preserving peace and friendship. In clear cases of
these kinds I have, so far as possible heard and re-
dressed the complaints- presented by fkeedly Powers.
There are, however, a large and, augmenting number
of doubtful cases upon which the Federal Government
is unable to agree with the Governments whose pro-
tection is demanded by the claimants. There are,
moreover, many cases in which the United States or
their citizens suffer wrongs from the naval or military
authorities of foreign nations which the Governments
of these States are not at once prepared to redress. I
have proposed to some foreign States thus interested
mutual conventions to examine and &djust such com-
plaints. This proposition has been made specially to
Englant France, Spin, and Prussia. In each case it
has been kindly received, but not yet formally
adopted.'
President Lincoln recommends an appropriation for
the owners of the Norwegian bark Admiral Riola. He
says that commercial and consular treaties have been
negotiated with Turkey, Liberia, and Hayti, and con-
tinues
Our relations with European States remain undis-
turbed. Our relations with the independent States of
the American continent remain unchanged, but more
friendly sentiments than have hitherto existed are be-
lieved to be entertained by these neighbours, whose
safety and progress is so intimately connected vt ith that
of America. This statement specially applies to Mexico,
Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras Peru, and Chili. T
have favoured the project of an Atlantic cable, and a
similar project to extend the telegraph from San
Francisco to connect by a Pacific telegraph with the
wire which is being extended across the Russian
empire.' _

The Message recommends extraordinary measures to
promote the development of the mineral regions of the
United States' territories, and continues
'Public expenditures for the suppression of the
rebellion have been met with promptness, and pub-
lic credit is fully maintained. The suspension of
specie payments by the banks made a large issue of
"United States' notes unavoidable.. The judicious
legislation of Congress, making these notes a legal
tender, has made them the universal currency, and
satisfied partially for the time the long-felt want of a
uniform circulating medium. A return to specie pay-
ments, however, at the earliest period compatible
with due regard to all interests should ever be kept
in view. The best means to reduce the fluctuations
in the value of the currency and insure its prompt
convertibility into coin is to organise banking asso-
ciations under a general Act of Congress. To such
associations Government might furnish circulating
notes on the security of United States' bonds,
deposited in the Treasury. These notes, being uniform
in appearance and security, and convertible always into
coin, would protect labour against the evils of a vicious
currency, and facilitate commerce by cheap and safe
exchanges. Public credit would be improved, and the
negotiation of new loans greatly facilitated by a steady
market demand for Government bonds, which the adop-
tion of the proposed system would create. It would
reconcile all existing interests by the opportunity offered
to existing institutions to re-organise under the act
.übstituting a secured uniform national currency for the
various circulations now issued.'

The receipts from all sources for the fiscal year ending
June, 1862, were 584,000,000 dols., being 49,000,000
doh. from Customs, 1,800,000 dols. from direct taxes,
and from loans 530,000,000 dols. The remainder was
the balance from last year. The aggregate disburse-
ments during the same ,eriod were 570,000,000 dols.
The 96,000,000 dols. expended for the reimbursement
and redemption of the public debt, being included in the
loans made, may be properly deducted both from re-
ceipts and expenditure.
A convention has been proposed to foreign Govern-
ments to simplify the rates of foreign postage and expe-
dite foreign mails.
President Lincoln urges the early completion of the
Pacific Railroad, and recommends the favourable
action of Congress on projects for enlarging the great
canals in New York and Illinois. The military and
commercial importance of enlarging the Illinois and
Michigan canals is presented in a report to the Secretary
of War.

In accordance with the purpose expressed in the
second paragraph of the Emancipation Proclamation of
September last, President Lincoln calls the attention of
Congress to what may be called compensated emancipa-
tion. He then argues upon the impracticability of dis-
union, and says :
There is no line, straight or crooked, suitable for a
national boundary upon which to divide.
'Our strife pertains to ourselves, to the passing
generations of men, and it cannot without convulsion be
hushed for ever with the passing of one generation.'
In this view the President reGommends the adoption
of the following resolutions and articles amendatory to
the Federal Constitution :

Resolved by the Federal Congress, two-thirds of
both Houses concurring, that the following articles be
proposed to the Legislatures or Conventions of the
several States as amendments to the Federal Constitu-
tion, all or any of which articles, when ratified by three-
fourths of these Legislatures or Conventions, to be valid
as part or parts of the Constitution.
'l. Every State wherein slavery now exists which
shall abolish shivery at any time before January of the
year 1900 shall receive the following compensation from
the United States:—

Presidents of the United States shall deliver to every
such State United States' bonds, bearing a certain
interest, for each slave known to have been therein by
the eighth United States' census; these bonds to be
delivered to such State by ins alments or in one parcel at
completion of abolishment, according as abolishment
shall have been gradual or at one time. Any State
introducing or tolerating slavery after having received
these bonds shall refund the bonds and interest to the
-United States.

2. All slaves who have acquired freedom by the
chances of war at any time before the end of the
rebellion shall be for ever free. Loyal owners will,
however, receive compensation. Congress may appro-
priate money and provide for colonising free negroes,
with their consent, at places outside the 'United
States.'

President Lincoln then enters into a long and earnest
argument to prove that the adoption of these amend-
ments to the Constitution are politic on the grounds of
justice, economy, and interest, and as a means which
cannot fall to restore the Union. He, however, says
that—

'The plan is recommended, not but that a restoration
of the national authority would be accepted without its
adoption. Nor would the war nor the Emancipation
Proclamation be stayed because of the recommendation
of this plan; but its timely adoption would no doubt
bring restor.tion, and thereby stay these proceedings.
This plan would secure peace more speedily, and cost
less, than if force alone is relied upon. Many objections
may present themselves, but the question is, can any-
thing h= tter be imagined or done?'
•
The Message concludes by saying that—
'Other means may succeed—this could not fail. The
way is plain, peaceful, generous, and just—away which,
if followed, the world will for ev— applaud, and God
must for ever bless.'

LATER FROM AMERICA.

DECZMBER 2, Evening.—The .New York Herald of to-
day thinks that the Radical party in Congress will not
listen to President Lincoln's proposed amendment to
the Constitution. The .New York World supports the
President's plan. The Commercial Advertiser is sur-
prised that President Lincoln's Message totally ignores
all military and naval sacrifices, and observes that it
containstnot one word ot sympathy for the past or cheer
for the future. Thee.yew York Times s4ys that the
President's proposal *ill not receive universal assent,
and thinks it doubtful whether Congress will pass the
amendment.

DECEMBER 3, Morning.—The report of the Federal
Secretary of War has been published. It states that the
Federal army at present numbers 800,000 fully armed
and equipped men. When the quotas are -filled the
army will number 1,000,000 men.
The report of the Secretary of the Navy says that the
Federal naval force consists of 323 steamers and 104
sailing vessels, carrying in all 3,268 guns. Thee Secr-
etary of the Navy refers to the depredations of the
steamer Alabama, and says :
The Alabama went forth from England to destroy
American shipping, and how far and to what results
this abuse may be carried with impunity to the Govern-
ment which tolerates it is matter of grave consideration.
This lawless rover, though built in and sailing from
England, has no acknowledged flag or recognized
nationality. Before the Alabama left England the
British authorities were informed by the recognized
official agents of ti e Federal Government of her character
and purposes. The British Government thus invoked
came too late to prevent her sailing. To what extent,
under these circumstances, the British Government is
bound in honour and, justice to make indemnification
for the destruction of private property is a question
which may present itself for disposal. It is alluded to
now from a s,re-e of duty towards American commercial
interests, and from the fact that recent intelligence
indicates that other vessels of similar character - are
fitting out in England.' •
The report of the Secretary of the Treasury has not
yet appeared. It is supposed in leading financial- cir-
cles that, although the Secretary of the Treasury may
recommend a new banking system, yet the necessities
of the Government will compel it to make a further
issue of legal tender currency. Several resolutions
proposed in Congress by the Opposition members to in-
quire into unconstitutional arrests have been voted
down. Congress has adopted a resolution directing the
Committee on Neval Affairs to report on the cheapest
and most expeditious mode of placing vessels of war
on Lake Ontario when tie ex.gency may arise, for es=
tablishing water commun cation from other waters to the
Lakes. General Burnside has visited Washington, and
had an interview with the President. Ile has returned
to the army. Nothing important has occurred at
Fredericksburg. The Confederate cavalry have crossed
the Roppahannock and captured two entire troops of
Fedealti cavalry. Five Federal gunboats are reported
to have proceeded up to the Rappahannock and anchored
opposite King George's Court-house. A successful cavalry
reconnaissance has been made from General Sigel's army,
in which 40 Confederate cavalry were captured.
The Legislature of Alabama has placed 1,000,000 dols.
at the di,,posal of the Governor, and has autho-
rised him to impress one tenth of the negroes in
Alabama to erect defences. The negroes will at once
commence to obstruct the channels leading into Mobile
Bay and in the rivers above the city. The Southern
journals assert that the Federals in West Tennessee
have forbidden the farmers to plant anything but cotton.
A meeting of the New York Chamber of Commerce has
been convened for the 4th inst., to consider measures
for the relief of the distress in Lancashire. A portion
of General Banks's expedition has sailed. The Federal
army of the South-West has commenced a general ad-
vance from Memphis and difierent parts of the Mississippi.
Preparations are being made at New Orleans for
an advance by land and water up the Mississippi. An
Union meeting has been held at New Orleans. The
correspondents of the New York journals describe the
proceedings as enthusiastic. General Butler is appoint-
ing overseers for the plantations which he has confiscated.
General Butler, in a letter permitting the National
Advocate to resume publication, says all persons express-
ing a desire for foreign intervention will be treated as
traitors. Nearly all the Democratic candidates have
been elected at New York city election. A resolution
has been offered in Congress to hold a convention of
delegates from all the States at Louisville in April next,
to consider the state of the country and the proper
means to be pursued for restoring the Union. General
Halleck's report contains a letter from General
M'Clellan, in which he strenuously opposes the removal
of the army from the Peninsula to Acquia Creek, de-
claring that it would be fatal to the Union cause.

NE-si Youx, Dec. 6, Morning.—Seveu transports and
two iron-clad steamers have sailed from Fortress Monroe,
under sealed orders. The Confederates appear to have
left the section of the country north of the Rappahan-
nock. The Federal expedition which has sailed from
Suffolk, Virginia, has recaptured the Federal battery
taken some time since, and has driven the Confederates
across the Blackwater River. The Federal gunboat
Ellis was blown up during the expedition up the New
River, North Carolina, to prevent its falling into the
hands of the Confederates. The Federal Commander
has informed the authorities of Fredericksburg that
as long as no hostile demonstration was made from
Fredericksburg he should not shell the town. Gene-
ral Stonewall' Jackson is reported to have
joined General Lee at Fredericksburg. The Confede-
rates are working on the defences ot Fredericksburg,
and the Federals are erecting fortifications commanding
the Confederate positions. The Confederates have cap-
tured a train of Federal waggons, with ordnance stores,
in Virginia.
.The naval expedition under General
Banks has sailed; its destination is still a secret. Federal
General Grant continues to advance in Mississippi, and
has occupied Abbeville, which had been abandoned by
the Confederates. The Federal expedition which went
up the Mississippi has discovered that the crop of cotton
remaining in the States of Mississippi, Louisiana, and
Arkansas has been overestimated. The destruction of
cotton having been very considerable, only a few
thousand bales remain in the counties bordering
the river. The new crop will be very small.
The Southern journals urge retaliation •for the out-
rage and plundering committed by General Burn-
side's army in Virginia. The Secretary of the Navy
has informed the Chamber of Commerce that there is no
authority to permit private vessels to cruise for priva-
teers. It is rumoured that the Alabama burnt another
bark on the 19th of November, in lat. 41. long. 66 16.
General Fitz,Tohn Porter is on trial at Washington for
not obeying General Pope's orders. During the trial a
letter was read from General M'Clellan, written during
Pope's campaign, Urging General Porter to give his
whole support to General Pope for the sake of the
country. The subscriptions for Lancashire have
already reached 40,000 dollars. The British residents
are also raising a subscription. The Chamber of Com-
merce of New York city has held a meeting to take
measures for the relief of the distress in Lancashire.
Some members thought that perhaps by inaugurating
this movement, some national vanity and enmity to
England might be attributed to the Chamber. The
majority of the speakers deprecated conducting the
movement in a way to obtain favour with one class in
England, but urged that it should be based exclusively
on the grounds of Christian charity. England was a
great customer of America for grain, and it was a plain
case that it was America's duty to feed a brother nation
in distress. Messrs. Griswold and Co. offered a new
ship of 1,800 tons burden to convey food to England,
not only as a relief for the suffering poor, but as a token
of respect for the Queen and her friendship for America.
A committee was appointed to collect subscriptions in
money and grain from all parts of the country. 26,000
dols. in cash was subscribed on the spot. A proposal to
aid the French operatives was voted down.
. . .

A resolution has been offered in Congress approving
President Lincoln's emancipation proclamation.
The Federal Commissioner Johnson, who was sent to
New Orleans to investigate the condition of affairs,
reports that persons in General Butler's command are
growing rich upon the necessities of the helpless people
of New Orleans by extortions offensive to decency, and
that the inhabitants of the city have been as much sin-
ned against as sinning since General Butler's rule. Mr.
Johnson denies that any money returned to the French
Consul was sent to Hav,nnah for the Confederates.

NEW YORK, Dec. 8 (Bvening).—An engagement has
occurred at Hartsville, Tennessee, between the Federal
advance force from Nashville and the Confederates under
General Morgan. Colonel Moore's. Federal brigade was
repulsed several times and finally captured. General
Morgan afterwards attacked the Federals at Gallatin, but
was repulsed with heavy loss. Both the Federal and Con-
federate armies at Fredericksburg are actively engaged in
fortifying at Fredericksburg. The Southern journals state
that a fleet of twenty Federal vessels sailed from Hilton
on the sth inst., for Georgetown or Wilmington. S, veral
Federal vessels had passed Charleston Harbour. It was
supposed that they were going to assist in attacking
Mobile. The same journals assert that thirty thousand
Federals are at Suffolk, preparing to move against
Petersburg, while a Federal force at Newburn, North
Carolina, will operate simultaneously against Wvldon.
The Federals occupy Granada, Mississippi. Large sub-
scriptions for the Lancashire Distress Fund continue to
pour in.

The Archdeacorny of Durham, vacant by the death
of the Venerable Charles Thorpe, D.D. (to which is
annexed a cannnry of Xl,OOO per annum in Durham. Ca-
thedral, with house of residence), has ben offered by
the B'shop of Durham to the Rev. Archibald Boyd. M. A ~
Rural Dean, and incumbent of the mother church of
Paddington,

articles.title: ATLANTIC TELEGRAPH.
articles.text:
THE ATLANTIC TELEGRAPH.

A report has been made to the Admiralty by Captain
Orlebar, captain in charge of the Newfoundland Survey,
on the proposed routes for the Atlantic Telegraph. He
says, writing from Prince Edward's Island on the 24th of
November:— -

Herewith you will receive the charts containing the
soundings taken in Trinity and Conception Bays, and
also eastward of St. John to the meridian of 50 deg. west.
A dotted red line indicates the route I consider best
adapted for th,‘ Atlantic telegraph cable, and for which
I beg to submit the following reasons :-
1. You will observe that it is only the most northern
line of offshore soundings that gives mu,tdy bottom, and
that this leads right in,o the mouth of Trinity Bay.
The soundings further south are more irregular, less &op,
and give stones, rocks, and sand. At the entrance of
Conception Bay the soondingi have the same character,
giving 50 fathoms less depth than Trinity Bay.
2. Also in Trinity Bay a channel with muddy bottom
five miles wick, and more than 130 fathoms deep, can be
carried from the offing more than 45 miles up the bay to
New Perlican, where it approaches within a mile of the
south shore.

3. The nature of the bottom was everywhere noted,
and specimens of it have been prepared for the microscope
by Mr. J. Leeming. The examination of these speci-
mens, and of the rocks on the shore of Trinity and Con-
ception Bays, which are of the silurian system, leads me
to suppo,e that there is nothing on the shores, or at the
bottom, likely to impair the working of the telegraph
cable. On this subject I enclose a memorandum by
Mr. T. J..Leeming, naturalist.
. _ _ _

4. Trinity Baiii twenty miles wide at the entrance,
and is well lighted by Cape Bonavista and Catalina Green
Island Lights on the north side, and Baccalien Island
Light on the south. Icebergs generally ground on the
shoal banks off Catalina and Cape Bonavista, and even
those that enter ihe bays are most. frequently driven
over to the north side.

6. In Fitters Cove, New Perlican, which is too exposed
for vessels to anchor, the bottom is sand, with scattered
rounded stones, and. at its head there is a beach of fine
sand on Nt hich the telegraph cable, if protected by a
sheath of iron near the land-wash, mightbe safely landed.
It would have to traverse for half-a. mile a rocky slope,
having a depth of 30 fathoms, decrea-ing to 11 fathoms,
but it appears tolerably even, and is too far within the
bay to be visited by icebergs, or disturbed by the ocean
swell.

6. On the northern side of the bay the soundings are
more irregular, and the bottom rocky, whilst there is
more ocean swell and more danger from icebergs.
7. For these reasons I think the western terminus of
the ocean telegraph cableshould be at New Perlican.

A VALIIABLE DISCOVERY. —A most important discovery
has lately been made by Mr. Anderson, the assistant-
superintendent of Woolwich Arsenal, of a simple process
by which steel is rendered as tough as wrought-iron
without losing its hardness. This change is effected in
a few minutes by heating the metal and plunging it in
oil, after which the steel can be bent, but scarcely
broken. The value of this discovery will be at once
appreciated by those who are aware of the difficulties
hitherto experienced in obtaining a suitable material for
the interior tubes of built up guns. The steel vent-pieces,
which cost several thousands of pounds and were virtually
condemned, can now be brought into use.—Army and
Navy Gazette.
ANOTHER COLLIERY ON FIRIL—An extensive four-
shafter colliery of Messrs. R. Hudson and Co., Stanley,
near Wakefield, about ten days ago was found to be on
fire, the coal at the bottom Of the furnace-shaft having
become ignited by the heat of the furnace. Efforts
were made to extinguish the fire, but without suceess,
and after the proprietors had consulted Mr. Holt,
mining engineer, and Mr. Morton, the Government coal
inspector for the district, it was resolved to fill up all
the shafts for a few yards from the bottom, so as to
exclude as much as possible the atmospheric air. That
work has been accomplished, but it is believed that the
coal is still burning, and it is probable that at least
some weeks, if not months, must elapse before the pit
is fully at wsvk again.
CHARLES DICKENS AND me LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.—
' The celebrated novelist Charles Dickens is in Paris,
and proposes to pass the winter there,' says a corre-
spondent of the Nord. 'lt is said that he intends to
organise in that city a series of readings from his own
works, the proceeds of which will be devoted to the
Lancashire operatives. These readings, as is well
known, are highly popular in England.
NEAPOLITAN BRIGANDAGE —The Naples journals
contain namerous accounts of encounters with brigands,
all of which appear to have ended in their dispersion by
the troops. At Caramanico, near Chieti, the police were
informed that three chiefs of brigands were feasting in a
house belonging to one Bracciarelli. A party of carbi-
neers was immediately sent to surround the house; the
brigands jumped out of one of the windows to make
their escape. The troops fired and killed one, the others
escaped, but from the trails of blood subsequently found
it is believed they were both severely wounded. Brae-
ciarelli was arrested. His house was found to contain
large quantities of arms and ammunition, and he
has made some important confessions.
The great Smithfield Cattle Show has passed off in a
most satisfactory manner during the five days on which
the public were admitted to gaze on the fat oxen, sheep,
and pigs; as many as 149,300 were admitted to the
capacious hall, which seems so admirably adapted for the
purposes of the show. It might, however, be better
lighted and better ventilated. On Friday evening the
place looked very misty, and the smells were not of the
sweetest. Some of the fat animals seemed tired of being
looked at, and by no means very comfortable. Pigs,
whose eyes are completely buried in grease, and whose
legs are entirely hid from view by enormous flanks of
fat; sheep, who pant laboriously for breath, and oxen,
whose legs can scarcely support their bodies, are by no
means very picturesque objects for artistic eyes. The
butchers and connoisseurs, however, seemed to look upon
them with interest—their mouths were evidently water-
ing in anticipation of a juicy steak or chop, and their
eyes twinkling with delight at the gains or pleasures
before them. One thing I could not understand, and
that was the great pleasure ladies evidently took in
gazing upon the fat pigs, and inhaling their (odoriferous?)
perfumes. The butchers' shops will be up till 'merry
Christmas,' in all their fatty glory. be,
from the
immense droves of cattle brought to London during the
last fortnight, there will be o lack of roast beef for the
annual great dinner. The cattle show is the first sure
and certain sign that Christmas is near at hand. The
London schoolboys know that the Christmas tree, the
plum-pudding, and the innocent frolic of Christmas eve
are not far off.—Our London Gossiper.
SEWAGE OF Towiss.—The commissioners appointed
to inquire into the best mode of distributing the sewage
of towns have made their second report, which con-
tains the result of numerous experiments and inquiries
made by them in various parts of the country. The
report concludes by repeating the recommendation of
the former report, That the only security for a general
and continued employment of such means of distribut-
ing the sewage will be by the establishing of responsible
conservancies throughout the country, armed with
adequate powers for preventing damage and for effect-
ing improvements. We believe that these powers would
be best vested in independent local authorities, such as
the present Commissioners of Sewers, acting under cer-
tain government regulations, in respect to borrowing
money and other matters. Our inquiry, however, has
of necessity been of too imperfect a character to enable
us to set forth for consideration any decided measures
in detail on so large and important a question. There
are many subjects to be inquired into, and vast inte-
rests to be considered, which are beyond our pre-sent
power or province to enter upon. We can only
respectfully but earnestly recommend that such inqui-
ries should be instituted into the various points bearing
on the subject, so that measures may be permitted which
will enable parliament to deal with the existing evil in
a way most conducive to public interests.'
FREE SPEECH IN THE PONTIFICAL ARMY.-0 wing to
warm discussions which are every day taking place
between the native and foreign officers of the Pontifical
army as to the political condition of the government and
the merits of the ministers, Mgr. de Merode the Pro.
Minister of Arms, has thought proper
.to publish the
following order of the day Inconsiderate and very
blameable expressions on political questions and on
personages of high rank are attributed to persons belong-
ing to the Pontifical army. The duty of the Pro-
Minister of Arms is to declare that if such facts were
proved they would cause great annoyance to his Holi-
ness, and that the officers, sub-officers, and soldiers who
had been guilty of them would incur the most formal
disapprobation. The Pro-Minister takes this oppor-
tunity of stating that, if military discipline everywhere
interdicts even the simple manifestation of political
opinions, that rule ought to be more particularly
observed in the Pontifical army, formed on the heroic
examples of complete abnegation and unlimited devoted-
ness. The sovereign independence of the Common
Father of the faithful is the only supreme interest of the
public mind, and ought to be considered by everyone as
the welfare of his own country. To the defence of that
.only and supreme good, each of you has come to devote
himself. Such is the general sentiment, and all must
therefore avoid even the slightest appearance that could
lead to a suspicion of sincerity. SEYERINO DE
MERODE

DISCOVERY OF A SKELETON.—Some labourers em-
ployed in the grounds of Mr. Roberts, market gardener,
Lower -Wool .vich-road, were a few days ago digging a
trench, when at a depth of nearly three feet they came

near it. In the opinion of a surgeon who examined the.
