articles.title: _AMARIC.AN WHEAT.
articles.text:
_AMARIC.AN WHEAT.

TO TRE EDITOR OP THE TIMES.

Sir,—As British farmers are now suffering from very
low prices, caused by American competition in wheat,
it may be useful and interesting to them to know how
the American farmer fares, and whether be is likely to
continue the competition at present prices. I therefore
request the favour of your inserting the accompanying
letter, dated 'M'Henry, Illinois, United States, Nov.
27, 1862.' I can guarantee its correctness and truth-
fulness, knowing the parties well. Matters must fare
worse with them when they have to add to their
enormous labour price direct taxation and the heavy
Customs' tariff.

Land has fallen much in value and is hardly saleable,
many young farmers having left their occupations for
the high bounty and pay of a soldier.
Under such circumstances, even Mr. Caird will no
longer recommend present emigration to Illinois.
I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
J. J. /11Ecill.

Tiptree-hall, Kelvedon, Essex, Dec. 15:
43{`Henty, County Illinois, Nov. 27.
'Dear Brother,—Your kind letter to Catharine was
duly received, and in reply I would say that, as com-
pared with us, you have the advantage in raising wheat,
for the present prices of that crop are ruining us, as we
only get from 50 to 70 (2s. 6d. sterling) cents. per
bushel of 601 b. here, the rest being consumed in trans-
portation. Wages are also very high since the war
broke out, labourers command readily about Bs. of our
money (equal to ss. of yours) and board per day. So
that you can see the position wheat growers are in here.
In fact, we are giving up wheat raising altogether,
and will only sow about 20 acres the coming spring.
We should have had very good crops here this year,
but just as we had our grain mostly bound and in shock
we were visited by a fierce tornado, which swept every-
thing before it, sweeping some fields of wheat entirely
away, sn.that on fields a .20 0r.40 acres you could only
get trora 5 to 50 bushels on the field.

- "fake it all in all, the ,fareaers are having pretty
hard tunes here. - Horses sell from 75 dols. to 90 dols.,
Milk cows from: 10'dols. to 12 dols., and other things in
pioportion. But we shall ,ee better times when the war
closes, and we bear our burdens cheerfully, knowing
that we of the North are fighting for the cause of truth
and freedom agrtinst falsehood and slavery, and I am
firm in the faith that we shall come out all right as a
nation. The North has only begun to develope its re-
sources in the fighting line, and I think you may rest
assured that the institution of slavery is doomed to de-
struction, and as that has been the cause of our national
troubles so its removal will work their cure.

'Yours very truly,

'A. W.'

CESSION OF THE lONIAN ISLANDS.—The telegrams
of this day bring from various quarters the assertion
that England is about to cede the lonian Islands to
Greece. This intelligence must be accepted with the
qualification that the cession can only be made with the
consent of the powers who signed the treaties of 1815.
The statement that the English Government is willing,
if it can ensure the stability and prosperity of the new
dynasty, to yield up its protectorate of the Septinsular
republic is, we believe, not without foundation. The
special mission of Mr. Elliot to the provisional govern-
ment at Athens has reference to this, and to other im-
portant questions bearing on the future of Greece.—
Morning Post, Dec. 15.
Importing Tea without colour on the leaf prevnnts
the Chinese passing off inferior leaves as in the usual
kinds. ilorniman's Tea is uncoloured, therefore always
good alike.
Corrox IN TIIRKEY.—His Excellency Savietti
Effendi, Minister of Commerce has ordered from Eng-
land an extensive supply of American cotton seed, for
gratuitous distribution in Roumelia and Anatolia. A
correspondent writes from Trikala :--4 The success of
our cotton crop this year has been remarkable, espe-
cially in the valley of Shiurpi, Carditza, and Ermia.
We only want adequate encouragement in the shape of
good seed and proper gins to place the cultivation on a
very satisfactory basis for the future.'—Levant Herald,
Dec. 3.

THR.EE GENERATIONS AT THE POLLS. The Hon.
Josiah Quincy, his son and namesake, and his grand-
son, Major Samuel M. Quincy, went together this
morning to the polls in Ward Four, and deposited their
Republican ballots. The senior, who was a candidate
for Congress sixty-two years ago, and the Major, were
on crutches. The former, at the age of 91, has re-
covered in a measure from an accident by which his leg
was broken, the latter, a fellow-cripple for a short time
of his venerable relative, was wounded bravely fighting
for the cause equally dear to both. All pasties united
in givinc, each of these energetic voters' thus determined
to discharge their duty as citizens, hearty cheers.—
Boston (U.S.) Transcript. .
THE ECCENTRICITIES OF BARON BRAMWELL.-At the
Chester assizes, on Friday last, two men, named Lloyd
and Cooper, were found guilty of burglaries committed
at Chester on the Bth of October. Baron Bramwell
proceeded to pass sentence on the prisoners. His lord-
ship said—' Prisoners at the bar, you have been found
guilty; you, Lloyd, of two serious offences, and you,
Cooper, of one equally serious offence. However,
there is this in your favour, you did not use any
violence, and this is what thieves ought to be taught to
do; they ought to be taught to run away when dis-
covered, as you were discovered. However, you are
both young, and I shallgive you another chance, and
sentence you both to six years' penal servitude.'
A Fox CAUGHT IN MANCHESTER.—A very- fine fox
was discovered on Thursday morning in the hayloft of
Mr. Greenwood's stable in College-lane, St. Mary's,•
Manchester. When found, the creature was wet, and
appeared fagged. Where it came from is a mystery.
REPRESENTATION OF CAMBRIDGESHIRE.—Lozd George
Manners' a brother of the Duke of Rutland, has an-
nounced his intention of offering himself as a candidate
for Cambridgeshire at the next general election. His
lordship, who has been elected a member of the County
Conservative Club, eat for the county in a former par-
liament.

A POSTMASTBR ROBBED ON THB HIGHWAY.—
SINGULAR CASE.—On Friday night last, on the arrival
of the driver of the Ridg fray and Chesterfield mail cart,
.he reported that he had been stopped on the road near
Handley, about four miles from Chesterfield, by three
men, one of whom seized his horse, while the other two
dragged him out of the cart. He stated that they
struck him a blowover the head (his cheek was swollen),
and rifled his pockets of between £5 and £6 in money.
They then suffered him to depart, and he made the rest
of his way into Chesterfield without hindrance. The
police are making a strict inquiry into the matter.—
Manchester Examiner.

Advices from Lyons state that the sale of raw silk
is difficult there. The merchants of Lyons, taking
into consideration the great increase in the quantity of
foreign silk imported into France, have decided, it is
said, on building storehouses for its reception. Japan
produces 3,000 bales of silk, being more than the pro-
duce of France and Italy. The East produces 300,000
bales. The greater part of these silks arrive in Lon-
don by the Cape of Good Hope, but it is expected that
when the canal across the Isthmus of Suez is completed
(if it ever be completed) silk from the East will first
arrive in France. Some considerable purchases of
fereign silki were made at Marseilles last week.
THE DUKE OF BEDFORD'S FAT STOCK.—The annual
sale of Christmas stock at the Park-farm, Woburn
Abbey, took place on Friday, the 12th instant. Mr.
Furze, as usual, being the auctioneer. There was a
very large attendance of buyers present, including
several leading salesmen from the metropolis. The
stock offered for sale consisted of 300 sheep of various
breeds, 70 oxen and heifers, and tt.bout 60 pigs. Mr.
Coleman, the bailiff, appeared to have taken much
pains to bring the animals up to the mark, and their
splendid condition when brought to the hammer testi •
fled to the success of his management. The Shropshire
sheep were knocked down at prices varying from
£2 17s. to £3 19s. each, and the Scotch wethers varied
in value from £2 9s. to £3 2s. The Oxford Downs
realized £3 ss. to £4, and the Southdowns £4 6s. to
£5 35., while some very extraordinary half-breds were
run up to £5 16.; the average price of the 300 sheep.
£3 7s. 10d. The Herefords sold rapidly, the prices
taking a range from £2l 10s. to £4O. The Scotch oxen
appeared to excite the greatest amount of interest ; the
btddings were spirited; the highest sum obtained was
£36, some of the primest being booked to the London
buyers. The pigs were of choice breeds, and sold at
good but not extravagant prices. The proceeds of the
sale were :—For the sheep, £l,OlB 6s. ; cattle, £2,043
155.; pigs, £312 2s. ; making a.total of £3,37435.
FEDERAL GENERAL SIGEL.—A pleasant incident
occurred at General Sigel's head-quarters the other
day. The general was surprised at his office by a visit
from his whole staff in full dress. He was conducted
to the porch of the house, and there beheld a magnifi-
cent black horse, richly caparisoned. Colonel Robin-
son, acting as spokesman for the party, presented the
animal and his trappings to the general as a birthday
gift fi cra the officers of his staff. The general was more
than surprised, and tenderly affected by this unexpected
present.. In accepting the gift the general remarked
that while the people of a great nation were engaged
in a war against each other, and thoughts came to him
of those who were sad at home because of the losses
sustained by this war, be had not felt it right to cele-
brate his birthday, as was the custom of those from
Fatherland. But the gift now ter dered him made him
doubly -happy, in that it proved that ethers had been
mindful of his birthday, and because of the renewed
aseirances of their confidence and esteem. However
he might regret to part with his staff, he could but
hope that a vigorous prosecution of the war would
result in its speedy termination. Until then, he was
proud to know that he had around him officers who
had so ably seconded him before, and all of whom he
knew would do their duty as soldiers and as men.

THE .iIfURDER, IN WALES.

On Thursday Thomas Edmund, the fellow-servant
of the deceased Jane Lewis, was committed by the
magistrates at Pontypridd on the charge of wilful
murder. The investigation before the magistrate, it
will be remembered, had taken place after the verdict
by the jury that the deceased committed suicide while
in a state of temporary insanity,' and numerous facts
had come to light to threw suspicion on the prisoner.
Deceased, a somewhat handsome woman, of about 21,
left her master's house at Tyntylla, in the valley of
the Rhondda, South Wales, between five and six
o'clock on Sunday evening, Nov. 2, and was found
about ten o'clock the same evening in a wood, about
180 yards from the farm, with her throat cut in a
most shocking manner, the wounds being such,
according to the medical evidence, that they could
not have been self-inflicted. It was shown that on the
night of the murder the prisoner left the house a few
minutes before the deceased, that soon after he called
at the house of a friend, and asked for a pocket-hand-
kerchief to wipe the blood from his face, alleging that
the wound was caused by the horn of a calf. On tho
same night the prisoner communicated to several per-
sons for the first time that he was to have been married
on the following week to the deceased, although it was
well known that she was on the eve of marriage to
another young man, named Thomas Williams, between
whom prisoner had seen an improper connexion, and
thus the motive of jealousy was made out. On the
other hand, no marks of blood were found on his
clothes, nor was there any direct evidence to show
that he was in the vicinity when the murder took
place. The decision of the magistrates has given
general satisfacticn, the verdict of the jury having
created great excitement in South Wales.

articles.title: 'WHIPPING-HOUSE.'
articles.text:
A 'WHIPPING-HOUSE.'

A correspondent of the Missouri De»zoorat, writing
from Helena, Arkansas, under date of Sept. 9, describes
as follows one of the beauties of the peculiar institu-
tion :'—

'Perhaps your readers are not aware that whipping
negroes is a regular business in some parts of the South;
but such is undoubtedly the case. Improved machinery
has been invented and putinto operation, and fhipping
is done by wholesale.

An institution of this kind is located at Mayena, 25
miles from this place, on the St. Francis road. The whip-
ping-house,' as it is called, is about 6 feet in diameter
and 10 feet high. A shaft runs from bottom to top ;on
the upper end is a small cog-wheel running horizon-
tally, into which a large wheel works. The propelling
power is a robust negro. Attached to the shaft are
leather thongs or straps about two inches wide. Lashes
are inserted in these, and when the shaft is in motion
they reach the neck. Near by is the office and strip-
pine. house. Here the victims are divested of their
clothing, and five or six are placed in the torture room;
the door being fastened, the negro on hold of the crank,
the proprietor, with v3atch in hand, orders the machine
to be put in motion. Around whirls the shaft, at the
rate of 200 revolutions per minute, with straps and
lashes extended, bruising and lacerating the poor
victim with thousands of blows extending from
head to feet. Fifteen minutes is considered by the
proprietor—Hampton &yr q—to be a reasonable time
to grind a batch of human flesh; and then it is so very
cheap, costing but a dollar per head! Ido think it
very nearly equals hell itself. Nothing for human
torture could be more terrible. A thousand scorpions
stinging their flesh could not inflict more punishment.
At the end of the time, the poor, bleeding, quivering
victims are brought out more dead than alive. The
plantations for miles send their grists to this mill to be
ground, and the proprietor had been doing a thriving
business until the Union troops came, and consequently
Othello's occupation was ruined.'

articles.title: ITALIAN AFFAIRS.
articles.text:
ITALIAN AFFAIRS.

The following is an extract from a private letter from
Pisa, Dec. 7:—
. _

It' is difficult to give news from this dreamy place,
and Garibaldi's presence is far from rendering the task
easier. All we know is that the classical bullet has
been extracted. It looks like an eagle's head in minia-
ture, and it is needless to say that it will have a relic's
career. It is too heavy for a lady's breloque, nor
could it in this age of gum arabic be used as a seal;
but it will be a nation's heirloom, and will be handed
down front generation to generation, long after the
sceptics that would not believe in its existence and
the fanatics that worship it have been reduced to
pulvis et umbra. Indeed I think it a most meri-
torious piece of metal, much as I regret the suffer-
ings it has inflicted upon one of the greatest of our
contemporaries. I cannot help thinking that it has
saved a whole nation from ruin and humiliation. lam
aware that this view is not popular in England. One
great good, however, has come from all this, which
everybody must admit. Both the Sicilian episode and
the subsequent demonstrations in Hyde-park have done
a great deal to clear the hitherto cloudy atmosphere,
and unless we take a morbid delight in mists and
uncertainties we must congratulate ourselves on the
change. The Sicilian sirocco which was threatening
bloody rain, has given way to a cold blast from Paris.
I still believe that Napoleon has not given up the
ambitious plan of destroying the temporal power of the
Pope, and I am not ready to blame him if he thinks fit
to do it gently and by degrees. He himself says, in his
Idees Napoleoniennes," that his uncle fell because
he attempted to do in a decennium the work of
a century;' and the lore of history and expe-
rience is not lost upon this docile man as it used to
be , upon the Bourbons. Is there nothing alarming
in the idea of having the old whining Pope let loose
upon the world a martyr and exile' and sure to become
the centre of a formidable reaction? Suppose the
Pope were to die a few weeks after his expulsion,
would it not be a matter of regret not to have waited
a little longer? But, fortunately, there are surer
means than expulsion. That 'moral revolution'
which Cavour hoped for (and Cavour was not a
dreamer) has actually begun. Passaglia's monster
petition, signed by 10,000 priests, shows clearly the
drift of coming events. The very rejection (which is
a matter of course) of this petition will ensure its final
success. The temporal power being the best antidote
to the spiritual one, the lenger they co-exist the better.
I grant there is danger irA this delay, the late revolu-
tionary twitchings in France show this. Fortunately
the continent can afford to lose its 'benefactor' (as the
Times called him the other day.) He has done a good
deal, but has now reached the age involution,' as
physiologists would say.

THE O'CONNELL FAMILY. The Kilkenny journal
states Mr. Finn, the brother-in-law of O'Connell, one
of the founders of the Catholic Association, and formerly
representative for the county of Kilkenny, died at
Tullaroan, on Tuesday night, at the advanced age of
78 years; and on the same evening, a few hours pre-
viously, Mrs. Finn, the sister of the Liberator, breathed
her last in an adjoining room.
AN EXTENSIVE EXECtiTIoNER.—The office of public
executioner at Graz, in Austria, having become vacant,
a considerable number of candidates presented them-
selves. A man has been chosen who proved that he
had already dispatched into the other world, by the
aid of the cord, not less than 135 criminals.

The late Mrs. Ann Cutts, of the Old Kent-road, has
left the National Lifeboat Tn stitution a legacy of £l,OOO,
free of duty. At the present period, when the demands
on the society are so heavy that it has just been com-
pelled to sell out £5OO iron, its small funded capital, this
legacy will greatly strengthen the hands of the com-
mittee to carry out the national and philanthropic objects
of the Lifeboat Institution.

A MISCHIEVOUS BOY. —A bird dealer, named Desjar-
dins, residing on the Quai de l'Ecole, having recently
noticed an unusual mortality among his stock, con-
cluded that the
ianimals must have been poisoned by
some evil disposed person. He accordingly kept
strict watch, and at length caught a boy named
N—, 15 years of age, an apprentice to a brass turner,
in the act of holding phosphorus matches to the birds,
which peeked at them, and no doubt swallowed particles
of the poison, a very minute quantity of which would
suffice to kill a bird. The lad was taken before the
commissaty of police, and it was then ascertained that
his only object was mischief, for which his parents, who
are responsible for his acts, will have to pay.
PRESEN CE OF MIND. —Mr. Rignall, ironfounder,
Chattcris, had been driving his pony some distance the
other day, and got out to run along the road. When
he was attempting to pet in again the step broke and
let him down, whilst the gig was in motion. With
remarkable presence of mind he seized the wheel and
lifted it completely over his body, thus escaping serious
injury. There was anotber person in the gig at the
time.—Peterboreugh Aciver/iscr.

AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

! The weather has been of the most variable character
! throughout the week—very mild for the time of the
I year, with heavy rains at intervals. After a consider-
able fall during the day .time, the night often was drier,
and as soon as the moon rose it became brgle er. The
week has been about half wet and half dry, but as little
wheat has to be committed to the ground, this has no
influence on field-work, which may be comddered as
finished in England.
It has been most miserable weather for thrashing -
wheat, and little can come to market now in fine con-
dition, which causes the trade to be worse than it
otherwise would be, and the damper the quality
of home-grown the more dry foreign has to 13€
ased to manufacture a passable seek of flour. Thf
average priqe was again lower, being 46s Pd. on t,
still smaller sale—the returned quantity was 83,231
quarters, against 60s. 4d. on 104,036 quarters the cor-
responding week. of last veer; a most disheartening
comparison, a.nl making a wonderful difference to the
farmers. This is sufficient ground for their holding
hack the supplies, and for their hoping to see an
provement in the spring. The imports from America
have been well kept up, and no doubt will he to the
close of the year; and until they cease or fall off greatly,
there is not much hope of revival. It appears pro-
bable we must get into the new year before any•
amelioration can be looked for with any tolerable
degree of certainty.
The deliveries of barley are of a very different cha-
racter to those of wheat, these have been very large
this week, amounting to 126,747 qrs., at 345. 10d..
Norfolk alone has supplied nearly one-fourth of the
quantity, and with a yield of fully six quarters-
per acre in that county, remuneration will re,ult from
last year's growth. This is, perhaps, about the,
most cheering account of any artiole on the farm;
and whilst the choicest qualities are command-
ing high prices, the growers cannot, do better
than meet the demand so long as they can find
any such fir delivery. After Christmas the maltsters
who have omitted to get into stock will have to pay
more for choice qualities weighing 54 to 551bs. per
bushel, calculated to make a sample of malt fitted for
even Burton-on-Trent or the Tetley's fine bright ale, so
much appreciated in the metropolis.
The best part of this week has been given up by
the agriculturists to the splendid sight of their cattle at
the new Hall; and that at least may be considered a
rumunerating and prosperous undertaking to all con-
cerned.—December 13.

articles.title: PUBLIC-HOUSE ADVENTURE.
articles.text:
A PUBLIC-HOUSE ADVENTURE.

An extraordinary row, which took place at midday
in the bar of the Colosseum Hotel, Great Portland-
street, is thus described by a letter in The Times, dated
Friday :

'This day, between twelve and one o'clock, four
suspicious looking characters entered the bar of this
betel, where I have been residing for the last month,
and asked to be served with a pot of ale, which was
given them, and they quitted the premises. Shortly
afterwards the whole party returned, requesting to be
served with rum' which the barman, an old servant of
some 30 years' standing, declined to serve them with,
as his suspicions were awakened as to the quality of
his customers and their intentions. Finding him
resolute, two of them each threw down half .a-crown,
demanding change, which the old barman refused to
give, at the same time requesting them at once to quit
the premises for he would have nothing whatever to do
with them, Observing that although there was, as he
termed it, a mob of four of them,' they would not
make him alter his determination. Upon this one of
the party began to threaten that he would 'leave a
mark' upon him and as he menaced him the old bar—
man perceived the handle of a bludgeon protruding from
under the back of the fellow's coat, and then saw the
knob like a hump between the rascal's shoulders, which
at once convinced him that the suspicions he enter.
tamed were well-founded, so he insisted on their leav—
ing the house directly. They defied him; but it sO
happened that on that side of the bar where these 'ugly
customers' stood was a dragoon end some cabmen, who
proceeded to eject the garotters (for such they were),
and a fight ensued, ending in the thorough discomfiture
of the offending parties. The soldier, on his own hook,
thrashed two so completely as to make them call
' Murder ' most lustily, while the other two were dis—
posed of by the cabbies, who took from two of them
their murderous weapons, for the retention of which
they fought, bit, and kick ' most desperately.'

THE SECOND EMPIRE AND THE CHURCH.—The

alliance of the church with the empire is creating again
the terrible phenomenon the eighteenth century—a
fanaticism directed against. religion. Every form of
scepticism is deepening in colour and incrpasing in
bitterness, and while good men weep over blasphemies
like that involved in the Bishop of Poicti3rs' sermon on
the Relics of Charoux,' the indifferent, are becoming
enemies to the church, and men like M. Michelet are
prepared for the second time to shriek out Ecrasez
l'infame!' The hatred of the soutane is growing, till
there is danger of hate to the Christian robe.—
Spectator.
BAPTISM OF MonmoNs.—lt will scarcely be credited,
but the veracity of our informant, who was an eye-
witness to the spectacle, is undoubted, that at this in-
clement season of the year the Mormons have been
baptising their disciples in the sea at Hendon. Last
Sunday afternoon, when walking along the beach below
the New Gas Works, he came upon a damp and dripping
batch of these Latter Day Saints'—for such, he says,
they told him was their correct designation, and not
Mormons—the name mentioned by him when he asked
one or two of them if they belonged to that body. The
disciples were fourteen in number, of both sexes, the
men being mostly young, and evidently of the class of
unskilled workmen. An elder' from Utah (so 'twos
said) conducted the business of the afternoon.—Sun-
derland Herald.
When the very nice couple (‘ Anonyma ' and her
companion) got to America they went to one of the
first hotels in New York, and took superb apartments.
The following evening they went together to the
theatre, and the little fool her companion was surprised
to see his fair friend making signs of recognition to a
decidedly ferocious-looking fellow opposite. He said
nothing, but the day succeeding she proposed a drive,
and away they went. When outside the town, the
stranger of the theatre again appeared, and while she
laid back in the carriage and smiled, the young gen-
tleman by her side was relieved of his seat, deposited
in the road, and then carefully protected by friends, to
whom he, at least, was a stranger; but he was not
permitted to return to New York for a week. The bird
had then flown, of course, and he was presented with a
bill as long as his arm—which he paid.

HEAVY GALE AT PLYMOUTTI.—A heavy gale from
the S.W. prevailed at Plymouth during Friday night.
On Saturday morning, about three a.m., the Norwegian
brig Emanuel, 274 tons, Captain Walloe' lying in the
Sound, went ashore on. the Batten Shoal. She filled
with water, and her cargo, 1,500 quarters of wheat,
consigned to Messrs. Bowden and Co., from New York,
was much damaged. The weather has since abated,
and hopes are entertained of saving about two-thirds of
the cargo. When the accident happened she was lying
at a single anchor, and drifted, her d tngerous condition
being only discovered by the crew by her bumping on
the shoal, heretvatch, it is said, being asleep. The cap-
tain and his wife and crew, nine in number, with their
clothes and bedding, chronometer, &c., were safely
landed in their own boat and a boat belonging to the
Phcebe, Brixham trawler. The lifeboat at this station
was launched, but the crew had left the vessel before
the lifeboat arrived out.
THE ARCHBISHOP or CANTERBURY AND TRE
ITINERANT DEALER IN GAME.—A rather curious inci-
dent happened to the Archbishop of Canterbury OR
Friday on his return journey to London. He left
Canterbury by the afternoon train which runs to Ash-
ford, and there leaves the passengers to be taken to
London by the Dover express. The archbishop, who
it may be stated had charmed every one he had met
by his genial affectionate manner, was standing on the
platform at Ashford, and conversing with a legal gen-
tleman, when a man in a blouse, who turned out to be
marched up to him and
awni iht i
snme raal nl tceremony
r e
qguarneseted him to have a brace of
wild ducks for four and sixpence. The archbishop did
not show any desire to accept the bargain, whereupon
the hawker fastened upon the archbishop's companion,
and with much volubility expatiated on the qualities of
the ducks. Now the legal gentleman is a very able
writer on the laws of nations and of commerce, and he
of the blouse found that he had met his match at the
settling of a bargain. Eventually the eminent lawyer
became the purchaser of two brace of ducks, but
whether at the price first asked by the seller is a matter
on which our informant expressed his doubts. His
Grace was amused at the incident, and the hawker
again importuned him to buy a brace of birds, where..
upon he fell in with the humour of the thing and made
the purchase, but without any haggling whatever. The
hawker then made the politest bow of which he was
capable and retired, in utter ignorance of the distin-
guished position of the gentleman with whom he had
done this little stroke of business.
SIR H. BULWER AT SUEZ.—The Malta limes of the
4th inst. says :---` We learn from Egypt that Sir H. L.
Bulwer paid a visit to Suez, and on his return to Cairo
left by a river steamer, placed at his disposal by
the Pacba, on a visit to Thebes and the cataracts.
Rumour states that the object of his visit is to inspect the
consular establishments; but it is believed, in addi-
tion, to have reference to the state of the yolks of the
Suez Call 11. Cairo is at present full of TsitOrs, and all
unusual number of travellers have already left for the
upper country •

_DISTRESS IN LANCASHIRE.

PRESTON.

In Preston the cotton trade seems improving. This
week some mills previously stopped have commenced
working, and others running short time have begun full
operations. It is expected that next week several
factories will start. There are still an immense num-
ber of people in distress. The, relief committee and the
guardians have, during the past six days, relieved
58,500. As I stated last week, some of the poor
get double relief. Making a proper deduction for these,
I estimate that there are now nearly 44,000 persons in
Preston in absolute distress. The fever, lam glad to
say, appears to be gradually disappearing—at any rate
it is cominc, down to the level of ordinary times. Sub-
scriptions of money and contributions of clothing, &c.,
continue to arrive on a very liberal scale. The Catho-
lics have at last got separated from the Protestants, but
a good deal of rancour, 'religious' animosity, and
Christian' hatred prevails in the town. The cottage
owners of Presi on this week memorialised the relief com-
mittee to make some allowanee to the poor for rent; after-
wards they memorialised the board of guardians to
join them in an application to Government tor a loan of
Z 50,000 from the consolidated fund. In both cases they
were unsuccessful. The school recently established for
distressed overlookers and managers is progressing very
well. The institute of the operative spinners and
xainders to which I referred last week, will, it is feared,
have to be closed. The committee say that they have.
appealed throughout the whole regions of wealth, and
right up to royalty, and that they have only met with a
miserable and insignificant response. In regard to the
operations of the reltef committee of Preston I may
state that this week they have relieved 10,229 cases,
comprising 40,331 persons, at a cost of £1,175 2s. Bd.;
or, as compared with last week, an increase of 129
in cases, 915 in persons, and £45 ss. 3d. in expenditure.
They have given sixpenny tickets, for exchange at the
shops in the town, to 14,581 persons. During the
week they have distributed to the poor 500 tons of
coal, £1,500 worth of bedding and clothing,, 34,250
loaves of bread, equal to 61 tons 3 cwt., 40,007 quarts
of soup, and 8,820 quarts of sconce (potato hash). The
entire expenditure for the week has been £3,100. Dr.
E. Smith, sent by the Privy Council, visited Preston a
day or two ago. Whilst in the town he visited amongst
other places, the kitchen,' or relief committee, in
Crooked-lane. He theze tasted the soup made for the
poor, and afterwards pronounced it the best of any he
had inspected in Lancashire. Arrangements are being
made in Preston to give the poor various treats at
Christmas.
WALTON-LE-DALE.

At Walton, which contains a population of 5,257 per-
sons, 2,286 individuals are in the receipt of relief from
the ,charitable committee. Their relief this week has
eost £146 7s. Old. Six hundred and. eighty of the per-
sons relieved by the committee get no assistance from the
guardians. At the sewing school in Walton there are
now 136 girls employed._ _

articles.title: litca HOLE
articles.text:
litca HOLE

The township of Much Mole contains a population of
about 1,000 persons. A report I have seen from bole
this afternoon says :—‘ There are 305 personsi here more
.or less dependent upon handloom weaving n their own
houses. The weavers latterly have had to go to and
from Preston and Chorley, a distance of sixteen or
eighteen miles, very frequently, in search of work.
i
They now seek for it n vain, and all their looms, except
aix, are silent.' I understand—and this will show the
position of the place—that not one person pays income-
tax in Hoole on real property, and but four on trades
realising £lOO a year. A relief committee has just been
formed here, and the farmers of the district have pro-
mised to cart a quantity of coal for the poor.

articles.title: GARSTANG.
articles.text:
GARSTANG.

The operatives in the district of Garstang are still
.suffering very severely. At Caldervale, Scorton' and
Catterall many of the operatives have no work at all.
The relief committee, established a short time since at
Catterall, appears to be doing much good. They have
distributed a considerable quantity of clothing, bedling,
4cc., this week, and are making every arrangement to
meet the coldness of the season, and the badness of the
times.

articles.title: D OLPHINHULAIE.
articles.text:
D OLPHINHULAIE.

This is a manufacturing village north of Garstang.
Small though the place is, there appears to be much
distress in it, and many of the operatives are'suffering
very keenly. A relief committee has been established
on their behalf, and this week a quantity of wearing
apparel, bedding, and food *has been distributed
amongst them. The poor of Dolphinholme appear at
present to be suffering more from a want of clothing
than food, and the committee
.state that contributions of
the former character would be most thankfully re-
-eeived.

articles.title: LANCASTER.
articles.text:
LANCASTER.

I have no particular change to report relative to Lan-
caster. The relief committee are engaged most assidu-
ously in meeting the wants of the poor. I think I told
you once before that the committee were rather of an
independent turn of mind, and that they had resolved
not to apply for any grants from either the Mansion
House or the central committee if they could by any
possibility avoid it. So far they have stuck to their
text. This week they have relieved 139 poor families
with food, fuel, and clothing. They have agreed to
make soup, or 'sconce,' every day in the week, and
have decided to expend at once £66 ss. in releasing
articles which have been pawned by the poor. The
industrial school established by the committee is
attended on the average by about 120 females. The
school organised by the Society of Friends is attended
by 80.
CATON.

In this village, which is situated pleasantly in the
Vale of the Lime, there is a good deal of distress. A
Lund has just been raised in order to provide every poor
family in the place with a cart of coals.

articles.title: HEAPY AND WHEELTON.
articles.text:
HEAPY AND WHEELTON.

Considerable distress prevails in these two places.
Until lately they have enjoyed a comparative immunity
from the evils of the cotton famine.' Now they are
experiencing the general results of the depression, and
many of the operatives are in exceedingly poor circum-
stances. Bedding, clothing, and food are much needed,
but an effort is being made to mitigate the prevailing
distress, and about £lOO has already been subscribed for
that object.
CHORLEY.

Distress increases at Chorley: The following statis-
tics will show the number of in and out door paupers
in the union: Indoer—Chorley, 88; Brindle, 91. Out-
door—Chorley, 1,964; Leyland, 1912; Croston, 626.
This week-the relief committee have distributed to the
Poor of Chorley 11,480 lbs. of bread, 3,600 lbs. meal,
3,120 lbs. flour, 300 lbs. soap, 113 lbs. coffee, 31- cwt.
Sugar, 4 cwt. bacon, and 1,600 quarts soup, at a total
cost of £2OO. The relief committee, at their last meet-
ing? decided 'that, as the present time of distress
Plainly affords a valuable opportunity for influencing
the operatives for good, it ought not to be allowed to
pass away unprofitably ; and it is therefore proposed
that some plan by which a moral and educational influ-
ence may be brought to bear upon those at present out
of employ be considered.' The committee subsequently
resolved that mixed schools for young persons between
the ages of thirteen and twenty-one be established in
the town, under lay superintendents.
D.A.ENEN.
The distress continues in Darwen, but it does not
appear to be so severe as it was a few weeks ago, and
there seems to be a better tone generally in the cotton
trade. The relief committee have just established a new
school for the unemployed operatives, who are taught
reading, writing, arithmetic, and grammar. The indus-
trial class established by the committee for females con-
tinues to be very well attended. A 'mothers' sewing
class' has been this week opened, and the average daily
attendance has been 130.
BLACKBURN.

This week there is—a—cTecrease of 252 in the number of
the unemployed; there are still, however, many opera-
tives out of work. 6,532 are working full time, 4,392
are on short time, and 16,349 tire totally out of work.
The relief committee have distributed during the last six
days 56,0401b5. of flour, 44,7601bs meal, and they have
made and sold at their kitchen, 5,377 quarts soup.
1113 wards of 10,000 articles of bedding and cloth-
„„ing have been given to the poor during the week.
-"ae distribution of the clothing contributed to
and purchased by the committee has not yet
been made. All the industrial and educational schools in
Blackburn are well attended, and appear to give great
satisfaction. The guardians have promised the cottage
owners, who
appear now to be suffering very severely
through high rates and losses of rents, to assist them in
effecting a lispension of the former, until they are in a,
better position than at present to pay the same. ,A few
weeks i ago t Nve:s decided that the guardians and the
charitable
. committee should relieve a certain number of
the poor,
independently of each other. The relief cora-
mittee, I believe,. will take charge of 20,000, and the re-
mainder will be in charge of the guardians. This new
sYstem, which comes into Operation next Monday, will
involve on the Part
of the relief comraittee an extra ex-
pendjtureof6Ooor7oOperweek. According to the scale
of the relief committee, all famihes entirely unemployed
vall be 'waisted at the rate of is. 6.d. per head per week.
The family income may be made into a suin not exceed-
ing 2s. per head per week, providing it requires not more
than is. 6d. to do it. All persons receiving parochial
aid are not to have any relief from the committee except
in fuel, clothing, and bedding. The. income of any
family from the
grants made by the relief committee to
the various classes will be reckoned as so much of that
family's relief. Thq,kresent weekly relief given by the
guardians of the to is twelve times more than that
expended in ordinary times, and if it Were not for 'volun-
tary charity (including, of course, the relief committee),
a rate e 30s. in !lile pc:l:net would ant be suffi'int tc

meet the requirements of the poor. In Blackburn the
operatives have not been the only sufferers through this
commercial panic. Since the commencement of the
depression eighteen firms connected with the cotton trade
have suspended payment, compounded, with their
creditors, or gone through the Bankruptcy Court; and
it is stated that there are now in Blackburn manufac-
turers iii the receipt of relief from the charitaltle com-
mittee.

articles.title: ACCRINGTON.
articles.text:
ACCRINGTON.

In Accrington the distress is still very severely felt by
the operative classes • it also seriously affects and em-
barrasses many of those engaged in business, such as
tailms, drapers, grocers, &c. The relief committee are
prosecuting their labours vigorously, and, on the whole,
the poor of Accrington appear to be tolerably well cared
for.

articles.title: COLNE.
articles.text:
COLNE.

This week the relief -committee of Coble have as-
sisted 1,068 persons, at a cost of £44 35. 6d.; a large
quantity of fuel has also • been distributed amongst the
operatives, and preparations are being made for a distri-
bution of bedding and clothing. The cotton trade of
Colne is slightly improving.

articles.title: ENFIELD AND OAKENSHAW.
articles.text:
ENFIELD AND OAKENSHAW.

Between 400 and 600 persons are in receipt of relief
from the charitable committee of Enfield and Oaken-
shaw, and this week the food, &c., distributed has cost
£39 ss. 9d.

articles.title: BURNLEY.
articles.text:
BURNLEY.

£444 14s. 3d. has been expended this week by Vie
charitable committee of Burnley, in the relief of 6,373
persons. The total expenditure of the committee, in-
cluding the educational, has been £509 us. 4d. The
distribution of £l,OOO in clothing to those whose earn-
ings do mot exceed 3s. per head per week, and who do
not receive relief from the gu3rdians or the charitable
committee will commence next week. This week the
committee have distributed an immense quantity of
bedding and clothing.
HIGHAM.

Higham, a manufacturing township in East Lanca-
shire, feels the present commercial depression very
severely. A relief committee has recently been estab-
lished here, and the members thereof have within the
last few days organised a sewing class. The attendance
so far has been good, and the girls appear to like their
new 'profession.'
CLITHEROE.

Cotton manufacturing and business of every sort seem
to have been at a standstill in Clitheroe. This week
621 persons have been relieved by the charitable com-
mittee, at a cost of £36 11s. 4d. The same committee
have relieved in the Low Moor district 103 families,
comprising 420 persons, at an average cost of is.
per head, or £24 12s. 4d. in the aggregate.

articles.title: BACUP.
articles.text:
BACUP.

No change of a noticeable character has taken place
at Bacup, so far as regards the state of trade. The relief
committee have introduced a plan of giving tickets to
the poor, which can be exchanged by them at the diffe-
rent shops in the town for whatever articles they may
require. The plan, so far, has given great satisfaction.

articles.title: CHURCH.
articles.text:
CHURCH.

Nealry 400 persons are now on the books of the
Church relief committee. A large quantity of bedding
and clothing has been given to the poor. ,The cotton
trade is slightly improving here and labour generally
seems to be more in demand than it was a few weeks
ago. - .

articles.title: 0 SWALDTWISTLE.
articles.text:
0 SWALDTWISTLE.

A slight alteration for the better has taken place in
the general trade of Oswaldtwistle. During the past
week the relief committee have assisted 243 poor
families, consisting of 1,093 persons, at a cost of
£37 19s. 6d.

articles.title: PfIOHISED .RETRENCILIfENT.
articles.text:
PfIOHISED .RETRENCILIfENT.

(From the Observer.)

Retrenchment in the military and naval expenditure
of the country is a question that is understood (we be-
lieve rightly) to be engaging the serious attention of the
Cabinet preparatory to the meeting of Parliament. We
think there is no doubt but that reductions to a consi-
derable amount will be effbcted ; and we are sure that,
under the control of a Government of which Lord Pal-
merston is chief, those reductions, in whatever direction
they may be made, will be effected without in any way
injuring the real efficiency of either service. The mili •
tary committee of the Cabinet have had several meetings
at the Horse Guards upon the subject, and search-
ing inquiries have been instituted to ascertain in
what direction savings upon the next year's esti-
mates may be most judiciously carried into effect.
We believe that ho vever great the desire for
economy in the national expenditure may be, the
wish to maintain our defensive establishments in
a condition of efficiency is equally strong in the
public mind.. Without pretending to know any-
thing of what must at present be shrouded in official
secrecy, it is not difficult to indicate some points at
which the present system offers the opportunity for
very material saving, without, in the least degree, im-
pairing the strength and efficiency of the national
forces. The administration of the army admits
of reforms which can be made to add to the
efficiency of the whole military machine, whilst leading
to such an amount of retrenchment in the expenditure
as may tell with very agreeable effect on the estimates,
and give considerable satisfaction to the taxpayer.
There is the extravagant staff in Ireland, of the
utility of which in these days of rapid communication
the most practical authorities entertain the strongest
doubts, and in curtailing which, • and the various
appointments connected with it, a judicious eco-
nomy may be freely exercised. Then, too, there
are the numerous district staffs, which seem to be
calculated more to complicate the administration of the
army than to be of any real use in the present day, but
all of which lead to enormous expense. There is here
an ample opportunity for the pruning knife to be applied.
On too many former occasions, when a season for re-
trenchment appeared to have arrived, a reduction of
strength was the rude expedient alone adopted. So
many thousands less of rank and file, so many men who
had been trained into effective soldiers at a great ex-
pense to be discharged; or so many ships to be paid. off,
and their crews dispersed. We hope that the circum-
stances of the times, when the estimates for the coming
year are prepared, will be such as to admit of some re-
duction in the personnel, both of the army and navy;
but we look to administrative reforms, especially in the
staff arrangements, for a more effective and more lasting
economy. In the military service of the colonies we
may expect that it will be found practicable to make
some material saving.
The transition state in which our navy still is will re-
quire a: continued outlay for purposes of construction
that will, in all probability, neutralise in a great mea-
sure retrenchments made in other directions. Increased
dock accommodation at Portsmouth is rendered indis-
pensible by the enlarged size of the ships that are taking
their place in the list of our active navy. Whatever
form the navy of the future may be destined to take,
there is one fact settled, and that is, that the new ships
will be vastly bigger than the old. Great lenghth is the
unvarying accompaniment of all the new forms. There
is scarcely a dock at Portsmouth long enough to receive
our new class of frigates, and it would be a matter, not
of economy but of penny-wisdom and pound-foolishness
to neglect this subject. We believe that provision for
improvements so much required will be made in the
next estimates; and we are sure that in no quarter can
it be pretended that expenditure for such an object is
unnecessary. The main and gratifying feature, how-
ever, of the estimates for both army and navy, we
think, will be found to be a material retrenchment of
expenditure, effected in such a manner as not to impair
in the least degree that high state of efficiency to which
both services have been brought. •

LOSS OF AN ENGLISH VESSEL WITH EIGHT HANDS._
On Saturday intelligence was received of the total loss
of the English schooner Caroline, of Salcombe, and all
hands with the exception of one. It appears that she
sailed from Great Yarmouth on the 22nd ult., for Leg-
horn, and on the 3rd inst. she struck ou a reef near Saint
Petre, a few miles to the westward of Cadiz, and almost
immediately capsized. She soon began to break up, and
the master, Captain White, his mate, and six hands were
drowned, only one of the crew being saved.

PATTERN POST BETWEEN THIS COUNTRY AND
FRANCE.—Samples of seeds, drugs, &c., which cannot
be sent in open covers must for the future be enclosed
in bags made of Imp, paper, or other material, tied at
the neck with strnig. Closed transparent oiled-silk
bags must no longer be used for this purpose, as the
officers of the Post-office . . France are all instructed to
treat packets of this description as letters, upon the
ground that they are hermetically closed, and cannot be
examined.

The 4TH DRAGOON GlTAB.ps.—Some couple of months
since we complained that Lieutenant Harran, who had
been removed from the adjutancy under circumstances
requiring no more particular reference, still held it nomi-
nally, thotght not really. Scarcely has our remohstance
brought about his formal removal, when we find him
again adjutant—this time really, but
.not nominally.
We must confess to a feeling of surprise that Colonel
Shute would suffer this, no matter from what quarter the
suggestion came. We cannot but attribute it to the
settled desire on the part of the authorities in Ireland,
especially those having the superintendence of the ca-
valry service, to run counter to the Duke of Cambridge's
decision, and as far as possible sustain Lieutenant Harran
against his Royal Highness. Along with this objection
we must think it highly impolitic to employ in a post of
such influence and authority an officer closely identified
with a party in the regiment whose Bitterness is naturally
not decreased by dis:lomfiture.—drtny and Gazette.

articles.title: COTTON GROWING IN -Mid.
articles.text:
COTTON GROWING IN -Mid.

We this week publish the last of a series of letters on
this subject, from the pen of Professor Syed Abdoollah,
of University College, a native of India, and one, there-
fore, well qualified to impart such reliable and valuable
information on the subj, ct, the result of his own per-
sonal observation. In taking a general survey of his
letters, we find that India is a country of which a great
portion is more peculiarly fitted than any other for be-
coming a great and productive cotton field. Profe•sor
Abdoollah brings forward in support and confirmation
of his statements, quotations from some of the most
celebrated In )ian statesmen bearing upon the question.
One quotation in particular struck us, in letter No. 3
(which letter, to our mind, contains by far the most im-
portant information of the series), in which the Marquis
of Dalhousie, during his Governor-Generalship of India,
urged the expediency of relieving England from almost
total dependency on a foreign country for so indispensable
a material for her trade as cotton. How expedient—nay,
how necessary—such a provision was, passing even's prove
sadly enough. The old cemplaint of the difficulties of tran-
sit, which sometimes renders valueless large quantities of
cotton now grown in the interior, by reason of the impos-
sibility of transportin g that commodity in a proper, reason-
able manner to the coast, is reiterated here. The Professor
shows us that native proprietors are not equal to the
work. It is English capital, skill, and example that are
wanting, but the native element is by no means to be
thrown out of the calculation. Fitted by constitution
and birth to endure the peculiarities of the climate,
which would be fatal to Eurepeans, combined with
labour, they offer to the English cotton grower not only
the most available and best, but the very cheapest labour
that can be procured. The peasantry are represented as
a class likely to respond to the wants and requirements
of settlers, and to be qualified and willing to accept the
employment which would be afforded to them by the
introduction of a class of settlers and capitalists having
cotton-growing as their object. But the learned gentle
man does not speak so highly of the generality of his
countrymen as he does of the peasantry. He says that
he is obliged to add his unparalleled testimony, much
against his will, that, in comparison with the English,
they exhibit human nature under a very degraded and
humiliating aspect; that they want truth, honesty and
goodfaith to an incredible extent; and that selfishness, un-
restrained by principle, reigns supreme. We are bound
to believe in the veracity of these statements, as we feel
assured that no man would render such an account of his
fellow-countrymen if painful truth did not compel him
to make such admissions. We gather, then, from these
letters, and the various confirmatory quotations they
contain, that native labour, directed by English capital,
which would rapidly introduce improved means of transit,
and regulated tariffs, would shortly convert India into a
vast cotton-growing country, with advantages equal, if
not superior, to those of any other country in the world.
—The Drapers' Weekly News.

articles.title: WILLS AND BEQUESTS.
articles.text:
WILLS AND BEQUESTS.

will of Sir James Francis Doughty Tichborne,
Bart., of Tichborne Park, near Alresford, Hants, was
proved in London by the executors and trustees, Wm.
Mostyn, Esq., of Cork-street, Burlington-gardens, and
Vincent Gosford, Esq., of Tan-y-llan' Flintshire. The
personalty was sworn under £lB,OOO. The testator be-
queaths to his relict, Dowager Lady Tichborne, a life
interest in a certain portion of the property, together
with a legacy of £l,OOO, a carriage, and the plate bear-
ing the Tichborne crest, which was purchased in France,
and is principally of French manufacture (the rest of
the family plate, furniture, articles of vertu, paintings,
statuary, &c., are to be retained as heirlooms with the
title and estate), and appoints his son and sacces,or to the
baronetcy residuary legatee. There are legacies to his
executors, and to some personal friends, and others;
also to his butler, bailiff, gardener, and other servants,
as well as to the poor Catholics of Tichborne and to St.
Elizabeth's Hospital, Great Ormond-street, London,
and the Reformatory, Mount St. Bernard, Leicester.
The will bears date the 6th of February, 1861, being
two months prior to the marriage of his (the testator's)
son and only surviving child, now in his twenty-second
year. The testator died at the age of seventy-seven.
The will of John Corrie, Esq. of Southington,
Southampton, was proved in London under £lOO,OOO
personalty, the executors nominated being the relict,
together with John Akers Hankey, Esq., of West-
bourne-terrace, Hyde-park, and Henry Rutt. Esq., of
Upper Clapton. The will was executed in 1855. To
his relict, who enjoys a life interest over £30,000 under
marriage settlement, the testator makes some further
provision; and, after leaving legacies to a few friends,
to his•executors, and to his servants, directs the entire
residue of his property to be divided into three parts,
bequeathing to each of his two nieces a third, and the
remaining third to the three daughters of his niece
Caroline by her former husband, in equal proportions.
The will of William Kentish, of Grove-villa, Bel-
ilLont-hill, Lee, Kent, was proved in the London Court
on the 14th ult. The personalty was sworn under
£lOO,OOO. The testator was of that highly-established
firm, Rowe, Kentish, and Osborne, 16, Change-alley,
Cornhill, engravers of bankers' security cheques and
bank notes. The will bears date April 16, 1861, and is
contained in a few lines, whereby the testator disposes
of the whole of his property, real and personal, to his
relict absolutely.

articles.title: TEST INDIA MAILS.
articles.text:
TEST INDIA MAILS.

The Royal Mail Company's steamer Avon, while
lying alongside the wharf at Colon -with two anchors
down, was driven ashore on the morning of the 22nd
ultimo, by a norther, and the heavy rollers setting in
the Bay. At the time of going ashore the Avon had
not received any of the cargo waiting at Colon to be
shipped by her, but she had received the bullion from
San Francisco, about 78 bars of silver, and 100 cases of
specie, value about £200,000. She also had about 300
packages of cargo from Grey Town, principally india-
rubber, all of which, it is expected, wane recovered.
The crew were landed by means of a warp from the
ship to the shore, and so passed along it through the
surf, which was running over the railway up to the
houses. On the 25th when the Tamar left Colon for St.
Thomas, the Avon was settling down aft, her rudder
post was gone, and it was expected she would become
a total wreck.

The United States brig of war Bainbridge also
dragged her anchors doling the gale, and drove towards
the shore (having thrown overboard her guns and
stores and cast away her masts) ; she made signals of
distress, and Mr. Dix, chief officer, Mr. Hodgson, second
officer, 35r. Garratt, fifth officer, Mr. Milne, fifth en-
gineer, and Mr. Olsen, fireman, all belonging to the
Avon, volunteereatiAnd put off to her assistance in a
boat, and ultimately succeeded in rescuing the crew.
The Bainbridge did not, however, go ashore, as her
anchors brought her up close to the reef after her crew
had left her.

Her Majesty's ship Jason, lying at Colon when the
gale commenced, succeeded in getting safely out of the
bay.
The American mail steamer Ocean Queen also suc-
ceeded in getting out, but with loss of paddle-box and
other damage.
The brig Bolivar, of Dundee, laden with coals, was
driven ashore, and became % total wreck.
The Tamar, with the English mails, arrived at Colon
on the 23rd, but was unable to communicate in conse-
quence of the .boisterous weather and heavy sea
running. She then bore up for and anchored at
Portobello, and there found the Ocean Queen which
vessel had succeeded in getting out of the bay when the
gale commenced; both vessels left on the 24th. The
Tamar succeeded in landing her mails and passengers on
the morning of the 25th, but was unable to land any
portion of her cargo. After receiving the Colon, Grey
Town, and Blewfields mails, she returned to St. Thomas.
In consequence of a heavy fall of rain and accumula-
tion of water on the railway from Panama to Colon
there are no mails, passengers, or cargo from the Pacific
ports or Panama by the Atrato. The line across the
Isthmus was quite impassable, in many places covered
with several feet of water, and it was expected to remain
Al for some days. The telegraph also was injured 4nd
not working.

Journal de Rouen states that 5,000 f. have been
sent by the Duke d'Aumale and 5,000 f. by the Count de
Paris and the Duke de Chartres to the subscription for
the relief of the suffering cotton workmen.

TEE :WI;NTER SEASON AT PAIT.—•A correspondent at
Pau writes 'After a short snap of very cold weather,
we are again luxuriating in an uncle.uded sun and a
temperature of 56 degrees of Fahrenheit. Our foreign i
colony is more numerous this season than even last year,
the English being, as usual, greatly in the ascendant,
and taking th.e lead in hospitable entertainments of
every description, while their kinsmen, the Americans,
are obliged, in consequence of the sad civil war afflicting
their native land, to keep somewhat aloof. Our railway,
a new theatre, and a circus will, it is officially announced,
be inaugurated in the course of another month. Four
deer have just been presented by the Earl of H. to his
countrymen of the 'Pau Drag run: These animals are
doubly valuable at this moment, when foxes for many
miles round are quite exterminated.'
It is stated that negotiations have been opened be-
tween the Swedish Court and Prince Christian of Den-
mark, of the house of Sonderburg-Glucksburg, and
future father-in-law of the Prince of Wales, respecting
a matrimonial alliance between the eldest son of the
Prince, born in 1843, and a captain in the Danish
army, and the Princess Louisa-Josephine, only daughter
of Charles XV. of Sweden, born in 1851. Another
throne to which will ascend, on the death of the reign-
ing sovereign, a member of the family of Glueksburg !

RASULTS OF THE WAR.

The New York Tribune, in noticing .the recent pro-
posal of Napoleon /11. to offer mediation, says :
AI. de Lb uys' vrop sal to intet fere between the United
States and the Confe,terate rebels assumes that we have
made no progress toward the overthrow of the rebellion.
Here are his words:

'From the commeticement of the war, an armed
force was set on foot by the belligerents, which, since
then, has almost constantly been kept up. After so
much bloodshJd they are now, in that respect, nearly in
the same position.'
Is this he fact? Let us consider.

The zoutbem Confederacy claims to be composed of
the fifteen Slave States, Delaware and Maryland ex-
cepted. It professes also to include the Indian territory,
New Mexico, and AI izona.
Let us—for the end of the year approaches—take a
hurried account of stook, and see just where we stand:-
1. The Confederates, though they recently invaded
Maryland in force, and have made petty raids into Penn-
sylvania, Ohio, Indiana, &c., do not hold at this hour a
single foot of ten itory outside.° what they claim as their
own, nor do they seriously threaten to acquire any.-2.
After having for months desperately contested the great
State of M ssouri, fought many important battles therein
--some of them successfully—they have been driven
out of it, so that only two or thee guerilla bands of
no importance now lurk in its swamps or forests and
occasionally steal out to commit depredatiOns.-3. Ken-
tucky has in like manner been in good part under rebel
domination, not only last winter but again two months
ago. Now they are wholly expelled from it, and likely
to remain so.-4. Tennessee is one of the States most
important to the slaveholders' Confederacy. Half of
it, includin7 the two most important cities, Nashville
and Memphis, have been held for the Union through-
out the last six months, and we are on the point
of trying to reclaim the residue.-5. Virginia is
the most populous State beloning to Jeff's Con-
federacy, and includes his metropolis. Very nearly
half of it is now in Union hands, including the cities of
Norfolk and Wh,eling, while its chief fortress, Monroe,
has never yet seen a rebel flag floating from its walls.
We expect to have a good deal more of it before the year
is out.-6. Of North Carolina, the Union has held Albe-
marle and the connected sounds, with their islands and
the beach outside forts Hatteras and Macon, the cities
of Newbem and outside,
with a considerable strip
of the main land, for sevel al months, almost without
resistance. We hold also the water line of transit thence
to Hampton Roads through the Dismat Swamp Canal.-
7. Of South Carolina, we hold the Sea Islands, in-
cluding the forts built by the rebels to guard the entrance
to Port Royal inlet or sound—S. Of Georgia we have
long held Fort Pulaski, commanding the water way to
Savannah, and the islands of Tybee, St. Simons, &c., are
actually or virtually in our possession. The whole coast,
with its inlets and mouths of rivers is in our possession.-
9. Nearly all the seaports of Florida (Pensacola, St.
Augustine, &c) have long been in Union 'hands.
All the fortifications also (Fort Pickens, Fort Taylor, the
!Tortugas) are and ever have been Union. 10.—Of
Texas we have Galveston and most of the seaports. We
can take the residue when we choose with little effort.
11.—Of Louisiana we hold Forts St. Philip and Jack-
son, which guard the ascent of the Mississippi, with
New Orlelns, the chief mart of the south-west, and a
large area of the adjacent sugar-growing region. And
we have held the city and, the forts more than half a
year undisputedly. 12.—We hold a considerable strip
of Northern Mississippi, and have a victorious army
there ready to fight all corners, only the rebels insist on
being goers instead. 13.—Ditto as to Arkansas. 14.
We have quiet.possession of all New Mexico and Arizona,
which, one year since, were mainly in the possession of
a triumphant rebel force. 15.—This is also the fact as
to the Indian territory.
It thus appears that nearly one-third of the population,
and more than a third the area claimed by the Con-
federacy, are to-day under Union control; meat of it
won by hard fighting within the past year. New
Orleans, St. Louis, Louisville, Memphis, Galveston,
Santa Fe, Lexington, Norfolk, Newbern, Pensacola—all
these are claimed as belonging to the Confederacy, and
most of them have been held by it; but they are now
all Union. More than one million people who were
under the Confederate flag a year ago, now peacefully
repose under the Union eagles. And we are just on the
point of marching on,' with larger and better disciplined
armies than ever before.

With what justice, then, with what fairness, does M.
Drouyn de Lhuys assert that the belligerents 'stand
nearly in the same position' as they did a year ago?
Where *is the square foot of ground we have lost?
Where is the Confederate offset for Kentucky, half of
Tennessee, Missouri, N9w Mexico, New Orleans,
Memphis &c., &c.? Why should he who proposes
friendly mediation between the contending parties in-
troduce the subject by assertions which prove him alike
hostile to the Union and singularly inconsiderate of
truth

articles.title: CORONATION OF THE KING OF MADAGASCAR.
articles.text:
CORONATION OF THE KING OF
MADAGASCAR.

The Moniteur contains the following details respecting
the coronation of King Radama of Madagascar :
'News from Madagascar' under date of October,
acquaint us with the result of the embassy to King
Radama, on the occasion of his coronation, with which
the envoys of France and England were charged. The
ceremony took place at Tananarive, the capital of the
island, on the 22nci. September. It was preceded by a
solemn mass, during which the royal crown, presented by
the Emperor Napoleon, was consecrated. The King was
crowned upon the Champ de Mars. In the centre is the
sacred stone which supported the throne. The King
wore a magnificent cloak given to him by the Emperor,
and the Queen.wore a mantle and a robe presented to her
by the Empress. An immense crowd thronged the city
and the neighbourhood champ de Mars. In the evening
there was a grand dinner and fireworks. The represen-
tatives of France and England met with the most cordial
welcome, and they speak in the most flattering terms of
the King and Queen. The best understanding has pre-
vailed between them.'

The Moniteur terminates its account by stating that a
treaty of commerce, upon the broadest basis, equally
favourable to all nations,' has been concluded, but that
no allusion has been made to any concession of territory,
as that might have occasioned grave difficulties.' The
French embassy quitted Tananariva on the 4th October,
and embarked on the 17that Tamalava, after having re-
mained more than two months in Madagascar.

articles.title: DESPERATE ENCOUNTER WITH SALMON POACHERS.
articles.text:
DESPERATE ENCOUNTER WITH
SALMON POACHERS.

Since the fresh weather set in in the beginning of
December, salmon have been swarming on the spawning
beds of the Earn, in the neighbourhood of Comrie, as
well as in the other streams of Perthshire, and a gang of
determined poachers have been killing the fish on the
fords almost nightly, and setting the watchers at defiance.
Late on Tuesday night, or early on Wednesday morn-
ing, a party of poachers, numbering 13, appeared on the
ford almost opposite the parish church, having their
faces blackened, and with torches and leisters.
They succeeded in a short time in killing seven salmon.
As soon as the poachers left the river they
were set upon by four watchers and two assist-
ants, when a serious and desperate encounter took
place between the two parties. Owing, however, to the
superior number of the poachers, the watchers were
severely maltreated, and one of them especially, named
Guthrie, was sadly cut about the face and head, and had
a narrow ecscapc from being drowned in the Earn. He
was attended to by a surgeon, who dressed his wounds.
During the melee two or three of the poachers carried
away the fish, and immediately returned to assist their
associates in the scuffle. The poachers were so audaci-
ous as, after the watchers had been rendered powerless,
to enter the river again in order to kill more salmon;
but they were not so successful as at first. On Monday
week a party killed a number of salmon at the bridge,
some of them weighing 301 b. The poachers, up to
Saturday afternoon, had not been discovered. The
fish are so numerous this season that the herd boys are
capturing them daily from the banks of the Earn with
cleeks.—Scotsman.

The last of the scaffolding in the interior of Notre-
Dame is now being removed, and the operation of fixing
stained glass in the windows is almost terminated.
There Is every reason to believe that the cathedral will
be restored to public worship on the 2oth, as announced.
On the 16th inst. the Crown Prince and Princess of
Prussia will visit Vienna, where they will be received
with considerable pomp and ceremony. There will be
a 'theatre pare' in their honour, a military review, and
a grand dinner in the Imperial Palace at Schoubrunn.

THE PRINCESS ALICE'S PHYSICIANS.—We learn that
Dr. Arthur Farre is appointed, in conjunction with Sir
C. Locock, to attend the Princess Alice in her confine-
ment, which is expected to take place next April. Dr.
Arthur Farre's appointment will be stamped by the pro-
fession with universal approbation, lie has earned his
reputation by study, hard work as a lecturer and clinical
teacher, and by an immense experience amongst the
patients of his hospital.—Medical Times.
