THE RED INDIANS OF AmEnrcA.HWe have often
th u,ght of th•• death of Mah lo tah Fe (the four bears),
who recovered from the disease, and sat in his wigwam,
and saw his whole tribe and family die around him,
then covered them with rushes, and went to the hill
determined to starve himself to death, remained thet e six
days, crept back to the gloom of his wigwam, lay down
by the side of his dead, and died after nine day'S' absti-
nence from food. The Red Man.. regards the white as
an essential and undoubted liar: probably, we may hope
not only because he has tested the veracity of his white
brother and found it wanting, but because almost every-
thing communicated must be opposed to his wall of
fixed ideas. But he possesses an instinctive grace and
grandeur of soul. What a pretty story is that which
Catlin tells of the Pawnee, who rescued the poor girl of
some hostile tribe from the stake, to whom some ladies
of New York sent the medal with the letter, Brother,
accept this token of our esteem; always wear it for our
sakes, and when you have the power to save a poor
woman, think of this and us, and fly to her relief ! ' and
the answer, so thoroughly Red Indian Sisters, this
will give me care more than ever I had, and I will
listen to tv:.ite men. I am glad I heard of the good
act I have done. I did it in ignorance; now I know
what I have done. I did it in ignorance, and did not
know I 4lid good, but by giving me this medal I know
it ! ' How great is that instinctive grandeur of soul
which does good and yet does not kno w it! We quite
agree with Dr. Wilson that the Red Man is one of our
greatest ethnological mysteries. Did he come from
Europe? Has he, too, Norse blood in his veins ?
Eclectic Review.

THE UGLY FEATURES OF WAR.—War has frightful
beauties whish we have not concealed; but it has also,
we must allow, some ugly features. One of the most
surprising is the rapid stripping of the dead after victory;
the dawn that follows a battle always rises on naked
corpses. Who does this? Who sullies the triumph in
t ids way? Whose is the hideous furtive hand which
slips into the pocket of victory? Who are the villains
dealing their stroke behind the glory ? Some philoso-
phers, Voltaire among them, assert that they are the
very men who have made the glory; they say that those
who keep their feet plunder those lying on the ground,
and the hero of the day is the vampire of the night.
After all, a man has a right to strip a corpse of which
he is the author. We do not believe it, however;
I re Ting a crop of laurels and stealing the shoes of a
dead man do not seem to us possible from the same
hand.—Les _Miserable& By Victor Hugo.
THE HAPPINESS OF THE BLIND.—To be blind and
to be loved is one of the most strangely exquisite forms
of happiness upon this earth, where nothing is perfect.
To have continually at your side a wife, a sister, a
daughter, a charming being, who is there because you
have need of her and because she cannot do without
you; to know yourself indispensable to a worn* who
is necessary to you; to be able continually toVgange
her affection by the amount of her presence which She
gives you, and to stay to yourself—' She devotes all her
I time to me because I possess her entire heart '—to see
her thoughts in default of her face; to prove the fidelity of I
a being in the eclipse of the world; to catch the rustling
of a dress like the sound of wings; to hear her come and
go, leave the room, return, talk, sing, and then to dream '
that you are the centre of those steps, those words, those
songs; to manifest at every moment your own attrac-
tion, and feel yourself powerful in proportion to your
weakness; to become in darkness and through dark-
ness the planet round which this angel gravitates—
but few felicities equal this. The supreme happiness
I of life is the conviction of being loved for yourself, or
I more correctly speaking, loved in spite of yourself; and
' this conviction the blind man has. In this distress to
be served is to be caressed. Dees he want for any-
thing? No. When you possess love, you have not
lost the light. And what a love! a love entirely made
up of virtues! There is no blindness where there is a
certainty; the grouping soul seeks a soul and finds it,
and this found and tried soul is a woman. A hand
supports you, it is her's ; a mouth touches your fore-
head, it is her's ; you hear a breath close to you, it is
she. To have everything she has from her worship to her
pity, to be never left, to have this gentle weakness to suc-
cour you, to lean on this unbending reed, to touch Pro-
vidence with her hand, and be able to takeher in your
arms. Oh! what rapture is this! The heart, that ob-
scure celestial flower, begins to expand mysteriously,
and you would not exchange this shadow for all the
light! The angel soul is thus necessarily there; if she
go away it is to return; she disappears like a dream,
and re-appears like reality. You feel het approach-
ing, it is she. You overflow with serenity, ecstasy,
and gaiety; you are a sunbeam in the nigtit. And
then the thousand little attentions, the nothings which
are so enormous in this vacuum! The most ineffable
accents of the human voice employea to lull you, and
taking the place of the vanished universe, you are
caressed with the :soul: you see nothing, but you feel
yourself adored; it is a paradise of darkness.—Les
Miserables; by V. Bug°.
THE DEATH OF HUSKISSON. - At Parkside, about
seventeen miles from Liverpool, the engines stopped to
take in water. Here a deplorable accident occurred to
one of the illustrious visitors, which threw a deep
shadow over the subsequent proceedings of the day.
The ' Northumbrian ' engine, with the carriage con-
taining the Duke of Wellington, was drawn up on one
line, in order that the whole of the trains on the other
line might pass in review before him and his party.
Mr. Huskisson had alighted from the carriage, and was
standing on the opposite road, along which the
'Rocket' was observed rapidly coming up. At this
moment the Duke of Wellington, between whom
and Mr. Huskisson some coolness had existed,
made a sign of recognition, and held out his
hand. A hurried but friendly grasp was given;
and before it was loosened there was a general cry
from flee bystanders of Get in, get in ! ' Flurried
and confused, Mr. Huskisson endeavoured to get
round the open door of the carriage which projected
over the opposite rail; but in so doing he was struck
down by the Rocket,' and falling with his leg doubled
across the rail, the limb was instantly crushed. His
first words, on being raised, were, I have met my
death,' which unhappily proved true, for he expired
that same evening in the parsonage of Eccles. It was
cited at the time as a remarkable fact, that the
'Northumbrian' engine, driven by George Stephenson
himself, conveyed the wounded body of the unfortunate
gentleman a distance of about fifteen miles in twenty-
five minutes, or at the rate of thirty-six miles an hour.
This incredible speed burst upon the world with the
effect of a new and unlooked-for phenomenon. The
accident threw a gloom over the rest of the day's
proceedings. The Duke of Wellington and Sir Robert
Peel expressed a wish that the procession should
return to Liverpool. It was, however, represented to
them that a vast concourse of people had assembled
as Manchester to witness the arrival of the trains;
that report would exaggerate the mischief, if they did
not complete the journey; and that a false panic
on that day might seriously affect future railway
travelling and the value of the company's property.
The party consented accordingly to- proceed to Man-
chester, but on the understanding that they should
return as sbon as possible, and refrain from further
festivity. As the trains approached Manchester, crowds
of people were found covering the banks, the slopes of
the cuttings, and even the railway itself. The malti-
trade becoming impatient and excited by the rumours
which reached them, had outflanked the military, and
all order was at an end. The people clambered about
the carriages, holding on by the door handles, and
many were tumbled over; but, happily, no fatal acci-
dent occurred. At the Manchester station, the poli-
tical element began to display itself; placards about
Peterloo,' &c., were exhibited, and brickbats were
thrown at the carriage containing the Duke. On
.the
carriage coming to a stand in the Manchester station,
the Duke did not descend, but remained seated, shaking
hands with the women and children who were pushed
forward by the crowd. Shortly after, the trains re-
turned to Liverpool, which they reached, after cen-
siderable interruptions, in the dark, at a late hour.—
Lives of the Engineers. By :Samuel Smiles.
SLEIGH-DRIVING.—SIeigh driving is the one grand,
unapproachable, unalloyed pleasure to be enjoyed in
i
Russia. There s nothing to be compared to a long
furious sweep in a good Russian sleigh, over hard, crisp,
clean snow, wrapped in good furs. With a great bear-
skin hanging over the back of the sleigh, arid its apron
another bear-skin, covering your legs, with your feet
encased in fur goloshes, resting on a doubled up Siberian
curly sheep skin, with a fur cap on your head, as tall and
straight and round as a very large English hat without
a rim, with your hands berried four inches deep amongst
the sable sleeves of your coat; as you lie easily back,
thus comforted, under a clear, frosty, bright sky, the
horses, in graceful silver-mounted harness, tossing their
heads, the bells at their necks tinkling merrily, the
driver in high wolf skin cap and sheep skin coat, over
which he has drawn a handsome blue 'caftan, trimmed
below the arms with silver-plated round buttons as large
as little eggs, and with a large parti-colourt d sash bound
round his waist—e, fellow all excitement, but coolly
managing three wild horses, who tear on at a whirling
speed, dashing the crisp snow in showers from their
hoofs, sometimes for a mentent or two half blinding you
with the fin it, cleanest, whitest powder in the world—
with these appliances, and you see and feel them all,
you know the luxury of sleigh driving. I am not
speaking of a drive through the streets of Petersburg,
but of a drive of thirly or forty miles over untroclden
virgin soil, through the forest, when the trees are
clothed in a dense fantastic folisge of hoar frost fes-
tooned with millions of stalactites, and when the pure
bracing air, as you rush through it, sends the blood
tingling through your veins.—Dickens's 'All the rear
Round.'

THE GREAT CHRISTMAS CATTLE MARKET.
DECEMBERIS —There was a wonderful supply of beasts
an to-day's market for Christmas consumption; three-
fourths of them, leaving out of the calculation the foreign
stock exhibited, were above average merit, not only were
the pure breeds, such as the Short Horns, Hereford,
Devons, Runts, and Sussex, fully represented, but the
number of Crosses was, if any hing, superior to last year,
both as to weight and quality. Lincolnshire, Leicestershire,
and Northauiptonshire forwarded the greatest number
of animals. The Shorthorns, taken as a whole, were
of a good type, and fully equal to former shows;
but we should have been more pleased to find some addi-
tions to their hindquarters. This slight deficiency—
which some persons may consider a characteristic of this
extraordinary breed was fully compensated by the
splendid symmetry of the crosses, some of which realised
£4O each; but our impression is, that, had the graziers
aimed at less fat and more consumable meat, the sales
effected to-day would have been more profitable to them.
There was one feature in this great exhibition worthy of
special notice. We allude to the very moderate number
of Herefords—pure breeds be it understood—exhibited.
Although the nurnbtr was far from extensive, the beasts
have been seldom, if ever; excelled in quality. Their
weight, condition, and symmetry were all that could be
desired. Those forwarded by Mr. Senoir, of Broughton,
near Aylesbury, but not consigned to any particular sales-
man, were quite equal to any previously exhibited here;
and, from the fact that some of them carried off all the
prizes for stock offered by the Bucks Agricultural Society,
It must be regretted—because the show of Herefords
in the Smithfield Club exhibition at the new Agricultural
Hall was of a limited character—that these noble animals
did not compete with similar stock in London. But £4O
each and upwards is a tempting sum to realise by a
grazier. The show of Devon stock was certainly a very
prime one; but, compared with some corresponding
markets, the number was only moderate. Mr. Senior
showed some remarkably prime animals; and, taken as a
whole, the supply, as regards the pure Devonshire breed,
was extremely good. The consideration of the Sussex
beasts proves conclusively that the breeders have made
great exertions to increase the number and quality of their
stock, the show in this respect being far superior to
any former year; but we may remark that some of the
beasts had the appearance of crossing with the Devon&
There was a good sprinkling of Welsh runte in the market;
but the show of long-horns was very limited. There was
rather a large number of Irish beasts on sale. Some few
of these are in good condition; but the remainder were of
a very middling character. The show from Scotland and
Norfolk, embracing as it did remarkably prime horned and
polled Scots, as well as crosses, was unusually prime.
Those most admired, however, were the fifty Scots belong-
ing•to Mr. M'Combie, of Tillyfour, some of which were
consigned to Messrs. Maidwell and Holyand, the remainder
to Messrs. Giblett and Son. They were disposed of at
very high prices, equal to fully ss. 4d. per Blbs., whilst
the general run of Scots was in request at, we should say,
remunerative quotations. Great credit is due to the
Norfolk and Scotch breeders and feeders for the prime con-
dition in which they exhibited their stock this morning.
The beasts exhibited by Mr. George Dickson, and for-
warded by Messrs. Marlin, Knowles, Thomson, Wishart,
Stodart, Kidd, Longmore, Bruce, Murray, Skinner,
Reeds, Frost, and other breeders and feeders in Scotland,
were remarkably prime in quality, and were readily dis-
posed of'at good prices. Mr. Vorley had a very good
show of beasts. Some of the stock was the property of
Mr. Cartwright, of Lincolnshire; Mr. Booth, of Norfolk ;
Mr. Martin, of Aberdeen; and Mr. Conglass, of In-
verary. Messrs. Giblett and Son had a very fine show
of beasts. A portion was forwarded by Mr. Martin,
of Aberdeen; Mr. Mennie, of Huntly ; Mr. Wortley, of
Norfolk, and Mr. Carwardine, of Leominster. At the
stand of Messrs. Morgan and Allday there were some very
good Scots, Devons, Shorthorns, &c. Those belonging to
Mr. Gillett of Halvergate, Mr. M'Carnock of Birmmg.
ham, and Mr. John Towers, of Ludlow, were much ad-
mired for their symmetry. Mr. Collins's stand was well
filled with good beasts. Other salesmen had likewise a
good show of stock. On the whole the supply of sheep
was good. Mr. Gurreer showed some extraordinary Cots-
wolds from the flocks of Mr. Herver, Mr. Walker, and
Mr. Craddock; also some Downs belonging to Lord
Radnor and Sir Thomas Throckinorton. Mr. John
Weall had some prime Downs and Gloucester sent
by Mr. Rowland, Mr. White, and Mr. Oakley, chiefly
from Hertfordshire. Some remarkably good Hamp-
shire Downs, bred by Mr. Canning, of Devizes, and
the Earl of Darley, were exhibited by Mr. Charles -
Burrell, who had also some very prime Norfolk
half-breds. Mr. Eland disposed of several heavy Lin-
coins, at and over £5 each. They were forwarded by Mr.
Chatterton, Mr. North, and Mr. Henley, the latter of
Croft, Messrs. Lintoll and Son brought forward some
very good Hampshire Downs belonging to Mr. Paull, Mr.
Fokes, and Mr. Tory; likewise several good sheep for-
warded by Mr. Cox, near St. Alban's, Mr. Sanders, of

Guildford. Mr. Dodd exhibited a fair number of Hamp.
shire Downs in good condition. Mr. Ben. Weal] had
some good sheep from Berkshire and Oxfordshire. He
likewise offered some remarkably good pigs

ISTRESS

THE DISTRESSED OPERATIVES AND
4,, CHRISTMAS

There appears to be a general desire through-
'out the country to make the Christmas week
Of 1862 a demonstrative one by doubling the
subscriptions to the distressed operatives in
Lancashire and bringing the full force of public
sympathy to bear upon the field of famine.
In concert with this movement we feel confi-
dent the working men and trades in general
will act as becomes them, and that all who
have not subscribed will hesitate no longer,
and those who have, will double their subscrip-
tion. Christmas in Lancashire will be robbed
of many of its old asBociations by the bitter—
ness of present sufferings, but every effort
ought to be made, and we are sure will be
made, to cause our destitute brethren to feel
as little as possible the disparity of fortune
which now exists between us and them.
Working men of England double your subscrip-
tions and permit us to have the pleasure in
Christmas week of announcing a large sum
through the BEE-HIVE. Forward them to the
Treasurer of the London Working Men's
Central Relief Committee.

Neft week being Christmas week, it will be
requisite that all Subscriptions, to obtain an
acknowledgment in the Bm-HivE on Satur-
day next, should be sent to the Treasurer, on
or before Wednesday night next.

'e tt-th

[REGISTERED FOR TRANSMISSION ABROAD.

SATURDAY, DECEXIBER 20, 1862.

SUMMARY.
The Greeks, under all discouragements,
proceed with their project to elect Prince Alfred
as their king; and meantime they are said to
have got their reward in a promise of the
lonian Islands from the British Government.
These islands may be a good, bad, or indiffer-
tout bargain to us, but they should not be

given away without the consent of the Par—
liament. G-overnment now stretch the prero-
gative of the -Crown too tight.
The :Emperor Alexander, of Russia, continues
at Moscow, meeting deputations now of the
nobility, and next of the peasantry, and he
employs these opportunities in urging both
parties to be good, that is to say, obedient
subjects, not avaricious of more reforms.

Gold, at the receipt in New York of the
President's Message, had gone up to 34
premium, receding to 32, where it remained on
the despatch of the mail.
Subscriptions for the relief of the distress
in Lancashire had been made in New York to
a considerable sum, chiefly by British mer-
chants; but by no means from those alone, for
munificent sums had been given by some of
the American houses. The local demands on
private charity were unexampled, and, there-
fore, the assistance from that quarter must be
accepted as coming out of much suffering.
The French forces are said to have made a
successful advance towards Mexico, although
experiencing resistance on the road, but the
Mexicans reserve their great defence for their
capital.

The Federal army of the Potomac remained
betweeu Acquia Creek and the Rapahannock
at the date of the last despatches, checked
by the flooded river in their assault on Frede-
ricksburgh. The latter place may be captured
ere now, but its possession will not materially
promote the march on to Richmond. General
Banks had left New York with a maritime
expedition comprising 30,000 to 40,000 men,
probably intended to act against Richmond
from the South and East.

The papers by the last Indian mail contain
reports of the proceedings at another great
meeting at Calcutta, called to adopt further
measures for the relief of the distress in Lan-
cashire. It is described as the largest and
most influential meeting that had ever been
collected in Calcutta. The G-overnor. General
of India had ordered the balance of the Indian
famine relief fund to be paid over to the
committees for the relief of the distress in our
cotton districts.

Cholera has been very fatal in some parts of
India, and several officers of the 93rd Regi-
ment, including the colonel, have died from
that disease at Poonah, where a Jewish mer-
chant, M. D. Sassoo, has just given-215,000
for the erection of a hospital.
A West Indian mail has arrived without
much important intelligence: and from
Western Africa the mail brings very little in-
formation. The Government were adopting
active measures for the improvement of
Lagos, their latest acquisition on the West
Coast.

The capabilities and prospects of British
Columbia continues to furnish materials for
a sharp dispute between those who do well
there and others who fail.

The Edmund's Main has now been flooded,
and in the process a second and fatal
explosion occurred, without causing any further
destruction of life, but involving the loss of
much more property. The recovery of the
bodies, and the resumption of employment in
the colliery, are not expected for several
months.

The number of persons still requiring relief
in Lancashire increases; although some autho-
rities now expect that the distress has reached
its maximum; but that no important reductiop
in its circle will be effected before March or
April. The sales of cotton at Liverpool now
exceed the arrival, and are reducing the stock.
A small quantity of Australian cotton has
been sold in London at 2s. to 3s. per lb. No
doubt is now entertained that Australia can
supply cotton not only equal but superior to
the celebrated Sea Islands.

We regret to notice the spread of similar
distress in the silk and ribbon trades around
Coventry, where the necessity of some measure
of relief has been acknowledged by the resident
landowners, and a considerable sum has been
collected through the instrumentality of Lord
Leigh.
All markets are dull, and Will now remain
so until the New Year. At the great Christ-
mas market here the number of cattle ex-
hibited was greater than in any former year.

CO-OPERATIVES OF LANCASHIRE
IN DISTRESS.

We have inserted a reply from Professor
BEESLY to the Rev. Mr. VERITY'S note in our
last number in which Mr. BEESLY requests pre-
cise information of the addresses and names of
any co-operatives or trades unionists who have
been refused relief during the present crisis in
Lancashire. Few men deserve more considera-
tion from the working classes than Professor
BESSLY, and as few will employ to greater ad-
vantage than him any information that may be
placed in his hands. We have endeavoured,
like our correspondent, to employ this great
calamity as a means of softening' asperities that
occasionally arise between different classes,
and of bringing good out of evil, by
raising up out of kindness and sym-
pathy for patience in suffering, an endur-
ing and permanent union. We cannot doubt
that in the relief of half a million of persons
errors of judgment and of opinion have been
committed; but, generally, we aso believe that
the funds raised by the public, And entrusted
to the committees, have been distributed in an
impartial
_manner.

Parochial funds cannot, under the existing
poor law, be employed to relieve a highly
deserving class of sufferers. The co-operative
societies had, in some districts, amassed a con-
siderable property before this crisis commenced
in their history. - The scrip, or shares, were
chiefly held by operatives of whom a part were
engaged on their own and some in other
works. The latter class, when they were
thrown out of employment, were obliged to
borrow upcn the security of; or to sell, their co-
operative property. They had no resources, for
their savings were placed in the co-operative
mill, or store, and as times became more
perilous, while cotton rose without carrying up
yarns, the spinners engaged in the co-operative
mills have been in some cases cast out of em-
ployment, and then found their scrip and
shares reduced to a nominal value. They have
taken a risk, and lost in the struggle. Many
other persons suffer in the same way. Ro-
mances of suffering in trade are many; often
distressing—sometimes attended with even
more absorbing interest than the romances
which occupy the pages of our cheap journals.
The frequency of this class of suffering does
not relieve its severity; and as the co-opera-
tive movement has been regarded with interest
by many classes, spoken of by public men in
and out of Parliament, in the most favourable
manner, and promises in its course to solve
some social problems, in addition to its elevat-
ing influences on the operatives, we hope many
persons in London will come to the rescue of
these co-operatives in distress.

The guardians of the ratepayers could not,
consistently with the parliamentary regulations
for their guidance, assist co-operatives until
their corporate property was sold and spent.
The state of the law cannot be questioned, and

it is not necessary here to discuss the policy
of its provision:. The absence of elasticity in
its plan may be regretted, and yet 'cannot now
be supplied; so that while we consider the
Lancashire case, and similar cases, to be
exceptional in their very nature, yet we are
unable to complain of the administrators of the
law, if they adhere to its conditions and terms.

The voluntary funds raised to supplement
local rates are altogether different, are elastic
in their purposes, are to be distributed in
equity rather than to be laid out according to
statute; and from them therefore some assist-
ance may be expected to the co-operators.
We do not believe that among the multi-
tude who have given of their means, from the
mite to one thousand pounds, in order to
relieve this distress, many can be found who
would make it conditional that saving and
thrifty persons, who have struggled hard to
show the power of self-denial in improving
the condition of the operative classes, should
be obliged to part with their earnings, not at
their cost, or their proper value, but to fling
them away in a drugged market, before any
relief be afforded to them. We are confident
that this was not the intention of those persons
who have piled up the gigantic fund for the
still more gigantic necessities of Lancashire;
and we are equally confident that the co-
operatives do not generally desire mere relief,
but would rrefer loans, to prevent the
sacrifice of their property, at a nominal
price far beneath its worth. Assistance
on this condition is within the power and pur-
pose of the relief committees; but if the
members entertain a different opinion, and
think that they should not give or lend money
on the security of co-operative scrip or shares,
we have reached a chapter in this Lancashire
history, when the distress of the co-operatives
may be prudently and safely introduced.
We expect no general relief from an improve-
ment in business much before April or May;
although as stocks wear out the prices of
material and productions must generally come
more nearly than now into harmony. The
relief funds are several weeks in advance of
their present engagements, and we hear that
the Governor General of India has authorised
the balance of the -Indian famine fund, amount-
ing from £60,000 to £BO,OOO, to be drawn out
for Lancashire.

The working classes of London may now
appropriate their means, at least for a time, to
the relief of co-operative distress, and the as-
sistance of those trade societies whose mem-
bers have endeavoured to stem the adverse
current by their own strength. The funds of
some of these societies are entirely exhausted.
The value of the co-operative shares is lament-
ably reduced. In pleading against the
dissolution of societies that have nobly
struggled to vindicate the independence of
their members, and against the sale of co-
operative property at a period when it is
impossible to realise one-fourth of its value,
we discharge a duty only less urgent than
advocating subscriptions to meet daily wants.
The ruin of these organizations would cast
society backwards for many years, would be
a great blow to every scheme for its elevation,
and the memory of the cotton crisis, and its
consequences, would cling to every plan, and
every proposal, for the advancement of the
operative classes by their own economy in
Lancashire and elsewhere through many years.

CAPITAL, COLONIES, AND LABOUR.
We stated some time ago that the people of
this country require the adoption of some dis-
tinct line of policy respecting the colonies which
the late Sir Robert Peel and the Earl of Durham
designated our working mens' domains. Their
opinion was never adopted in the legislation of
Parliament; and the "domain " was given
away for nothing to the settlers in the colonies
who had paid for and improved part of the land,
and had value for their money and their work.
This course was adopted only towards the
solonies under constitutional government, for
the crown colonies continue to be the domains
of the people!
The British American colonies have used
their land funds in payment of roads, general
improvements and in discharging the common
burdens of the revenue.
The African and Australian colonies, but
especially the latter, have employed a large por-
tion of their revenue froM land, in defraying the
cost of emigration. In this manner they have
made "the domain of the working classes of
Britain "in some measure useful to these
classes; although the rules for aiding emigra-
tion adopted by the Government Commis-
sioners have not been drawn up in the most
favourable manner for home interests.
The British-American colonists do not ex-
hibit any churlish desire.to keep this colossal
land or its proceeds exclusively for their own
purposes; but on the contrary, excellent
blocks of their soil are offered on admirable
terms. The Canadian legislature give a hun-
dred acres' block of land on the Ottawa to any
settler for nothing. This plan does not exhibit
selfishness but ignorance of home society. An
agricultural labourer derives no good from the
free distribution of land on the Ottawa, because
he cannot get there; and he has not
capital to improve the land, sow the seed,
and support himself and his family until
it grow and ripen, if he were there.
We suggested the co-operation of capital and
labour on the soil, and no question need be
raised regarding its quality or quantity. Land
adequate to employ a population of six or
seven hundred millions, and probably a
thousand millions, is included within the
British Empire. It waits for cultivation, and
the cultivators wiat for it; but a chasm
exists between the land and the men that can
only be bridged by capital. Money cannot be
expected without some return and good
security, The capitalist has his money, and
the labourer has his skill and strength, each
weak when alone, but strong when both to-
gether.

rProsperity depends on thiee conditions—
first, the material, and of that, land, abund-
ance exists at our disposal as our national
property; second, labour and skill, but both
are abundant, and looking for employment;
third, capital, and money is plentiful for a
limited return on fair security.
These three conditions only require to be
associated to make prosperity.
Another union is perhaps requisite in order
to produce that of capital, labour, and land, on
fair terms for all—the union of commercial
principles with philanthropy. It is not re-
quisite for more than the first, second, or third
operation. After each successful report of any
new project imitations spring up. A dividend
of ten per cent, on one scheme, however
limited its field might be, would secure the
formation of twenty schemes, for success in
any path soon makes it a beaten road.
Land is the basis of society, and commerce
follolvs agriculture and manufactures at some
distance. For some time past praiseworthy
efforts have been made to put heart and vigour
into our agricultural population by the im-
provement of their cottages, and rewards to
meritorious labourers; but these plans may

be excellent, yet they are not equal to the
object.

Rope is an essential ingredient of activity
and intelligence among any population, but our
agricultural labourers are left often hopeless.
They cannot advance in this country to the
position of employers, in their own department
of life, except in a few isolated cases, not de-
pendiug on the proceeds of labour. The
colonies could afford the agricultural 'labourer
land on low terms, and capitalists might supply
the means of their support until the land were
made productive, on its security, in addition to
such security as character always supplies.
We advise the formation of a company on a
small scale, experimental perhaps, to assist
emigrants, not only in passages, but in'the im-
provement of their farms, on the security of the
soil and the buildings. The operation would
be simplified by treating with one of the colo-
nies for some legislative privileges,"respecting
securities and titles. The conditions of assistance
might properly include some payment from the
applicant towards his own passage and that of
his family. The payment must be either ,
small or prohibitive, to many; but, if confined
within narrrow limits, it would form a certifi-
cate of economical habits, or the esteem of the
applicant's neighbours.

-71'he chief object of this scheme is, however,
to render emigration to one of our colonies,
and a farm there, the hope and the possible
object of an agricultural labourer. The pur-
pose infers the loan to him of the necessary
means for getting to the land, living on the
land for a time, clearing a few acres, and put-
ting up the absolutely requisite buildings.
The security for the repayment of the loan
consists in the applicant's character, partly
provided for, in the improvements effected on
his land, in its gradually increasing value, and
of course in the soil.

As the company would necessarily have an
agency in the colonies where the advances were
made, they would be given in monthly or
quarterly sums, and some provision would thus
be afforded for their application to the improve-
ment of the property. When repayment corn-
menced that also would be taken by instalments
and not in a lump, so as gradually to extinguish
a debt that had been gradually and beneficially
formed.

A homestead might pass away from a family
by the early death of its head; if this company,
his creditors, were not extremely indulgent;
but provision could be made against that
calamity to the family or embarrasment to the
company, by a policy on his life, not neces-
sarily equal to the advance, although that
might be easily arranged; but sufficiently
large to give his widow or his children a
substantial interest in the family farm.
While this plan would assist agricultural
labourers, we must remember that 'a district of
farmers require tradesmen, who might be
assisted on the same principles. This co-
operation i of capital and labour, would give to
the first a fair return upon a fair security;
and to the second, means of securing perman-
ent employment, and a permanent home on
equitable terms. The hope of independence
would thus be made the heritage of many in-
dustrious men, to whom at present it is un-
known.

This co-operation would extend from the
original parties in the transaction to all colonial
and home interests. The colonists are our
best customers; . and we can never have
too many men on limited means at home
turned into independent although colonial
farmers. All interests in the state would
be served by the triple alliance between
capital, labour and land; Which would elevate
many families and lower none, but pro-
mote the equality of independence .by taking
nothing from any person, while even adding
to the value of all existing property.
Our purpose, is, however, very modest and
experimental. A small company and a small
capital would adequately test the scheme,
although from small operations we cannot look
for large returns.

PRESIDENT LINCOLN'S MESSAGE.
THE Times says that President LINCOLN'S
message to Congress recalls his proclamation
of emancipation to the slaves in the rebel
States on New Year's day. The statement is
erroneous, for the President refers in his
message to Federal, and in his proclamation to
Confederate States. To the former he suggests
emancipation, during the interval between
1862 and 1890, or twenty-eight years. He
offers compensation in United States bonds,
bearing interest, but the rate is not fixed.
As this scheme requires the consent of two-
thirds of the legislature, and then of three-
fourths of the States, we shall not probably see
its adoption. Although in twenty-eight years
an adequate margin is afforded for these '
operations. It is a legislative measure not
connected with the military proclamation of
January- next.

articles.title: GARMENT DYERS.
articles.text:
THE GARMENT DYERS.

' We have received from T. G COLLING, " Ip.te
Secretary of the Garment Dyers' Short-time
Agitation," a letter in reply to Mr. HARTWELL'S
remarks in our last on "The Ingratitude of
Working Men." Mr. HARTWELL complained •
that as the Dyers wanted our assistance at one
period of the year in their measures, they had
advertised their collection for the relief of the
distressed operatives of Lancashire, not in
this, but in Lloyd's paper. Mr. COLLING
admits the assistance rendered, but says that
as a business matter the advertisement was sent
to the quarter which he thought had the largest
circulation. As a business matter no necessity
existed for sending the advertisement to any
quarter; and as to circulation, Mr. HARTWELL
must be correct in assuming that ours must be
the larger circulation among garment dyers;
unless we suppose that he is also correct in
supposing that they are not very grateful as a
trade.

PROFESSOR BEESLY AND THE REV. MR.
VERITY ON RELIEF TO CO-OPERATIVES
AND UNIONISTS.

TO THE EDITOR OP THE "BEE-RITE."

SIB,-Mr. Verity does not give what- I asked
for—namely, names, dates, and circumstances. I
gather from a paragraph in the Observer that the
relief committees have refused to supply funds to
trades unions and co-operative societies, but not
(so far as I see at present) to relieve unionists and
co-operators. The distinction is perfectly plain.
Unionists cannot expect to be relieved on different
terms, or in a different way from others. If that
is Mr' Verity's case, it is a pity he did not state it
plainly. I ask him to prove it, and he merely
answers that he is "in possession of proofs," that
"he will undertake to prove," &c., which is a very
different thing. As t 3 his assertion "that paupers
are not relieved, and that relief is not sufficient," it
has nothing to do with the question. I still repeat
my demand. Prove to me that individual unionists
or co-operatives have been refused aid when they
needed it, because they were unionists and co-
operators, and I will denounce the iniquity as
loudly as any one. I wilt find means to sift the
facts if Mr. Verity will only furnish them.—,
I am, Bce., E. S. BEESLY.
University Hall, Gordon-square, Dec. q 6.

THE LONDON SEAMSTRESSES AND THE
LANCASHIRE
.SPINNERS.
TO TRH EDITOR OF THE " BEE-HIVE."

SlR,—The exertions made in some quarters to
redeem the clothes of the Lancashire operatives
have been eminently successful. They have shown
already how easily all the difficulties on this sub-
ject might be surmounted. It is, therefore, the
utterest folly to go on making clothes when they can
be had made and ready, and fitting thoroughly, for
less money than would be needed to buy new cloth,
whfle all the time required to make the clothes would
be saved; and this is a question of time, for the
fresh of this day may be turned into frost of to-
morrow.
If any step of this kind be approved, it must
be now taken. The public have not a long time to
consider, and discuss, and talk, and think over
their duty. Whatever is to be done requires to be
done now, and not at another time.
Depend upon this that we shall soon hear of the
London sufferings; therefore, what is to be done
must be done with knowledge and prudence. A.
Peer of the realm is advertising the sale of ready-
made clothes, shirts, I suppose, and such like, in a
bazaar of London. He is chairman of a committee
for the relief of Lancashire spinning girls. This
work is their work. By buying it the public are
expected to contribute some thing towards their
support. At the risk of being considered hard-
hearted and narrow minded, I object to this relief
at the expense of London stitching girls. Have
they had too much employment, or too good wages,
that they should be exposed, at the commencement
of the winter, to a dire competition with the bene-
volence and the charitable subscriptions of the
metropolis ? If they give, as some have given out
of poor earnings, a portion to support their
northern sisterhood, is it becoming to bring work
paid for by general contributions into competition
with them? Not for .a moment do I believe
that the nobleman in question is allying
himself with the slop shops, or those
of them that press down wage-, in order to deprive
our London sewing girls of some part of their pre-
sent wages, but that is the inevitable result of per-
sistence in his scheme. I have no wish to believe
that he. desires to deprive industrious females in
London of work, but no other conclusion can come
of his plan of relieving Lancashire, a plan that
should at once be abandoned, and should not have
been proposed. The effect of these projects is
obvious. The female operatives here will have
less wages and less work; and the work done here
for the benefit of the poor by the Dorcas societies,
(never too much) will be given to another quarter,
for an impolitic purpose that should be altogether
unnecessary. If I have written aught that any one
may construe into a light word, regarding our'
Dorcas societies, allow me to put that right. I
believe them to consist of persons, young and old,
who cheerfully give money and time to help others
in one manner, that is to say, t'o clothe the poor.
And on these unpaid labourers who manifest their
faith by their works, may many a blessing fall on
their way through the world.
I have been charged, in perfect innocence on my
part, with making light of our Dorcas Societies in
my last letter. No other idea could be more
unfounded, however my parentheses and Aurora
Borealis-like way of writing—excepting the
brilliancy of these casual lights, and only appropri-
ating their characteristic of not being very steady—
may give it a foot to stand upon. lam so far from
desiring to take an inch from the ell of estimation
in which I hope the public hold these Dorcas
Societies, that I would rather add a foot of good
measure thereto.
Apostolical succession may be a doubtful ques-
tion, but there can be none respecting the succession
of good women from Joppa to London, although
perhaps, it comes alonc, with the memory of weary
tapestry working in the middle ages.
If we only could bring all our population into one
right and unselfish habit, we all should be the
happier therefore, the habit of giving some little
skill, time, work to the general good. It is a
grand thought that many thousands of our counttit'S
female population give a little of their life, that is,
of their strength and their time, in each week
without fee or reward, to somebody's work. It is
that they only know it to be somebody's work
which gives beauty to the business. It is work
perhaps for some little child, born into cheerless
cold realities, and the worker has never seen
may never see, the creature who is to
be clothed and warmed. Years will come
and go, as this year is going, and the worker
will "fade as a leaf "—the leaf of her life will wither
away, and the night to her will come when no
woman can work. Her memory and name may be
forgotten, when the grass covers her, and the leaves
of autumn fall, or the daisies of spring bud over
her; but always and ever will live this labour done
for somebody unknown yet not unloved, for is it
not to one of the least of these little ones?
Last Saturday evening, I noticed in a London
street three large spirit shops extremely close to
each other, so close that the population there were
evidently snffering from habitual want of refresh-
ment, a thirsty people, ever keeping Lent on salted
stock fish. In one of the houses the men had
a majority, so far as could be seen through
the open door, and were in a row regarding two
public men of Italy, Garibaldi and the Pope, while
one young woman, apparently married though, was
endeavouring to cut figures eight in the air with a
sold ier's " switch," inquiring " Who's the Pope?
what's the Pope? I should like to know that?'
Now, she was not sober enough to be told that; or
to appreciate the information if any one had entered
on the history of the Pontiff and his ecclesiastical
office. It was not possible to notice the scene
without a thought of the wretched homes and the
pitiable children of these people : their own selfish-
ness burned into their very hearts ; and their own
peace so sacrificed for a momentary excitement that
the first case resembled the idea which one might
form of the infernal region in a good humour; and
the second of that place turned back to its more
natural state.
Our Dorcas societies are just at the moral anti-
podes of this selfishness which, at any cost, gratifies
a depraved and morbid taste. So far, therefore,
nobody can know without liking them. They are
human; imperfect therefore—improveable there-
fore; but they are in the onward, upward line, doing
good very quietly, very laboriously, and usefully.
All this writing is the washing out of a joke;
which may be called a mistake by gome. I wish
all other mistakes might be as easily washed away.
The benevolent labours of the Dorcas societies
never compete with those of professional seam-
stresses, whose number in London is a multitude ;
whose labours are severe; whose wages are
never high; whose interests have been assailed by
machines that pay no tax on tea or sugar, and
need no clothing, and whose means of living are
now threatened by the rivalry of the charitable.
At the cost of any misapprehension, this mode of
helping buyers from the earnjugs of the operatives
must be exposed and resisted. It is not necessary
for the poor of Lancashire ; it is cruel to a great
indhstry of London. It is no more free trade than
the partial payment of wages out of parochial rates
is free trade. It is the conversion of charity into
gall; it is the turning of good-heartedness into
oppression ; a robbery done with charitable funds.
Those who have tried to live by sewing and ,
stitching in London, know best the difficulty of
living well in that way, and it is unnecessary to
increase the labour by taking from its rewards, for
already the work is more than many females can
long endure. 'EVELYN LE.

NEW YORK, Dec. 12.
The Housr! of Representatives has passed a bill in-
demnifying President Lincoln for suspending the writ
of habeas corpus.

It is semi-officially announced that the Federal
Government has received information that France will
not further prosecute her proposal for an armistice or
mediation.

A battle has occurred at Fayetteville, Arkansas, be-
tween 7,000 Federals and 24,000 Confederates. The
fight lasted all day, until the Federals were reinforced
by 5,000 men, and fell upon the Confederate rear.
The Confederates were then repulsed, and retreated
across the Boston Mountains, the Federals remaining
in possession of the field. The Federal loss is stated at
1,000; that of the Confederates at 2,000 men.
The Confederates have again been repulsed in an
attack upon Cane Hill, Arkansas.
It is rumoured that the Federal expedition under
General Banks has been landed at Petersburg, Vir-
ginia.

General Burnside having succeeded in constructing
bridges across the Rappahannock, the Federals crossed
and drove the Confederates out of the city to their line
of works outside Fredericksburg. Since then no
further news has been received.

articles.title: ITALY.
articles.text:
ITALY.

Tunny, Dec. 17, Evening.
In the Chamber of Deputies to-day the Minister of
the Interior stated that the Government, in acceding
to the proposition for an inquiry into brigandage, has
by no means intended to encroach upon the privileges
of the executive. The Government was determined
to make every effort to repress brigandage and prevent
its recurrence in the coming spring. The principal
object which it had in view was the re-establishment
of the authority of the law.

Dr. Bertani proposed that the Chamber should declare
that it regarded the arrest of the deputies at Naples as
an offence against the majesty of the sovereign parlia-
ment. Signor Rattazzi demanded a full discussion of
the subject, but the Chamber adopted the order of the
day.

TURIN, Dec. 18.
The Opfnioize of to-day asserts that 111. de Sarfiges,
in an interview with the President of the Council,
touched upon the Roman question. The Minister is
said to have replied that the present policy of France
renders it little probable that fresh negotiations would
bring about a satisfactory solution. It is also asserted
that the Chevalier Nigra, Italian Ambassador at Paris,
has made a similar statement to M. Drouyn de l'Huys.
In the Chamber of Deputies, the committee of inquiry
into the question of brigandage was appointed. Baron
Ricasoli and General Bixio are among the members of
the committee.

DEC. 12.
The Italian Government respectfully declines further
negociations with France respecting the Roman ques-
tion at present.—The Government entertains uneasi—
ness about the Emancipation Societies; they remain
dissolved till a right of association is established by
law.—The Muralist party has been utterly unsuccessful
at Naples.

LISBON, Dec. 12 (via France).
A terrific accident has occurred on the Eastern

THE YELVEI?TON 314RRIAGE CASE...

EDINBURGH, Friday Night.
The decision in the Yelverton marriage case was
given to-day by the Court of Session. The Court,
by a majority of two to one, declared Theresa Long-
worth or Yelverton to be the lawful wife of Major
Yelverton according to the law of Scotland. The
judges in favour of the legality of the marriage were
Lord Curriehill and Lord lleag. The Lord President
was unfavourable. The judgment was received with
great cheering both inside and outside the court. The
only step which can now be taken to bring this re-
markable case to a final conclusion is that of an appeal
to the House of Lords.

TRADE S' INTELLICrENCE.

THE DISPUTE IN THE SHIP-BUILDING

TRADE.

It will be in the recollection of our readers that on
the breaking out of the dispute between the Chatham
Dockyard authorities and the iron ship builders at
work upon the Achilles, the Times, true to its in •
stincts, took part against the workmen, heaping all
sorts of calumny upon them, ridiculing the idea that
wooden men were not as capable of building an iron
ship as the iron men, and • stating that the
authorities need be put to no inconvenience. After a few
days the Times went further still, and wound up a
furious and frothy article, 'full of sound and fury, sig-
nifying nothing,' by saying, that not only 'was the
work of the wooden men already equal to that of the
iron men,.but it was expected in a few weeks to sur-
pass it.' All practical men bad a hearty laugh at
this statement. Even our friends, the shipwrights
themselves, could not help smiling at the rubbish thus
uttered by their newly-found friend. The Times, ever
consistent in its inconsistency, has now gone on the
Opposite tack, from what cause we know not, but it is
evidently eating the leek.' On Thursday morning,
under the head of Naval Intelligence, appeared the
following paragraph :
' The further progress in bending and preparing the
armour plates for the Royal Sovereign at Portsmouth
is put a stop to for a few days, owing to a portion of
the travelling tubular crane having given out. The
accident is, fortunately, but trifling, and might have
happened under any management; but it shows what
may follow if the present course is persisted in. The
shipwright department is doing good service in the con-
struction of our iron-cased ships, but if proficiency in
driving and clinching an iron rivet is thought by
the Admiralty to be a sufficient qualification for taking
charge of and working machines of unusual power, and,
to them, of novel design, in preference to men having a
professional knowledge of the structure and manipulation of
metals, the ultimate cost of our ships' armour-plates
will be dear indeed. As an annexe to the steam fac-
tory departments, the full powers of the machinery
would have been brought into use. Under present ar-
rangents matters will soon be brought to a dead lock,
our ships will be kept waiting for their plates, and a.
heavy bill for damages will probably have to be pre-
-seated. There is plenty to do for both the iron and
wood men of Portsmouth yard, and if ths Admiralty
confine each branch to their own proper duties, the public
- purse will considerably benefit by such an order, and
the Royal Sovereign and. Alfred be much earlier afloat
than they can be under presen,t arrangements.'
This is cool, being exactly the reverse of what the
Times has' said. on previous occasions. The iron ship
builders, and their warmest advocates, have never said
more. All that they have contended is, that men
without the professional knowledge of the structure
and manipulation of metals,' could not work iron with
the same facility and cheapness as those who had that
knowledge. The Times now confirms it. All that
they asked for was that the Admiralty should confine
each branch to their own proper duties.' The Times
now says this is necessary; or the public purse will
suffer, and the completion of the vessels indefinitely
postponed. The very .words the iron ship builders
• used. at the commeneemeni i3,f the dispute.! Are we to
; •.- late the Times on awakening to common sense,
or e some hidden motive in the background
' . e latter. We have no faith in the Times or
- its hone: .

THE LONDON BOOKBINDERS' STRIKE.
The following letter has been sent by Mr. Bone
to the editor of the Stationer, which appeared in
the last number for Dec. 10 :
We beg to hand you the following particulars con-
nected with a dispute which has. arisen .between our-
selves and the men employed by us, and which un-
happily has tetMinated in at strike. Abob.t a fortnight
ago we set up a steam 'cutting machine for dividing
sheets, advertisements, plates, &c., in order to expedite
the work in the women's dewtment, and placed ,a
man at it who has been with filr.itome years, but who
has not served 7 years' apprenticeship as a bookbinder,
-Which the men assume to be .requiaite for mastering
the intricacies of so simple a machine. When we in-
form you that there is scarcely a shop in London or
the country where such a thing as employing skilled
• labour for this process is thought of, we are only
telling you what every one knows. Again, another of
the reasons alleged for their present conduct is this.
We prepare our work by,. otheNs than journeymen—
that is, we employ porters to pump up the hydraulic
presses in place of men who have servedltheir seven
years' apprenticcship: Surely in these clays of im-
elovement we ought to advance, and not to retrograde.
We offered to arbitrate the matter, and abide by any
decision that might be awarded, without avail.
W. BONE and Sox.
'London, 187, Fleet-street, Dec. 4, 1862;
In reply to the above we beg to say-
1. That the work at tlio steam-cutting machine, re-
ferred to by him as being a process in which the em-
ployment of skilled labour is not thought of' either in
town or country; that in scarcely a shop in London is
other than skilled labour employed thereat—the neces-
sity of which Mr. Bone must by this time be aware,
as the porter has already spoiled a quantity of plates'
in consequence of this want of skill.
2. There was never any objection to the employment
of porters to pump up the hydraulic presses. There
was certainly an objection to the work being prepared
by gangs of boys instead of skilled workmen, but that
objection was withdrawn; although in no other large
shop did such practice prevail.
3. There was no offer of arbitration. The under-
signed, accompanied by another, waited upon Mr.
Bone with a view, if possible, to heal the existing dif-
ferences. Mr. Bone, however, refused to hear a single
word. He certainly gave as a reason why he would
hear nothing, that if any communication were made
by proxy on the part of his men, that he also ought to
confer by proxy; but he expressed no wish for an
arbitration.
Upon the subject of arbitration, as well, indeed,
as on many others, Mr. Bone's% ideas sebm to be
peculiar to himself. To a deputation of his men on
this subject, he said he bad no objection to appoint
representatives to meet the same number on part of
the men, to treat upon matters; but,' continued he,
if any question arises upon the porter at the machine '
—the only point remaining in dispute—' I would
sooner shut up my shop than agree to any modifica-
tion.' Mr. Bone had certainly a right to refuse all
compromise but he has no right afterwards. to say
that 'he offered to arbitrate the matter, and to abide
_ l'Y any decision that might be awarded.' Is it pos-
sible that he cannot see that what he called an offer to
arbitrate, was absolutely a refusal to do so? This,
however, was all the arbitration he offered.
Mr. Bone, has expressed his intention of employ-
ing :unlimited boy and porter labour wherever it can
be Introduced, and to discharge the skilled book-
binders as soon as they had taught the porters and
boys their work. It need not be said that this was
attempted to avoid paying the regular wages of the
trade. Skilled labour would be employed only when
absolutely needful, and then supplanted whenever a
porter, or a man at miters' wages, could be got to
perform the work. The constant desire to gain by
this practice being the avowed intention of Mr. Bone,
the men saw in it only the alternative of leaving
at once/ or waiting to see which should be last
devoured; and they preferred the former.
T. J. DUNNING.
No. 5, Raquet-court, Fleet-street, Dec. 16.

• We understand that out of the 32 members of the
London Consolidated Lodge, who left Mr. Bone's
employ, last week, there are only 12 on the society
books, the remaining 20 having obtained employment.
Mr. Bone's shop or ' factory ' is, as might have been
expected, in much admired disorder.' May it con-
tinue so, while he acts thus unjustly towards a body of
respectable tradesmen.

articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 20, 1862.

TRADES UNIONISTS' MANHOOD SUF-
RAGE AND VOTE BY BALLOT ASSOCIA-
TION.

A numerous meeting of the members and friends of
this association was held at the Brown Bear, Broad-
street, Bloomsbury, on Tuesday evening last, Mr.
Eglington in the chair. Correspondence, favourable to
the movement, was read from Bristol, Birmingham,
Sheffield, &c.
The secretary, Mr. Fa,cey, read a paper on the
Suffrage,' reviewing it as it exists on the restrictive
and exclusive basis of properly, and arguing that the
present electoral laws practically ignore human intelli-
gence, learning, and genius; that they cripple the
political capacities of all classes; that they engender
and spread class prejudices and animosities, and en-
danger the safety of property; that, by depriving the
great masses of any representation of their sympathies,
aspirations, aud interests, they prevent the government
acquiring such a knowledge of the physiology of labour
and capital, and their relations and interests as is
necessary for the proper development of the industry
and resources of these kingdoms; and that they are un-
just, inasmuch as, by the uncertain tenure of property,
the present holder of the franchise may undeservingly
be deprived of it, and, because they compel the un-
recognised and unrepresented majority to obey laws
made by the minority, without their consent, and to
pay taxes and imposts over the levying of which they
have no control. kThe paper discussed the several
schemes of franchise proposed by various parties, show-
ing their impolicies and insufficiencies, and concluded
with powerful arguments in support of manhood suf-
frage, as a natural right, as an expediency, and as a
policy.
An earnest And interesting discussion followed the
reading of the paper, in which Messrs. Waverly,
Petherbridge, Beats, Rowe, and several others, took
part.
An unanimous vote of thanks was given to Mr.
Facey, for reading the paper, and the meeting was ad-
journed until Tuesday, January 13, 1863, when Mr.
Petherbridge will read a paper on The Ballot: the
necessity for obtaining it, and the advantages of its use.'

WORKMEN'S PRESENTATION TO MR.

H. G. REID, OF EDINBURGH.

On Thursday night week Mr. H. Gilzean Reid,
formerly editor of the .Edinburgh, News, was entertained
at a fruit soiree by &number of his friends in Buchanan's
Temperance Hetel. The chair was occupied by Mr.
J. Ogilvie; and amongst those present were the Rev.
Dr. Begg, and several representatives of Trades Unions
and Co-operative Societies. In the course of the even-
ing Mr. Colville (manager of the Edinburgh Co-
operative Building Co.) presented Mr. Reid, in name
of the working men present, with a massive gold Albert
chain and a writing desk. The desk, which was a
handsome and beautifully finished article, bore the fol-
lowing inscription Presented to Mr. H. Gilzean
Reid, along with a gold Albert chain, by a.
few working men, as an acknowledgment of ser-
vices rendered in connection with the nine hours'
movement co-operation, and other movements for the
social and intellectual advancement of the industrial
classes.' In presenting this testimonial, Mr. Colville
made particular reference to the prominent part taken
by Mr. Reid in advancing the interests of the working
classes, and the readiness with which he tendered his
advice to them on all occasions of difficulty. Mr.
Reid replied in suitable terms, and gave a history of
the nine hours' movement in Edinburgh, and the rise
of the Co-operative Building Company. The meeting
was afterwards addressed by the Rev. Dr. Begg, who,
after referring to the deep interest taken by Mr. Reid
in every movement calculated to promote the welfare
of working men, spoke at some length on the advan-
tages of co-operation to the industrial classes. The
co-operative movement, so far as it had progressed in
Edinburgh, had been attended with complete success;
and there was no reason to doubt that it would continue
to prosper, and raise working men both in their social
and moral conditions. Short addresses and songs
fokinwed, which rendered the entertainment of a most
pleasant and harmonious nature.

THE SENTENCE ON THE LATE SECRETARY
OF THE PAINTERS.
TO THE EDITOR OP THE BEEHIVE.

Sta,—As you will in due course report the deferred
sentence at the Middlesex Sessions on the late Secre-
tary of the Painters' Association, the subject matter
may induce a series of reflections. We have little for
congratulation, much for regret. We az; humbled by
the fact that one of our members, who, by virtue of the
office' he held, should have been beyond suspicion, is
nowfstiffering the penalty of the law for defrauding his
fellow workmen. It is truly lamentable, when a man
is honoured with the confidence of those with whom
he is connected, that he should abuse his trust. We'
may now hope that the lesson in this instance may not
be forgotten. It must be clearly understood that while
weettnite to assist each other in the hour of need, we
likewise combine to punish—at whatever cost—any
person guilty of a dish....t action.
I a. yours respectfully,

MINERS' STRIKE AT KILMARNOCK.—In terms of the
resolution come to at the last colliers' meeting, the
men at Gauchalland Colliery last week demanded the
advance of 61. per day. As yet the masters have not
seen fit to give it, and, accordingly, on Saturday, the
men stopped work, and refuse to give in till they re-
ceive the advance. They have agreed to remain on
the ground till Wednesday, after which they will go
and seek work elsewhere. They are however, hopeful
that they will get what they want, as their masters
have already offered it to one of the pits.—Glasgow

GRAND COLLIERS' DEMONSTRATION AT WIGAN.—On
Monday morning one of the largest and most orderly
assemblies of colliers known to this neighbourhood
took place in the Mesnas. The object of the gathering
was to receive a deputation from the council of the
British Miners' Association who are making a tour of
the mining districts, with the object of enlistin,g the
co-operation of the colliers in the efforts which the
society purposes to put forth for the amelioration of
the condition, of the mining population of Great
Britain, and for the better instruction or the rising
mining generation. About 10,000 members of the
class specially appealed to assembled. Lord Raynham,
one of the &Imitation, addressed them, and resolutions
pledging the meeting to support the association were
passed, and votes of thanks brought the proceedings to
a close.

NORTHUMBERLAND AND DURHAM MINERS' PERMA-
NENT RELIEF FUND.—The workmen of Walker Col-
liery held a meeting on Wednesday night, in the Col-
liery School Room, in connection with the above fund.
Mr. George Mitford was called to the chair. He
briefly stated the objects of the meeting, and then
called upon Mr. Alexander Blytb, Secretary of the
Association, to give an account of the progress and the
general working of the society, which was done in a
very lucid manner. Mr. John Richardson, accountant,
Royal Arcade, Newcastle, next addressed the meeting,
expressing his conviction that there was sufficient in-
telligence amongst the miners themselves to carry on
such a society without waiting for foreign aid. He
concluded his very eloquent address by urging the
men present to join the fund before leaving the meet-
ing. As a proof of the effect of his advice being
taken, forty members were enrolled. A local sosiety
was formed, Mr, Robert Brown being chosen secre-
tary, and Mr. John Shiel treasurer. The meeting
closed after a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman
and speakers.

RAILWAY PORTERS' TEA. PARTY.—OR Saturday
evening upwards of 700 railway porters and their
wives sat down to tea in the Corn Exchange, Man-
chester. The men were all in the employ of the
Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. The party was
got up at the suggestion of the Manchester City
Mission, who have appointed Mr. Chadwick as a
missionary labourer amongst the men. Addresses
of an encouraging nature were delivered by a number
of the gentlemen present. The New Windsor Tonic
Sol-fa singing class was present, and, accompanied
by a piano, gave a number of songs with good effect,
several of which were encored. The proceedings,
which were of a most interesting nature, closed at an
early hour.

I WINDSOR CASTLE, Dec. I.7.—The conseciation of the
Royal Mausoleum at Frogmore took place this day.
Her Majesty the Queen, previous to the ceremony,
went from the Castle to Frogmore-house in the most
private manner, and, when the Bishop of Oxford, the
clergy, and members of the Royal Household, and
others had assembled, walked to the Mausoleum,
accompanied by their Royal Highnesses, the Prince
of Wales, the Prince and Princess Louis of Hesse,
the Princess Helena, the Princess Louise' Prince
Arthur, Prince Leopold, and the Princess Beatrice.
The Queen entered the Mausoleum at five minutes past
twelve o'clock. The Bishop of Oxford (Bishop of
the diocess), Archdeacon Randall (Chaplain), Sir
John Phillimore, D.C.L. (Chancellor of the diocess),
the Dean of Windsor, the Dean of Christchurch, Res;.
Dr. Stanley, the -Vicar of Windsor, the Rev. Lord
Wriothesley Russell, and the Rev. James Blunt, Vicar
of Old Windsor, then, commenced the consecration by
passing round the external walls of the building, with
Dr. Elvey and the choir of St. George's Chapel sing-
ing (Tallis's Chant) Psalm xlix., 0 hear ye this, all
ye people.' Earl Granville (Lord President,) Viscount
Sydney (Lord Chamberlain,) and the gentlemen of the
household, followed in the procession. The psalm
having been chanted, the Bishop, clergy, and gentle-
men entered the Mausoleum, and the Bishop continued
the ceremony, Dearly beloved in the Lord,' followed
by the prayer 0 God, who hast taught us in Thy
Holy Word.' The choir sang the Amen Chant, and
afterwards a hymn from In Memoriam. The Bishop of
Oxford recited the prayers. A hymn of four verses,
from In Memoriam, was sung (the Old Hundredth) by
by the choir.
His lordship, sitting in his chair, directed the Chan-
cellor to read the sentence of consecration, which was
then signed by the Bishop. The Queen, with the
members of her family, quitted the mausoleum, and,
unattended by the Lathes and Gentlemen in Waiting,
walked back to Froginore.
The mausoleum has a central dome, an octagon, 61
feet in height and 30 feet in diameter. The ground
plan of the building is formed of four recesses, with
connecting circular corridors, the space between the
opposite recesses measuring also 64 feet. There is an
entrance porch projecting from the east side, ap-
proached by a flight of steps. Although the building
is not yet completed, the central portion in which the
Royal sarcophagus is to be placed is enth ely closed.
The exterior of the mausoleum will be nearly covered
with granite of various colours. The interior will be
finished by coloured marbles and frescoes. The build -
ing has been designed by Mr. Humbert and Professor
Gruner. The contractor is Mr. G. Dines. •

articles.text:
FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.

FREEMASONRY.

A Grand Lodge of the Province of Northumberland
and Berwick-upon-Tweed, to which all Master
Masons were invited, was opened on Wednesday at
noon, in the Assembly Rooms, Newcastle. The
brethren afterwards walked in procession from the
Assembly Rooms to St. Nicholas Church, the spectacle
being a very gay one, from the number ot richly
embroidered scarves and aprons worn by the brethren,
and the banners which were carried in the procession.
The prayers were read by the Rev. S. Atkinson, P.G.,
chaplain; the lessons by the Rev. T. Brutton (in the
absence of the Vicar of Newcastle, P.P.G., chaplain),
and the sermon by the Rev. E. C. Ogle, P.G.M.
The revlegentleman preached an eloquent and forcible
discourse from Luke xi., 41. At the close of the
sermon a collection was made in aid of the distressed
Lancashire operatives amounting to about £l2O.
Headed by the splendid band of the Ist Northumber-
land Artillery, under Mr. Watson, the brethren
marched back to the Assembly Rooms, where they
dined together.
MASONIC LODGES AND THE LA.NCASHIRE DISTRESS.
—A contribution has been received by the Edinburghl
Distress Committee from the Celtic Lodge of Edin-
burgh and Leith, No. 291. Probably other lodges who
have funds at their disposal for charitable purposes
will consider this a proper object for which to vote a
subscription.

ODDFELLOWS (MANCHESTER UNITY.)
THE FORTHCOMING DELEGATE DIEETING.—The de-
putation appointed by the Board of Directors (Mr.
Woodcock, Present Grand Master, Mr. Gale, P.G.M.,
and Mr. Buck, P.G.M.,) visited Leamington on
Wednesday last for the purpose of inspecting the rooms
most suitable for holding the meetings in Whitsun
Week, and they decided upon the Public Hall. The
local committee are making every arrangement to
carry out the affair in a manner that will give satisfac-
tion to the delegates who assemble here to represent
nearly half a million of members, who form this great
Unity, with credit to the entire district.
.HULL.—PHILANTHROPIC LODGE, No. 242.—At a
meeting of the members of this lodge on Monday, Bth
Dec., it was unanimously resolved that £5O be distri-
buted amongst the distressed members of their lodge
and the cotton operatives of this town. A relief com-
mittee was appointed, which will meet every Wednes-
day, at the Odd Fellows'-hall, at eight o'clock in the
evening, to relieve distressed members who make
application.
BATH.—The Ancient Order .610adfellows gave a ball
at the Guildhall, on Wednesday, the profits to be
devoted to the. Lancashire distress fund. There were
about 250 young people present: and a very agreeable
evening was spent.
FORESTERS.

ELLAND, YORKSHIRE.—The Court Temperance, held
at the New Inn, met on Saturday evening, and passed
a resolution to subscribe £lO out of the funds of the
court for the relief of distressed Foresters in Lanca-
shire. Should the distress continue, another similar
contribution will be made.
DRUIDS.

HORNSEA.—On Wednesday the officers of the -Hull
district, Messrs. Thos. Bygate, Jas, Wriggleswortb,
and M. Rosenbaum, assisted by P.A. John Pickering,
and Sec. John Atkinson, of the Burton Constable
Lodge, Sproatley, proceeded to open a new lodge at
Mr. Dawson's, Victoria Hotel, Hornsea, called the
Victoria Perseverance Ledge,' No. 478, when thirty-
two members were enrolled. The ceremonies were
ably conducted, and attentively listened to, and at the
close the D.C. Secretary announced the proceeds of the
first evening to be ss. 6d.
SKIRLAUGH.—On Thursday the members of the Earl
of Shaftesbury Lodge, Hull district, celebrated their
third anniversary, at their new lodge-room, just com-
pleted for the better accommodation of its members,
Sun Inn, Skirlaugh. Fifty-five members and friends
sat down to an excellent supper, provided by the host,
Mr. Westerby. After the cloth was drawn, Mr.
Ed wd. Burnham, the lodge surgeon, was voted to the
chair, who, with some of the leading members, ad-
dressed the meeting, alluding to the satisfactory
position of the lodge, which keeps continually on the
increase in members as well as in funds.

APPREHENSION or THE SECRETARY OF THE DON-
CUTER BUILDING SOCIETY.—On Friday, John Hastie,
late secretary of the Doncaster Building Society, was
brought up at the Doncaster borough police-court
before Wm. Sheardown, Lg., charged with defrauding
the Doncaster Building Society of a large sum of
money, and appropriating the same to his own use.
Mr. Smith (for the prosecution) tailed Mr. Thomas
Wood, the present secretary of the Society, who stated
that the defalcations amounted to more than £4,000,
and he feared that this sum would not cover the loss
that the shareholders would- sustain. Mr, Smith
applied for a remand, which was agreed to. The
prisoner observed that he had drawn out a statement,
which be had handed in to the superintendent of
police, Mr. Gregory, and this would, he believed, place
his transactions in a different light to what had been
represented.
