articles.title: ALARMING FIRE IN THE STRAND.
articles.text:
ALARMING FIRE IN THE STRAND.

At a quarter past eight on Monday evening a fire
broke out on the premises of Mr. Page, shellfish ware-
house, in the Strand, next door but one to the entrance
of the Adelphi Theatre, causing the greatest excite-
ment throughout the neighbourhood. The report
quickly spread that the theatre itself was on fire,
causing an immense assemblage of people, completely
blocking up not only the Strand itself', but all the
thoroughfares in the locality. It being a benefit night
at the Adelphi for the band fund of the London and
Westminster Rifle Corps, and the performance of the
'Messiah' taking place at Exeter Hall, the Strand was
at the time of the outbreak thronged with carriages,
and the confusion and uproar that took place were
almost indescribable. The reserve of the F division
of police from Bow-street, and all the available con-
stables from the neighbourhood, were brought into
request, but it was some time before anything like order
could be restored. On the arrival of the engines it was
found that the flames had got firm hold of the upper
and back portions of Mr. Page's premises, occupied as
supper and bedrooms, and were rapidly extending to the
theatre, which stands immediately in the rear. The
danger to the latter building now became so imminent
that the management deemed it prudeut to close the
performances. Mr. Webster informed the audience
from the stage that there was a fire raging close to the
theatre, which rendered it necessary that the house
should close at once, and he requested them to retire
as orderly as possible. Some alarm was excited, but
the house, which was much crowded, was speedily
cleared, without any accident. The same course was
parsued with the company at the Cider Cellars, which
are immediately in the rear of Mr. • Page's premises.
In the meantime, the firemen exerted themselves to the
utmost to prevent the spreading of the flames, and
after an hour's labour they were fortunately successful.
The whole of the upper and back portions of the pre-
mises of Mr. Page were destroyed, together with the
billlard-rooms of Mr. Beckingham adjoining, on the
west side, and the back part of the house occupied by
Messrs. Batt and Co., florists, on the east, and the
whole of whose premises were much damaged by water.
The theatre was not injured.

articles.title: FEARFUL OCCURRENCE IN THE BOROUGH.
articles.text:
FEARFUL OCCURRENCE IN THE
BOROUGH.

On Monday a scene of the greatest excitement took
place in High-street, Borough, near the Hop Pole
beer-shop, which has resulted in serious if not fatal
consequences to one or two persons. From the in-
quiries made it appears that a number of persons had
been playing during the evening at some house in the
neighbourhood at dominoes, and during the game an
altercation ensued, and from words they resorted to
fighting in the open street, which drew together a vast
crowd of spectators, Find whilst fighting one of the men,
named James Denham, of 1, Pleasant-row, Lower
Kennington, unperceived by the bystanders drew a
knife from his packet, and plunged it into the body of
David Casser, of 4, St. Margaret's-court. The latter
cried out that he was stabbed, when the mob rushed
upon Denham, took the knife from him, and commenced
to carry out Lynch law, and there is no doubt,
judging from the wound in his head, and the great
quantity of blood that flowed, that he was also
stabbed. One of the sufferers was taken to Guy's
Hospital, where his wound was dressed. The injury
was on the left side, near the ribs; but unless erysipe-
las should supervene, it is not likely to prove of a
serious character. Another man, named George Wood-
mason, was found to be dreadfully injured, and Denham
himself also; in fact, blood flowed in copious streams.
Whilst they were in the Stone's-end Police Station-
house, Mr. Inspector Mackintosh at once sent for Mr.
Evans, the divisional surgeon, who promptly attended,
accompanied by his assistant, Mr. Henderson. These
gentlemen, after stanching the blood, strapped up their
wounds, but ene was in such a dangerous state that it
was deemed advisable to have him removed on a
stretcher to Guy's Hospital, where he at present is
likely to remain for some time. The would be assassin,
upon being taken to the police-court, did not make any
attempt to deny the charge, but boasted of what he had
done, and said he would do the same to any other per-
son if they attempted to ill-use him. Upon being cau-
tioned by the inspector, he replied, Well, I did it,
and must suffer for it.'

CHILD MURDER. IN POPLAIL—Mr. Walthew re-
sumed an inquiry at the spotted Dog, High-street,
Pdplar, on the body of a female child, which was
found, shockingly mangled, lying in a garden in
Union-place. Mills, the officer of the court, said the
conclusion arrived at was that the deceased had been
brought from the station of the Blackwell Rtilway,
which was close at hand, in a bag, and throw g into
the garden, where it certainly had been but a very
short time previous to its being found. The police
stated that they had used every endeavour to dis-
cover those who were implicated in the murder, but
without any prospect of success. The coroner
said that .the present was unquestionably the most
brutal case of child murder that had ever come
before him. The jury returned a verdict of
Wilful murder against some person or persons un-
known.'

WORKING MEN'S CLUB.—The second anniversary
of this institution was celebrated on Tuesday night at
its premises, in Duck lane, Westminster. The chair
was occupied by Sir R. W. Carden, at whose side was
seated Miss Adeline Cooper, a lady whose benevolent
exertions in connection with the club are beyond all
praise. Established to afford working men an oppor-
tunity for social intercourse, away from the tempta-
tions of the public-house, the institution has been a
complete success. Its members, originally numbering
only forty, have increased to four hundred. From the
report, it appears that the temperance cause has been
materially aided by the establishment of the club,
about 300 persons having taken the pledge in the im-
mediate neighbourhood. A loan society, a penny
savings-bank, and a fund to provide costermongers
with barrows, have also been established. Deposits
to a considerable amount have been made, numerous
loans have been granted, and there has not been a
single defaulter. On the whole, the Working Men's
Club enters upon the third year of its existence under
the most favourable auspices.

COURT OF COMMON PLEAS.
(Before Mr. Justice Willes and Special Juries.)
LLEWELLYN V. IVYNDHAM.

This was an action brought by the plaintiff against
Mr. Wyndham, of Felbrigg Hall, for board, lodging,
&c., and goods supplied. The defendant paid £25
into court, and pleaded infancy with regard to the
remainder. When the special jury were first called,
ten gentlemen only answered to their names. Both
parties declined to pray a tales, and the learned judge
had the names again called, and fined the absentees
£lO each. Another special juryman answered to his
name the second time. Both the plaintiff and defend-
ant still declined to pray a tales for the odd man—the
twelfth juryman—and the consequence was the with-
drawal of the case and the discharge of the attending
special jurymen without their fee.

articles.text:
ASSIZE INTELLIGENCE.
NORTHERN CIRC-UIT.—LIVERPOOL.
(Before Mr. Commissioner Gurney.)
MURDER.

Thomas Edwards, a butcher, was indicted for the
murder of Isabella Tongue, a woman with whom he
had been cohabiting for onwards of eleven years. The
woman was a prostitute, and lived in a court off Nor-
man-street, Liverpool. Before she became acquainted
with Edwards the deceased had, it appeared, an inti-
macy with a man named Sullivan. Sullivan, how-
ever, had been compelled to leave the country, and
only returned in November last. Then the connection
between him and Tongue was renewed, and in conse-
quence Edwards became dreadfully excited and jealous.
On November 27 Edwards came home in the evening,
and on finding that Tongue had been out with Sullivan
all day, he became very angry, and began to drink ale
and rum. During the evening he went out and got
more drink, and finally lay down on the sofa. Early
in the morning Sullivan and the deceased returned to
the house, and Edwards angrily asked where Tongue
bad been all day. The deceased made no reply, but
Sullivan said to the prisoner, 'What is that to you?
She has been out with me.' The prisoner then stabbed
Tongue furiously in the neck and other parts of the
body, and she died very soon afterwards.—The jury
found the prisaner Guilty,' with a recommendation to
mercy.—Sentence of death was passed.

articles.title: MURDER OF A SHERIFF'S OFFICER.
articles.text:
THE MURDER OF A SHERIFF'S OFFICER.

Neal O'Donnell and James Coyne were indicted for
the wilful murder of a sheriff's officer, James Morris,
on the 15th of September last. Evidence having been
taken in support of the opening, the jury retired, and
after an absence of forty minutes returned with a
verdict of manslaughter in the case of O'Donnell, and
of acquittal in the case of Coyne. His lordship re-
marked that, though he did not find fault with the
verdict of the jury, this Was a case so near one of
murder that he Mt bound to sentence the prisoner
to penal servitude for life. Coyne was discharged.

articles.title: OXFORD CIRCUIT.—GLoucEsTER. (Before Air. Justice Mellor.) MURDER.
articles.text:
OXFORD CIRCUIT.—GLoucEsTER.
(Before Air. Justice Mellor.)
MURDER.

William Mealing was charged with the wilful murder
of Sarah Moss, at Rendcombe, on the 23rd October.
The prisoner, whose age is 26, is tall and thin in
person, has nothing ferocious in his looks, but has
more of the animal than mental qualities in his aspect.
The prisoner was found not guilty, on the ground of
insanity.

THE CASE OF CAPTAIN CONROY, THE BIGAMIST.

James Summers, alias John Alexander Conroy, was
charged on three indictments with forgery and bigamy;
bigamy in having married two young ladies—Miss
Emily Dawson Graham, at Windsor, and Miss Jane
Cowley Dale, at Cirencester, his wife Margaret being
living. The other charge was that of forging a cheque
for £lOO on Messrs. Hepburn and Co. Mr. Dale, land-
lord of the King's Head Hotel, .Cirencester, deposed
that the prisoner came to his house on the 16th April
last, and remained there till July. He paid his addressas
to Miss Dale, representing himself as Captain Conroy,
of the Indian army. Witness looked in the Army
List,' and not finding his name there he called the
prisoner's attention to the fact, when he expressed his
surprise, and said he should write to his friend Sir J.
Lawrence. He accordingly wrote to Sir John; and,
in a day or two, Mr. Dale and the prisoner received
letters purporting to be from Sir J. Lawrence, (but
which were proved to be forgeries), vouching for the
fact that the prisoner was a captain in the Bengal
Infantry. This he (witness) considered satisfactory,
and. the prisoner became the accepted suitor of Miss
Dale, and they were married on the 9th July. His
lordship summed up with great care, and. the prisoner
was found guilty. He was then charged with bigamy,
and pleaded guilty to both cases. Sentence, fifteen
years' penal servitude.

NORTH WALES CIRCUIT.—CHESTER.
(Before Mr. Baron Bramwell.)
THE BIRKENHEAD RIOTS.

Patrick Fahey, the elder, 66; Patrick Fahey, the
younger, 24; Thomas ,Shovelin, 19; James Tracey,
23; Thomas Buckley, 40; John Gorman, 26; Michael
Fahey, 18; Thomas Larkin, 46; Michael Hogan, 18;
Michael Martin, 47; Michael Hoare, 35; James Fynan,
65; Henry Lennon, 37; Catharine Larkin, 44,
Bridget Burns, 32; Margaret M'Guire, 30; Bridget
M.'Donald, 22; and Elizabeth Curtis, 36; were
indicted for unlawfully and riotously assem-
bling, with divers other persons, to disturb the
public peace, and making great riot and distur-
bance at Birkenhead on the 15th of October last.
These disturbances arose out of the attempt of the
Catholic party at Birkenhead to prevent a meeting of
the friends and admirers of Garibaldi being held in the
room of the Young Men's Debating Society at Birken-
head, the facts connected with which are fresh in the
recollectiva of our readers. Evidence having been
given as to the part taken by the prisoners in the dis-
graceful proceedings, his Lordship summed up with
great care; and, after an absence of an hour and a
quarter, the jury returned a verdict of guilty against
all the prisoners with the exception of Fynan. The
learned Baron then ordered Patrick Fahey the elder to
be discharged on his own recognizance, Catherine
Larkin to be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for
twelve months, and, the other female prisoners for six
months each. Shovelin, Patrick Fahey the younger,
and Michael Fahey and others he sentenced to one
year's imprisonment, Buckley and Hogan to two
years' imprisonment, and Lennon to 16 years' penal'
servitude.

articles.title: CENTRAL CRIMINAL COURT.
articles.text:
CENTRAL CRIMINAL COURT.

(Before Mr. Baron Martin.)
MANSLA:UGHTER.

Frederick Pearce, 36, described as a smith, was in-
dicted for feloniously killing and slaying Th )s. Searle.
Hannah Wheatley, a single woman, said that she occu-
pied a room at 12, Wood's-buildings, Gravel-lane.
The prisoner, with his wife and three children, occu-
pied a room above that of witness. On the night of
the 22nd of November, between nine and ten, she
heard singing in the prisoner's room. She saw her
daughter, Hannah Pearce, with some beer in a can.
Soon after she heard voices, and a gruff voice said,
Give me my change.' She then heard the prisoner
say, 'I will not.' The voice she first heard replied,
Then I will have it out of you.' A scuffle ensued, and
the table was turned over. Presently she heard a man
fall down stairs. He was bleeding. She saw him
afterwards at St. Thomas's Hospital dead. A police
officer who was called said that when he first saw
Searle he had three severe wounds on his head. The
prisoner admitted that he had committed the assault,
and added that Searle should not have come after his
wife. He also told the police that Searle had two or
three times got his wife away from him, and that he
had had great difficulty in getting her back. The
prisoner was found guilty. Baron Martin sentenced
him to nine months' imprisonment with hard labour.
FATAL EFDECTS OF LARKlNG.—Willialll Cairns, 62,
carpenter, pleaded guilty to the charge of man-
slaughter. It was stated that some of the shopmates
of the prisoner, employed at Ashby and Sons Bishops-
gate-stregt, were engaged larking,' and throwing
pieces of wood at each other, and one of the pieces
struck the prisoner, and he snatched up a chisel and
threw it at the deceased, and inflicted an injury that
caused his death. The prisoner had confessed the
deepest regret at the occurrence, and it appeared that
he had been thirty-two years in the service of his
master, and bore a most excellent character. Judg-
ment was postponed.
ALLEGED CHILD MURDER. Salome Newman, 17,
was indicted for the wilful murder of her infant child.
It appeared from the statement of Mr. Sleigh, the
prosecuting counsel, that the prisoner was a domestic
servant in the employment of Mrs. Bolton, of 14,
Navarino-road, Dalston. In October last her mistress
heard a noise downstairs, and found that the prisoner ,
was suffering great pain and evidently in labour.
Afterwards she gave birth to a child, but concealed
the birth, and denied the fact. Subsequently, the
body was found wrapped up in an apron, and laid upon
the top of the register of the stove in the room she
oceupied. A staylace was tied tightly round the neck.
No preparation was made for the birth of the child.
The jury acquitted her of the murder, and found her
guilty of concealing the birth of her child. Baron
Martin sentenced her to eighteen months' imprison-
ment with hard labour. -

articles.title: MIDDLESEX. SESSIONS.
articles.text:
MIDDLESEX. SESSIONS.

(Before Mr: Bodkin.)
Wm. Pike, late Secretary to the Amalgamated
Painters Associati,m, was brought up on Monday last,
to receive judgment for embezzling several sums of
money belonging to the above association.
In answer to his lordship, the present Secretary said
that since the prisoner's trial there had been no attempt
made by his friends to pay back any part of th..; money
to the Association.

His Lordship then asked tbe prisoner what he had to
say for himself.
The prisoner said he would pay the money as soon as
he was able.

His lordship considered that nothing. I deferred
(says his lordship) passing sentence upon you until this
sessions, in order to give your friends a chance to pay
back that portion of the money upon which you were
acquitted. I thought they would have done so, as it
was represented that you had borne a good character
previous to this offence. But now I shall treat the case
as if nothing of the kind had taken place. The sen-
tence of the court is, that you be imprisoned with hard
labour for six calend r months.

articles.title: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

CLE RKEN WELL.

FATAL ACCIDENT IN Sr. PANCE.AB-11.0AD.—ThODAS
Elliot, aged 42, a drayman, was charged with causing
the death of William Edmonds, 44, a house painter,
by running over him with a brewer's dray and two
horses. From the evidence it appeared that on Satur-
day night the prisoner was driving a dray, belonging
to Messrs. Whitbread, along the St. Pancras-road,
when nearly opposite the Model Lodging-houses,
deceased was crossing, and before the driver could pull
up the horses the dray went over the unfortunate
man. Mr. Sutherick, surgeon, immediately attended,
and pronounced life to be exthet, stating that death
must have been almost instantaneous.

The defence set up was that it was an accident.
Mr. Barker remanded the prisoner.
BOW-STREET.
,

A DESPAVADO.—John Hare, a powerful looking
young man, was brought before Mr. Henry, on a,
warrant granted in July last, charging him with
assaulting Police •constables Ackrill and Miles, of the
F division, and rescuing a prisoner from theigeustody.
It appeared from the evidence that the priallner is a
most desperate character, anè that he has committed
several street robberies attended with violence. For
one of them he had been sentenced to three years'
penal servitude, but was liberated before his time.
Mr. Henry inquired if his sentence had now expired,
and was answered in the affirmative. The prisoner
was then committed for trial, Mr. Henry offering to
accept bail, which was not, however, forthcoming.

articles.title: GUILDHALL.
articles.text:
GUILDHALL.

ILLEGAL CONDUCT OF A DETECTIVE-Wm. Jarvis, a
detective officer of the City police force was summoned
before Alderman Humphrey for unlawfully detaining
a set of furs, value £lO, and a dishonoured cheque for
£30,. the property of a young lady, the complainant.
The case against the defendant was that he had gone
to the house of complainant and induced her to gyve
up the property above mentioned, which had been
presented to her by a young man of the name of
Parker, without having any authority beyond that of
his own card. Alderman Humphrey said the defen-
dant had no right to go into a person's house in such
a manner without a magistrate's warrant. If it was
to be tolerated for one moment that police-officers in
plain clothes might go into private houses, charge
persons with complicity in an act of felony, and possess
themselves of property without any other authority
than their own cards, no one would be safe. The case
was adjourned in order that a warrant might be issued
against Parker.

articles.title: WORSHIP STREET.
articles.text:
WORSHIP STREET.

AN UNFIT CAB DRIVER.—John Leclgeyett, a cab
driver, badge No. 9,182, was charged with drunkenness
and assault.—Mr. John Champion, residing in Buck-
land-street, New North-road, stated that on the
previous evening he, in company with a friend,
engaged the defendant near Southgate-road, to drive
them to the City-road. He very quickly became
aware, however, that the man was intoxicated, as he
drove in a wrong direction. Suddenly he received a
severe cut across the eye, and sprang from the cab,
followed by his friend. He moved forward a few
paces, holding his hand to the injured part, without
any thought respecting the fare, when the driver came
up to him, knocked off his hat, thrust him against
some railings so violently that his knuckles were
grazed, and used such grossly insulting language that
he gave him into custody.—A. sorgeant and two con-
stables of the N division spoke to the scandalous con-
duct of the defendant while taking him to the station.
He kicked most dangerously at those near him, and
tore the coat of the officer.—Mr. Cooke fined the
prisoner 10s., with the alternative of ten days, for the
first assault; and 205., or fourteen days, for the others,
and also ss. for the damage done to the coat.—The
cabman was removed in the prison van.

articles.title: WE-STMINS PER.
articles.text:
WE-STMINS PER.

THREE WEEKS AFTER WEDLOCK —A very genteel
looking young woman, but who appeared to be in a
delicate state of health, besought the magistrate's
assistance. She said that her husband was constantly
ill-treating her, and, however unpleasant it was, she
had felt compelled to seek the protection of the law.
I have been married only four months, and I am, of
course, very sorry, under such circumstances, to come
here; but I don't know what to do, I am so illused.
He hats me; he continually knocks me about, and
began to do so three weeks after we were married. I
give him no provocation that lam aware of. He says
he wants to get rid of me, that he don't want me any
longer, and I am sure, if that is his wish, I am quite
ready to part, for lam very unhappy. My health is
very indifferent, and he tries to tread me under foot
instead of using me kindly. Yesterday he struck me
in the back with his fist because there was something
he did not fancy in the dinner I had provided, in
which I had done all that I thought right. He hurt
me much, and after he had given me a blow in the
back he struck me about the head.—Mr. Paynter : I
don't think bringing a husband to a police court does
any good, if it can be avoided. You may have a sum-
mons.

articles.title: LAMBETH.
articles.text:
LAMBETH.

ANTI-GAROTTE Tilo—v;;;;;;;:-211-enry Rawlings, clerk,
and William Hine, a simple-looking youth, appeared
to answer to a summons, charging them with dig-.
charging fire-arms in the public highway, to the
terror and danger of her Majesty's subjects. The
defendants pleaded guilty to the offence, and admitted
they fired off the pistols they carriel with them for
their personal safety before they got home. Inspector
Smith, of the Brixton station produced one or-the
balls that had been fired, which he said had cntered
the window of a lady's drawing-room, knocked off a
portion of a stove cornice, and fell back into the
apartment, to the great alarm of the lady and her
family. Mr. Elliott observed that it was a very silly
and dangerous act, and convicted the defendants in a
penalty of 10s. and costs, which they paid.

articles.title: THAMES.
articles.text:
THAMES.

Golding Jones, a bricklayer, about 49 years of age,
was charged with attempting to commit suicide. Mr.
Woolrych said he should remand the prisoner to the
Clerkenwell House of Detention for a week, and that
it would depend upon the report of the officer whether
he should then let him go at large or not. •

THE CITY SOLICITORSHIP ELECTION.—At a Court of
Common Council, held on Thursday, this office was
filled up by the appointment of Mr. T. J. Nelson.
There were nine candidates, only two of whom went
to the poll. The numbers were—Nelson, 114; Crosby,
59; majority, 65.
MYSTERIOUS DEATIL—On Wednesday morning con-
siderable sensation was created in Norwood in conse-
quence of a report that a gentleman had been found
murdered under the following circumstances: —lt
appears that some person passin, through the wood
observed a gentleman on the ground in a rico' of blood,
and, calling the police, had him conveyed to the
Beulah Spa Tavern, where medical aid was procured,
but life was found to be quite extinct, death having
been caused by a deep wound in the body. The follow-
ing description has been issued by the police :—About
55 years of age,
,six feet in height, grey hair, grey
eyes; wound in the body four inches long; dark coat,
tweed waistcoat, white shirt, Wellington boots, white
stockings ; on his person were found a pair of steel
spectacles, 31d. in copper, powder-flask, four bullets, a
duelling pistol loaded with ball, and a dagger in a

PROTECT] 1111 ASSOCIATION _

articles.title: :THE STARTING OPERATIVES.
articles.text:
:THE STARTING OPERATIVES.

On Friday, Dec. 5, 1862, a meeting of the operatives
of Liverpool was held in Hope Hall, Hope-street, in
order to consider the existing calamitous distress in the
manufacturing districts, and to take steps for the more
effectual alleviation thereof. The meeting was nume-
rously attended. Among the gentlemen • who occupied
seats on the platform were the Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D.,
the operative's friend,' Rector of Habergham, near
Burnley Mr. James Denbigh, of Padiham ; Mr.
Lewis Mr. Anderson, Mr. J. G. Brown, Mr. Lynch,
Mr. Lawson, Mr. Dobbs Mr. Dagnall, Mr. Glenville,
Mr. Swinnerton, Mr. Watkin, Mr. Winstanley, Mr.
Lewin, and Mr. Charles Williams, secretary of the
Liverpool United Trades' Protective Association.
Mr. Lynch was called upon to take the chair. He
read the following notice 'convening the meeting :
anis LIVERPOOL 'UNITED TRADES' PROTECTLVE Asso-
CATION AND TEE STARVING OPERATIVES.—The above
Association beg leave to inform their fellow working
men and the public that in consequence of the St.
George's Hall being required for balls, &c., they were
refused the use of the Hall to hold a Public Meeting
in Aid of the Distressed Operatives, and the inclement
season of the year presented them applying for the
use of Gill-street Market, as kindly suggested to them,
they will hold a Public Meeting in Hope Hall, Hope-
street, on Friday evening, Dec. sth, when the meeting
will be addressed by the Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D.,
(the Operative's Friend, and Rector of Habergham,
near Burnley) when the causes and consequences of
the present Cotton Famine will be reviewed from the
position ef the working classes, and suggestions made
of relieving the present appalling distress. Working
Men of all classes are earnestly invited to attend.
Chair to be taken at seven o'clock. Other gentlemen
will address the meeting.—' Remember those who are
in adversity, as being yourselves also in the flesh.'—
Hebrews.
The Chairman also read the following letter, which
had been received from the Town Clerk in reply to
the application of the United Trades' Protective A.sso-
elation for the use of St. George's Hall
'Town Hall, Liverpool, 13th November, 1862.
SlR,—Your letter of the 7th instant, addressed to
the Mayor, requesting the use of St. George's Hall for
a public meeting in aid of the distressed operatives,
was laid before the Council at their meeting on Mon-
day last, and referred to the St. Gcorge's lan Com-
mittee; that committee met to-day, and I am directed
to inform you, that as the wooden floor is now laid
down in the Hall, in consequence of applications for
the use of the building for balls, and cannot be removed
without considerable expense, the Hall is not now avail-
able forthe intended meeting. I would suggest, however,
that you make application to the Finance Com-
mittee on an early day for the use of Gill-street Mar-
ket for your intended meeting—l am, sir, your
obedient servant,__ _

"W. SnurrixwonTn, Town Clerk.
'Mr. Charles Williams, Secretary to the Liverpoo]
*United Trades' Protection Association.'

The Chairman said: Ladies and gentlemen, the reason
of our applying for the use of St. George's Hall for
this meeting was, that it was in a central situation, and
had an attraction calculated to bring together a large
number of persons. I myself and two others were
deputed to wait upon the Town Clerk and make appli-
cation for the use of the Hall. We were received in
the most friendly manner by Mr. Weightman who
said that our object was a most laudable one, and that
our application should be laid before the committee
who managed the letting of the Hall. From the letter
I have just read you will learn the answer we received.
Now we know perfectly well that the mere fact of the
boarded floor being laid down would not prevent our
meeting being held; therefore I hold that the refusal
of the use of the Hall to the men who built it was most
ungenerous and unhandsome. (Hear, hear.) Various
meetings and balls have been held since, and even a
ball in aid of distressed foreigners. They grant the use
of the Hall for the relief of distressed foreigners, and
refuse it for the distressed operatives at home!
(Hear.) The men who built the Hall, and worked
at it from morning till night, were refused its use
for such a noble object, and shamefully excluded.
(' Shame!) We were told to apply for Gill-street
Market. Now, we know what Gill- street Market is
—cold and unhealthy, with scarcely a perfect pane
of glass in the entire building. lam sorry to say
that our superiors do not show us that respect to
which we are entitled. How different was the con-
duct of her Majesty the Queen towards the men
who reared the building for the International Exhi-
bition. She said that they had a right to go through
as soon as any one to inspect the contents, and as
soon as the building was opened she purchased
tickets and presented them to the operatives who
had erected that wonderful structure. St. George's
Hall will stand for ages as a proud memorial of the
skill and talent of British workmen—and how un-
seemly it is that British workmen themselves should
be debarred from its use. The cther day I read a
placard announcing a grand assault at arms' to take
at St. George's Hall. There were two lines of
at the bottom, as a motto—
'lll fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates and men decay.'
lines made a great impression on my mind,
with the reflection that there were hundreds
honsands of men, women, and children now
ng bread and the bare necessaries of life.. I also
_emembered that the strength of the nation was the
happiness of its people. Now, here is an opportunity
to promote that happiness, and an opportunity for the
wealthy classes to come forward and assist the
working classes. There has been a meeting of the
great landowners of Lancashire—a very important
and significant one indeed. Those noble lords, after
returning to their dwellings will call their stewards
before them and give them their directions.
Would not the stewards proceed with willingness
to carry out the will of their noble masters? Yet
let the noble lords themselves remember that ,
they are but stewards of what they possess, and ,
that the richest as well as the poorest will have to give
an account of his stewardship. The property they
possess belongs not (to. any of them they brought
nothing into the world, and nothing shall they carry
out of it. I would also say to the wealthy clasees,
that there an opportunity now presents itself, which
• 'may never occur again, for cementing everlasting
-friendship between the poor and the rich, and showing
:that the rich really and truly sympathise with the
poor in their poverty. (Hear, hear.) Lord Derby on
one occasion related a story of a noble fellow who,
when parish relief was tendered to him, replied in-
di.gnantly, No; sooner than I would take parish;
relief, I would " clem" first.' The expression was
highly significant and characteristic of the high feel-
ing of the distressed operatives in the manufac-
turing districts. But let it be remembered that if
things continue long in this deplorable condition
there will be a change in the feelings of the poor
operatives. Seeing such a meeting as this of working
men, I say to you, no cause for which you could have
met would be more noble or more charitable than the
objet for which you have met—to sympathise, not
merdly b. words but by deeds also with your fellow-
sufferers. Some of the cleverest and the most generous
of the sons of toil are now walking about the streets,
for they have no work. The hum of machinery is no
longer heard in the busy hiv.-2s of industry. In the
homes of the working men are now seen fnelless grates,
empty cupboards, and scant furniture. We call upon ,
working men b-night to assist working men. In con-
clusion, I beseech you all, whatever you have to give,
to give it cheerfully; and all will be laid up for you
where the rich man will not be classed for his riches
nor the poor man be classed for his poverty. (Loud
applause.) The Chairman concluded by introducing
the Rev. Mr. Verity.
The Rev. Mr. Verity, on coming forward, was re-
ceived with great applause. He said—The subject of
discussion this evening is one which for magnitude
and extent cannot find a parallel in the pages of
history. It is one which has moved the hearts of the
people of England, the people of Europe, as well as
the people of the far-distant colonies. It has moved
the hearts of strangers as well as friends. (Hear.)
As regards the extent of the distress, I take it for
granted that you are fully acquainted with it. There
can be no question that Lancashire now is very different
from what it was twelve months ago. Then thousands
of families were obtaining their daily bread, and in no
scanty measure: workmen were receiving £3 to Di
per week for skilled labour. Who could have prophe-
sied that in a few months so dark a misfortune and
one that would fling so ToanY into such distress,
would have been possible? But if the distress is
great, lotus thank God that the efforts put forth are
adequate for the relief of that distress let us
thank God that no exertion will be needed for
the relief of the distress. But at the same time,
while we commend all classes of society for their
benevolent efforts, do not let us run away with the
idea that the distress is already relieved. The distress
in Lancashire is by no means relieved as it ought to
be, and the great want, in order to accomplish it
thoroughly, is left unsupplied. It is my duty to bring
the nature of that want before you this evening, and
to enforce its claims on the working men of the great
town of Liverpool. (Hear.) We have in the field
two central committees, which are moving heaven
and earth to obtain funds. They are—first. the Man.
Sion House Committee, which sits in London; and
secondly, the Manchester Central Committee. Allow
me to sketch the rise and mode of proceeding of those
two committees. When Lancashire became greatly

place
Poefry

depressed, in February last, an appeal was made to the
manufacturers for some funds to meet the pressing
urgency ofahe state of things. To that appeal the
manufacturers were deaf. They said there was
I no distress. They closed their ears to the
voice of suffering, and turned a deaf ear to
the agony of the poor. But there was one
man who heard the cry, and hastened to the relief.
All honour to Sir William Cubitt. (Cheers). Though
two hundred miles away from the scene of the suffer-
ing, he responded to the cry. But those in the locality
who might be expected to be the first to take steps for
the relief of the distress buttoned up their pockets, and
saidAat the suffering was not sufficiently painful.
The -Lord Mayor of London heard the cry, and help
came into Manchester. Committees were then formed,
and the Lord Mayor's committee had a ready ma-
chinery for .dispensing the funds at their disposal.
When our friends at Manchester found that relief was
coming to them from distant parts without their seek
ing it they were alarmed; then they came forward
with a most remarkable wish to supersede the Lord
Mayor's committee, and take out of his hands the dis-
tribution of the funds which had been entrusted to
him. Now, the Lord Mayor received the universal
support of the whole country. At that time strictures
were made upon the Manchester committee. When these
individuals found the stream of benevolence
setting in they wanted to control its direction
in a manner agreeable to their own wishes;
then they proposed to take charge of subscrip-
tions. Those subscriptions came in nobly. At last
the manufacturers were moved to contribute; and now
it must be said they have contributed nobly according
to their means. Cf course there are some exceptions,
some defections from the general benevolence; but,
on the whole, I repeat, the manufacturers have con-
tributed nobly. But if you ask me whether private
or public benevolence can really relieve the distress,
I say No, it cannot. There is only one mode
which can permanently relieve the distress and meet
the exigencies of the case during nine months'
distress. That is not a grant from the benevolence
of the outside public, much less is it the borrowing
system which, I regret to say, the manufacturers
have begun to patronise, although they deprecate the'
borrowing system in business. What is the reason
for their adoption of this measure? It is to avoid
the healthy action of that excellent measure, the
rate in aid. will explain the excellency of this
measure. The rate in aid is intended to supply the
means of supporting the poor by extending the-burden
from the manufacturing to the agricultural districts.
Now, the squires and nobility are generally found in
the agricultural districts, and manufacturers in the
towns and villages. The consequence is that the
nobility refuse to allow the rate in aid bill to be ex-
tended so as to include their property. But if by
borrowing they can manage to mortgage the future,
the earnings and wages of the working classes will pay
off the burden. I think it is proper to put the saddle
on the right horse; and therefore I trust that the
working classes will have their eyes open to this great
fact, that the distress cannot be properly and ade-
quately relieved, by borrowing money, but by the rate
in aid measure, which is a legal, just, and proper re-
moval of the burden from the manufacturing districts
and equalising it by putting it ppon the nobility and
gentry. (Heir, hear.) I have already said there are
two committees. Let us see how they work, and
examine the principles upon which they extend relief.
The London committee profess to distribute their
funds equally wherever distress presents itself. They
set out with the priviso that the poor persons who are
to be the objects of their bounty must be poor trades-
men, poor co-operatives, poor working men, or any
proper person standing in need of relief. The Lord
Mayor's committee deserve public confidence and ad-
miration. The greatest error was that they did rot
give liberally, so as effectually to stem the tide of dis-
tress and keep the workmen really out of the workhouse.
By funding portions of their subscriptions I consider,
also, they were opposing the wishes of the subscribers..
We know that charities are usually in debt, and that
instead of having a large balance at the banker's be-
nevolent societies, should be Dr. to Cash.' Demand
usually creates a supply in these cases besides affording
a beneficial stimulus to the exertions of the promoters.
Now, the Lord Mayor kept his coffers full, and the
consequence was the public did not augment them.
But while he was making this mistake-and sending
£2OO to the poor of Blackburn, what was the Man-
chester committee doing? They started with most
admirable principles it must be admitted, but it must
also be added they afterwards quite abnegated them.
They proposed not to relieve the pauper relieved by
the parish, but assist the sober, intelligent working
man in his great necessity by granting him suffi-
cient food, fuel, and clothing, during the crisis. The
object was that he might never have to apply to the
parish, and thus lapse into the class of a pauper. These
were noble principles. But how have the Manchester
committee carried out those principles ?: They could
only see their way to giving £2OO or £3OO per week.
The result was, as Mr. Farnell showed in his reports,
that the distress gradually and surely increased in
intensity,, and the poor were daily nearing destitution..
5,000 of the steadiest and most spirited workmen were'
left unrelieved, and actually fell into the hands of the
poor-law guardians. (Cries of 'Shame.') This com--
mittee went on in this way for about two months. Five
weeks ago, after collecting from all sources, and even
begging of the working classes themselves, the Man-
chester committee had accumulated the vast sum of
£129,000 in their hands ; and five weeks ago they only
distributed £4OO. (Shame.) Such a fact is enough to
make the blood boil to see funds accumulate in such a
manner, with half-a-million of people threatened with
starvation is a most deplorable spectacle. Mistakes of
the same character have occurred before in the cases
of other benevolent organisations, and they have be-
fore called forth the censures of the public. The Times
the other day told us of a balance- of £BO,OOO which
remains undistributed from the, Indian Relief Fond.
And this grievance, letrust, and confidently hope, will
be removed by Lerd,Derby. (Applause.) T.he noble
lord will not allow of such a mal-administration as
funds accumulatingat the bankers, when the necessity
for their distribution is so pressing. The Earl of
Derby's labours in the cause of the starving operatives
deserve to be generally known; to my knowledge,
his attendance at the committee meetings is most eon-
stant and attentive. This was not only most com-
mendable but highly necessary, for the distribution of
£30,000 at one sitting required some attention and
administrative talent. (Hear, hear.) The question
now arises, hove is all the wealth that flows into the
coffers of the- committees,. distributed?' The local
relief committees, as you are aware, receive grants
from the central committee, and distribute the relief
to the distressed poor. Now, I have paid great
attention to-the sufferings of the poor in my own
.dis-
trict. I have also paid attention to the applications
made for relief. And I have also paid attention to the
constitution of the local relief committees: I will tell
you of what classes those committees are almost en-
variably composed. As. a general rule the local relief
committee is composed of the squires and manu-
facturers of the locality. Working men are invariably
excluded from sitting on these committees. Working
men are not considered competent to bear apart in
the deliberations of these committees! Working men.
are too insignificant to have any right to sit at these
boards! Sir J. Kaye Shuttleworth said:—' Working
men must not be allowed to send deputies to these
committees, because the squires and manufacturers
will not sit at the same board with them!' (Shame.)
Now, I myself wanted to remedy this gross abuse.
I considered that working men had a right to serve
on local relief committees. I maintained that they
were perfectly able to do so creditably and effi-
ciently. I believe that equal duties confer equal
rights, and that if you tell working men it is their
duty to contribute to the fund, working men have
a right to have some voice in the distribution of
that fund. (Hear, hear, and applause.) And I have
no hesitation in saying that if working, practical men,
had been sitting on the committees, many mistakes
into which they have fallen would not have occurred.
And that if one or two working men had sat at the
Manchester board the gross abuse of allowing such a
sum to accumulate would not have occurred. I will
now look at the result of the present system of distri-
bution. The object was to prevent the artisan lapsing
into the pauper, and skilled workmen drifting into the
workhouse. What is the case? Men are tumbling
into the workhouse weekly. They are falling into
pauperism at the rate of 7,000 per week. And at the
present -time 275,000 workmen are subsisting on the
paltry pittance of fourteen or fifteen pence per week.
And this is the case with 150,000 lying idle in the
Bank! (Shame.) Now I will give you a specimen of
how the committees act. They assemble, say on a Mon-
day morning. The doors are then thrown open and
the poor applicants for relief flock to state their cases.
Now suppose the case of a poor woman. She goes to
the committee and tells them that the parish only allows
her 28. per week to relieve three persons. What will
the committee say to her? Why, that Sir James
Shuttleworth has toid us not to give relief to cases
where the parish afforded relief.' So they refused re-
lief altogether. I will now take a case which has actually
occurred, and is not a mere supposition. In the town of
Padiham there was a woman named C. 8., (the rev.
speaker gave the full names, but we do not think it is
desirable to give them publicity.) This woman has
two children. She called upon the relieving officers
who referred her to the middle-class relief fund.
Several justices of the peace sat upon the bench.
The woman was first asked as to her condition.
Her destitute condition was undeniable. This woman
was next asked how many children she had. She
stated that she had two. In what condition are they?
The woman was rather puzzled at the question, and

said, They'rone on e n'em rotten.' As soon as the
Board heard that, one or two of them, especially one
who was hiring apart from his wife owing to his con-
jugal incontinence, coloured up, and dismissed the
woman with you may go now, my good woman.'
(Shame.) Let us take another case. J. B.'s family
consisted of his wife and six children. They were re-
lieved neither from the parish nor from the middle-
class committee. They came starving to the working-
men's central committee. We relieved them, and are
doing so now. Another case. E. W., a widow with
live children. Her income was Bs. per week, to main-
tain six people, after paying 2s. per week for rent. She
went to the parish, and got no relief. She went to the
Assembly-rooms where the middle-class committee sit,
and got no relief. At last she came to us, and we re-
lieved her with 2s. 6d. per week. (Applause.) Now I
need hardly tell you that the fact of there being a work-
ing man's committee, and of working men distributing'
relief, created much jealousy. It was a very sore
affront to those who sat on themiddle-class committee.
And they soon resolved to have revenge on us. In
selecting the recipients of relief, the committee of
course do not include any who have refused to work for
them, who have joined a strike, or who belong to co-
operative societies which have started mills of their
own. (Shame.) Thus some of the best and worthiest
workmen have to go without food and clothidg. There
was a man with eight children who was connected
with our committee. This man applied to the middle]
class relief committee for a blanket, a bed, and a pet-
ticoat for one of his family. As soon as he made his
appearance, a manufacturer said to him J. H. is your
name, is it not?' It is." Don't you sit on the
working men's committee?' I do.' Well, as long
as you are connected with that committee, you get
nothing from us!' Another case was that of E. K.,
who was the brother of one of the members of the
middle-class committee. He went to the committee to
beg for food and clothing. The secretary, when he
heard the man's name, said, there is your brother.'
The brother nodded his head. You had better fill up,
that form, and then get your brother to sign it to cor-
roborate the trath of your statement, or you can have
no relief.' But the brother refused to sign it, and the
poor man was sent away. The explanation of this
was, that in a trade dispute sometime previous the
man, who was an operative, refused to allow his three
children to work as knobstice' for his brother who was
the manufacturer. But worse than all these cases
is the case of the poor co-operator. Now we
all know that in order to be a co-operator, a man
must be industrious and frugal. These men save
from their earnings what they lay out in stock and
shares. We know what great things have been
accomplished by co-operation—of the mills which
have been erected, and the extent of business trans-
acted by some of the societies. Several of the
societies have been so successful as to realise 40 or 50
per cent. on their capital. But now, when employment
has ceased, the condition of the co-operator is deplor-
able in the extreme. He finds his little capital locked
up. Efe cannot realise except at such a disadvantage
as will throw away, perhaps, the savings of years. He
cannot borrow money on the security of his scrip on
account of its inconvertibility. These circumstances
must entitle the co -operator, at this crisis especially, to
the sympathy of all who have the interest of the work-
ing classes at heart. But what is the case? The poor
man goes to the middle class relief fund, and asks for
food or rairaent. The committee composed of manu-
facturers, turn round and say, have you fast; you
have sunk your capital, and need not expect relief till
you have sold your scrip.' Perhaps the man, says,
But we cannot sell our scrip. Will you lend us some-
thing on the security of the scrip ? ' The answer is,
We are not pawnbrokers.. Go to the parish.' ('Shame').
The man goes to the parish. The relieving officer says,
Are you a co-operator?' "I am." Then we won't
relieve you." But,' the maa may add, we cannot
ear bricks and mortar.'•Then we cannot do any--
thing for you.' Will you lend me anything if I de-
posit my scrip ? "No, we cannot; you are not a
pauper, and we cannot give you relief.' So the poor
operative falls to the ground.. Many men have thrown,
their scrip into, the fire; others have sold £lO worth, ,
for 10s. ; some have trampled it under foot, because it
stood between, them and the bare necessities of sub-
sistence. Theease of one man which has come before
my notice is extremely hard. This man actually
destroyed his scrip in order that its possession might
not prevent him, receiving relief. The relieving
officer gave the man relief to. the amount of Aix
or eight shillings. In, the course of time the
case came before the board of guardians. The
guardians heard of the particulars of the case. They
went to the secretary of the co-operative society, and
examined the books. The man had, forgotten to have
his name erased when he destroyed his scrip. His name
was, consequently, remaining on, the books. Im-
mediately the man was taken up and imprisoned for
receiving relief, because his name was on the books of
a co-operative society at the time that he received the
parochial relief. I might give you the particulars of
other cases to show yonthe gross injustice, inadequacy,
and niggardliness of these locali relief committees.
I must, however, say that all are not alike nor all the
manufacturers of the same character. The Fielclings,
of Todmorden, who give away £2OOO, per week to their
hands—the Armitages, of Manchester, who provide
their people daily with a good dinner—are bright ex-
ceptions to the general rule. (Applause.) What I
complain of is the .general action of these middle-class
committees. The temptation that exists forrevenging
themselves on successful workmen for old grievances
and union disputes ie, very great,. And now I come to
the means that ought to be adopted in order to prevent
the evils I have named. I say at the outset that unless
working men themselves sit on these committees there
can be no justice.. (Applause.) I have a working
man's committee in my own parish. I applied to the
Lord Mayor's committee for a grant, and received a
grant of £5O. But as soon as the squires and manu—
facturers saw that we were relieving,the victims of the
middle-class committee they wrote to London and
stopped the supply. The men of Burnley established.
a working men's committee: They were refused a grant..
The working men of Padiham were refused a grant.
So we applied to the Manchester central relief fund.
MreMaclure, the secretary, sent us word that the con-
sideration of the application, was postponed until there
were local subscriptions in, proportion to the assess-
ment of the parish. It was further necessary that we
should fill up the form to be sanctioned by the
manufacturers, the squires, and the poor-law guar-
dians. This of course,, we could not do, and we
,replied to that effect, but that we were willing to send
ithe balance-sheet and a statement showing how the
amount would be expended. The reply we received
was, that if we wanted any more forms we might have
them—(laughter)—so, we. gave that up. The real
obstacle to our obtaining a grant was the presence of
working men on our committee. I wrote then to the
Lord Mayor's committee, applying for another grant,
and asking whether he could get it if we received the
sanction of the manufacturers and squires& the locality.
They said they would, and not say anything about the
forms to be filled up. (Hear.) So I applied to the
manufacturers for their sanction. They refused, because
they could not sit on committees with working men.
One squire said he could not possibly sit on our com-
mittee, because another gentleman in the parish would
not join with working men. I then asked this
squire if he would give us the use of his name. He
said he could not, for he would have nothing to do
with working men. Such are the obstacles which
impede us. I am glad that I have first stated my case
to the working men of Liverpool. I have confidence
in the trades of Liverpool that they will sympathise
with the sufferings of their fellow working men. The
question is, Are working men capable of distributing
relief funds? I contend they are. In proof of this
assertion I say working men have friendly societies and
trades' societies which they managewith credit. (Hear.)
Working men receive 115,000,000 in wages, with
which they maintain their families, their trade socie-
ties, and their benevolent olubs. They are faithful in
much; it is unlikely they will be unfaithful in little.
(Applause.) The fact is the middle classes want to
receive all the credit of your subscriptions; and they
want to distribute the fund as they please, without allow-
ing you the management of one farthing of it. Will
you submit to this? (Loud cries of 'No, no.') Will
you have your subscriptions taken from you to a fund
over which you have no control? ('No.') Will you
have your funds administered by committees who
refuse relief to the prudent co-operator and the honest
trade-unionist? (.No.') Why not have your own
Working Men's Central Committee for Lancashire,
and thus fill up' the great want—a want that is felt in
every working-man's home in the cotton' districts?
(Hear, hear.) I submit this to your serious considera-
tion. Weigh well the resolution. What 1 wish to do
is to inaugurate a central committee of working men.
As they will not admit you into the local middle-class
committee, haver locallcommittees of your own, and
thus supply the wants and exigencies of the distress.
(Hear.) As a friend to the working classes, I say this
is one of the most important considerations that can be
brought before you. The Corporation of Liverpool
will not assist you. You are told that you are net able
to take up your subscriptions. My advice is, button
up your pockets, and contribute to a working men's
central committee. Let each trade send up its dele-
gate, and see the fund properly distributed. You will
thus do the work of charity and vindicate your psi.
tion. You will thus prove that you are able to manage
a relief fund, and relieve adequately and justly the
wants of your brethren, who are now suffering so
grievous a calamity. (Loud and continued applause,
during which the rev, gentleman resumed his seat.)
Mr. Williams, in rising to move the first resolution,
said he approached the duty with an amount of diffi-
dence which be could hardly account for; but, after

listening to the address of the rev, gentleman who had
just sat down, and hearing the remarkable statements
adduced, and also knowing by his own practical ob-
servations the great truism involved in Mr. Verity's
speech, his soul recoiled within him to find such con-
duct and such distinctions exhibited by those gentle-
men of whom better behaviour would have been ex-
pected. (Applause.) He begged to move the follow-
ing resolution
That this meeting views with the deepest sym-
pathy the increasing distress amongst the operatives
in the manufacturing districts, and is of opinion that
every effort should be made by all classes of the com-
munity for obtainining continuous contributions
towards the alleviation of the present unparalleled
crisis.'

The first question was, are the parties for whom they
were about to appeal worthy of sympathy? Hfdeclared
distinctly that the persons spoken of deserved their
sympathy, their co-operation, and their admiration,
for the manly fortitude they had exhibited during this
awful and unparalleled crisis. (A pplause.) He ap-
pealed to the working men who heard him whether the
Lancashire operatives were not always ready to assist
their fellow-workmen when a difficulty arose. (Cries of
yes, and hear, hear.) They were always most liberal
in their collections; they only needed to be asked to
hasten to the rescue—(hear, hear)—and on the grounds
of their liberality and brotherly fellowship he con-
tended they were deserving of the warmest sym-
pathy. (Applause.) He did not wish to say one
word disparaging the labours of the central relief
committee; but the questions were whether the
money provided by the public was properly dis-
tributed—whether it was administered in such a
a manner as to constitute a premium upon idleness and
mendicancy—and whether the relief that was intended
for honest sons of toil was really afforded to them.
(Hear, hear.) The instances which Mr. Verity had
given answered these questions. (Hear.) The case of
the co•operator, for instance, was most significant, and
afforded a correct idea of the existing state of affairs.
(Hear.) The only remedy was that working men
should take the matter up, and prove to the world that
they were capable of managing finances. (Cheers.)
Some people said that working men were not capable
of doling out benevolent funds. But he would take
the case of the Ironfounders' Society of Great
Britain. In .the annual balance-sheet of that body,
whiclt. embraced a period of 21 months—viz., from
January, 1861, to September, 1862—were the following
facts

Donations to members out of work L26,408 12 6
Donations to members in cases of
, accident
Superannuations .
Sick and funeral allowances .
Making a total of 21 months' disbursements of £35,187
7s. 7d. (Loud applause.) Could they not dole out a
, few pounds to those deserving it; and might not
working men, who had managed such a grand sum as
that, be entrusted with the distribution of relief to their
starving fellow sons of toil? (Hear.) It was high
time to do something. They ought to have been in
the field a month ago, and they would have been but
for the ungrateful and ungenerous conduct of the local
authorities. The delegates were received by Mr.
Weightman with every respect; they waited for an
answer, and received for reply a suggestion to take
Gill-street market! They applied for the Concert
Hall, but it had been pre-engaged. At last they
thought of Hope Hall. All honour to Mr. Perkins,
who, when told the objeet of the meeting, not only let
it most reasonably, but induced another party who had
previously engaged it to waive their claim. (Hear.)
lie (the speaker) called upon the working men to come
forward and do their part.. How should they like a
pittance of one' shilling a week to maintain their little
ones? The fact was enough to freeze their blood. It
was their bounden duty to, do something in such an
emergency. Let it be one promptly, liberally, and
continuously.. (Cheers.) (Mr. Williamaconcluded by
• reading the resolution.)
Mr. Winstanley seconded the resolution,. which was
carried unanimously.
Mr. John Gough Brown moved the following resolu-
tion That we, the representatives of the various
Liverpool Trade Societies, pledge our societies to do all
in their power, either by levies or voluntary subscrip-
tions, as each society may for itself determine, to assistl
as promptly as possible, and in a permanent way, our
distressed brethren in Lancashire.'

The meeting'had heard of the manner of distributing
the large sums-of money collected for the relief of the
distressed. It had struck him for some time that all
things wore not going on well; but he could have
formed no conception of the real state of things, if he
had not heard the extraordinary statements of the
P.tv. Mr. Verity. , (Hear.) It was most important that
the working people should. know how the. money was
doled out to, their fellow-sufferers. If better mean%
were not taken for relieving the distress a terrible
future was in store; for famine loomed in the distance,
and fever was borne on famine, and the judgment of a
just God would inevitably fall upon those-who would
permit such a direful calamity. (Cheers.)‘
Mr. Dagnall seconded the resolution, which was put
to the meeting by the Chairman and carried unani-
mously.
Mr. Lewha, moved the following resolution:—
'That the Executive of the Liverpool -United Trades'
Protective Association resolve itself into a committee,
to be called the Liverpool central committee, for the
purpose 0 collecting subscriptions for the relief of the
distressed Operatives, and that Liverpool be divided
into districts to act in concert With, and forward their•
subscriptions to the central coramittee,.and shall be em-
powered to send a delegate to see the funds properly
and equitably divided.'
• Mr. Glenville in seconding the resolution, thought
that if the working men present would only put their
shoulders to the wheel and work harmoniously they
would be able to assist considerably in relaxing not
only the distress in the cotton districts but the distress
among the cotton, porters of our own town, (Applause.)
The resolution was carried unanimously.
A vote of thanks was cordially given to the Rev.
Mr.. Verity, and also to the Chairman.
After a numben of subscriptions from persons in the
room had been promised and announced the meeting
dispersed; it being understood that steps would be im-
mediately taken, to remedy the abuses spoken of by

YOTJNG SMlCPBaixacm—Young. though he was, George
was now of age to be able to contribute something
towards thefamily maintenance;, for in a poor man's
house every child is a burden until his little hands
can be turned to a profitable account. That the boy
was shrewd and active, and, possessed of a ready
mother wit, will be evident enough from the following
incident :—One day his sister Nell went into Newcastle
to buy a bonnet; and Geordie went with her for
company; At a draper's shop in the Big Market, Nell
found a 'chip' quite to her mind, but on pricing it,
alas t it was found to. be fifteen pence beyond her
means. Girl-like, she had set her mind upon that
bonnet, and no other would please her. She accordingly
left the shop disappointed and very much dejected.
But Geordie bravely said, Never heed, Nell; come wi'
me, and I'll see if I canna win Biller enough to buy
the bonnet; stand ye there, till I come back.' Away
ran the boy and disappeared amidst the throng of the
market leaving the girl to wait his return. Long and
long she waited, until it grew dusk, and the market
people had nearly all left. She had begun to despair,
and fears crossed her mind that Geordie must have
been run over and killed; when at last up he came
running, almost breathless. 'l've gotten the siller for
the bonnet, Nell!' cried he. 'Eh, Geordie,' she said,
but boo hae ye gotten it!" Iluddin the gentlemen's
horses!' was the exultant reply. The bonnet was

in triumph.—Lives of the Engineers. By Samuel
Smiles.

THE LATE MR. JONAS WEEI3.—A well attended
meeting of the leading agriculturists of the United
Kingdom has been held at the Agricultural Hali,
Islington, for the purpose o deciding on the best means
of expressing the appreciation by the agricultural in-
terest of the country of the high character of the late
Mr. Jonas Webb, and the services he has rendered to
the cause of agriculture. The Hon. E. T. Yorke, M.P.,
presided, and among those present were Mr. W. Cox,
M.P., Messrs. J. Clayden Fisher Hobbs Simonds,
Jonas Bruce, Rigden, Sidney, Peck, &C. Mr. J.
Clayden, having explained the purport of the meeting,
stated that he had received letters from Lord Bernars,
and many gentlemen residing in Norfolk, Essex' Berk-
shire, &c., regretting their absence. The Chairman,
the Hon. E. T. Yorke, warmly eulogised the many
virtues of Mr. Webb, both as a friend and an agricultu-
rist, and proposed the erection in the hall of a statue
which would defy criticism, and do justice to him whom
they might call, in the language of Thomson, their
Shepherd King.' The following resolution was then
proposed by Mr. Turner, and s-conded by Mr. Fisher
Hobbs :—"lhat it is desirable that the agriculturists of
the United Kingdom, as well as the numerous personal
friends of the late Mr. Jonas Webb, of Babraham,
should mark their sense of his admirable public and
private character, and of the inestimable services he has
rendered to the cause of agriculture, by some permanent
memorial.' Resolutions providing that no subscription
should exceed 5 guin, as, and appointing a committee, to
be called 'The J onas Webb Memorial Fund Committee,'
comprising among many others the Hon. E. T. Yotke,
M.P., Lord Hardwicke, General A. N. Hood, Lord
Walsingham, &c., and requesting Professor Simonds
and Mr. S. Sidney to act as hon. secretaries, &c., were
then passed, and a vote of thanks to the chairman con-
cluded the proceedings. Upwards of £l6O towards the
proposed statue was subscribed by tbe meeting.

COPYRIGHT IN PICTURES.

COURT OF COMMON PLEAS, DEC. 12,

GAMBART V. BALL.—Both the parties to this suit were
printsellers, the plaintiff being in business at Pall-mall,
and in Paris, and the defendant in Holborn. The action
was to recover damages for an alleged infringement on
the plaintiff's copyright by photographing his pictures.
Mr. Collier, Mr. Prentice, and Mr. Thompson appeared
for the plaintiff, and Mr. Coleridge and Mr. Rew for the
defendant.

Mr. Collier, in opening the plaintiff's case, said that
his client, like many other picture dealers, was in the
habit of purchasing oriFinal pictures at large prices, and
afterwards of engaging—also at great expense—
engravers for the purpose of producing engravings of
those pictures. He was the owner of two celebrated
pictures, The Horse Fair,' by Mdlle. Rosa Bonheur,
and The Light of the World. For The Horse Fair,'
he gave the artist £1,600, he having outbid the French
Government; and he also engaged Mr. Thomas Land.
seer to engrave it, and paid him 809 guineas for so doing.
He purchased the copyright in The Light of the
' World,' for £2lO, and paid the owner £l3O for the loan
of it; and, in addition, Mr. Symonds had £3OO for
engraving it. The engravings were thus obtained at
an enormous expense. The present action was founded
upon the 17th Geo. 111. cap. 57, which gave the owner
of copyright in a picture a right of action against any
person who infringed it; and the circumstances which
he should prove against the defendant were, that he had
exposed for sale in his window and had sold photographic
copies of the pictures which he had mentioned, and this
without having the permission of the plaintiff to do so.
When applied to he refused to give the name of the
photographer, and he also declined to give any infor-
mation as to the number of copies which he had sold.
Mr. Gambart, in his evidence, said: lam the plaintiff
in this case. I purchased the copyright of Light of
the World' of Mr. H. Hunt for £2lO, and I
paid Mr. Combo, of Oxford, £l3O for the loan of
the picture. I likewise paid Mr. Symonds £3OO
for engraving it. The plate is not destroyed. The
publication line is on the plate; it was on the
plate before any copies were struck off. The photograph
produced (a small one, about four inches long and three
inches wide) was purchased at the defendant's shop. It
is a copy of my engraving, and must have been photo-
graphed from it. There is no other engraving but my
own in existence. The painting is still in the pos-
session of Mr. Coombe. A photograph could not have
been taken from the original, because it is too dark. If
the photograph had been taken from the original the
colours would be different, because there are some dark
colours in it which must have come out light if it were
photographed from the painting. I never gave the de-
fendant or any other person permission to copy the
engraving. I purchased The Horse Fair' of Rosa
Bonheur, and I sold it since to an American gentleman,
reserving to myself the copyright. There were two
pictures of 'The Horse Fair;' one I sold, and one is
still in my custody. I purchased the picture for £1,600,
and I paid Mr. Landseer 800 guineas for engraving it
The date of the publication line in that picture is the
20th February, 1857. The photograph produced (the
same size as the other), must have been taken from my
engraving; it could not have been photographed from
anything else. I never gave the defendant or any other
person permission to copy the engraving. The Horse
Fair' and The Light of the World' were very suc-
cessful pictures. They are worth £l,OOO a-year to me
as long as I live. I lose money by ninety out of every
hundred pictures I publish, and, therefore, when I get
a trump like these two pictures I make them pay.—
(Laughter.)
Mr. Collier ;--So you lose by the other cards and win
by the trumps.—(Laughter.)
Witness: Yes; the sale of these engravings was very
successful down to the time that the photographs were
published.

Mr. Collier: To what extent did the sale fall off after
the photographs were taken?
Mr. Coleridge objected to this question being put, in-
asmuch as the plaintiff could recover for the loss
which be had sustained at the hands of the defendant,
and not for losses through other people selling photo-
graphs. The defendant did not himself photograph
the pictures, but bought the photographs of a
traveller who came round to sell them to stationers and
printsellers. It was probable that hundreds of other
people had sold the photographs' and the defendant was
not to be affected by what they done.
Mr. Justice Willes suggested that the parties should
arrange the arrange the amount for which the verdict
should be taken in the event of the plaintiff recovering,
and that thg question whether the plaintiff ought to
succeed should be reserved tor the Court.

Some discussion took place, which resulted in £lO
being agreed upon as the amount of damages.
Mr Justice Wiles expressed his opinion that a
verdict should be entered for the plaintiff for this
amount, and that the defendant should have leave to
move the full court to set that verdict aside and enter
one for himself, upon two points; first, that what he
had done amounted to no "nfringement of copyright;.
and, secondly, that photographing from an engraving
was net a thing that was a violation of the statute.

Mr. Collier s-aid that the plaintiff had consented to
the damages being fixed at £lO, because this was the
first action which had been brought, but if any one
photographed from pictures in which he had copyright
in future, he would press for the full amount which he
could recover.

A verdict was then taken for the plaintiff for £lO,
subject to the opinion of the court.

Garibaldi, in reply to a letter addressed to him by a
friend in Glasgow, states that if he had agreed to draw
his sword in the cause of the Federal States, 'it would
have been for the abolition of slavery, full and uncon-
ditional.' Garibaldi's correspondent remarks updn this
letter it proves that the general did not mean to take
part with the Federals,, who, he knows, never dreamed
of honest negro emancipation.'
The railways are introducing gas. The Scottish Cen-
tral line has commenced; and, as it is the easiest thing
passible to arrange—by the means of pipes passing along
the roof—there is no excuse for any of the railways
not following the lead. It will be a very agreeable and
useful adjunct to these lines that are in the habit of
having accidents in the tunnels; and it may be sug-
gested to those who are ingenious enough to apply it,
that the gas may be made on, the premises; that
is to say, by the locomotive as it proceeds on its journey.
A company is being formed for the construction of a
harbour at St. Petersburg. After so many unsuccessful
attempts to realise this important design, a metropolitan
port remains as great a desideratum as ever, the larger
vessels being still compelled to unload at Cronstadt, and
the greater part of the cargoes having to be conveyed to
St. Petersburg in barges. Mr. Gladstone, the banker,
has alone subscribed 1,500,000 roubles towards the
capital required, an equal amount being guaranteed by
twenty Moscow firms. It is also said that M. Schneider,
of Paris, takes an interest in the matter, in which he
has advised the Russian speculators to avail themselves
of the assistance of M. Gache, a submarine engineer at
Marseilles, whose skill and experience have been re-
peatedly tested on similar occasions in France. No
Government commission, however, has been as yet ob-
tained.
HEn MATE= AND Da. NORMAN MACLEOD.—
The North British Mail has been 'informed of another
instance of the affectionate solicitude felt by the Queen
for those honoured by her acquaintance. Iler Majesty,
on reading in the newspapers of the death of the late la-
mented Dr. Norman Macleod, of St. Columba's, ex-
pressed her deep sympathy and regret that he had
been cut off in the full career of a life of wide-spread
usefulness—a sympathy intensified by his connexion
with memories of her visits to Balmoral both as wife
and widow. One of the ladies in attendance expressing
her Majestys' feelings on the event, the words fell on
the ears of a Scotch lassie,' a servant to Lady Augusta
Bruce, who ventured to remarlethat it must be the father
of Dr. Norraan Macleod who preached before her Majesty
at Balmoral. The Queen, being informed of this, desired
the girl to be sent into her presence; and the lassie, who
came from Glasgow or its neighbourhood, having
been ushered in, was asked by her Majesty regarding
the whole matter. She explained the points that she
i
thought inconsistent n the short and inaccurate
paragraph her Majesty had been reading. In conse-
quence a telegram was dispatched to Sheriff Sir Archi-
bald Alison, of Glasgow, who confirmed the girl's story;
and soon after a feeling letter of sympathy was sent to
Dr. Norman Macleod by the Marchioness of Ely by her
Majesty's command.'
A medical student, on his way to an hospital at. the
East end of London, where it was his turn of night
duty, carried in his hand, for purposes of self-proteci ion,
an operating knife belonging to his ease of instruments.
In one of the narrow streets which he had to raverse he
was seized round the throat in the approved fashion;
but, having his knife ready, he struck out vigorously,
and his assailant released his hold and dropped. Only
waiting to take one look at him for purposes of identifi-
cation—for garotters like laywnas, seldom attack singly,
—he made his way at speed to the hospital, and related
his story to his fellow students. Not twenty minutes
after his arrival there, a crowd of men and women
escorted to the door a respectable carpenter, poor fellow!
who had just met with a sad accident in his workshop
by 'overreaching himself and falling on P. e edge of one
of' his tools.' The interesting patient was admitted and
put to bed, and, it is ha,-Ily necessary to sac, was
promptly recognised as the baffled garotter. No re-
marks wf re made on either side, but the police authori-
ties were apprised of the circumstance ; and, as soon as
the recovery of the wounded carpenter is comdete,
which will not be retarded by any hints of coming
trouble, he will be handed over to the e ire, not of his
fri, nds, but of members of the police force, who will he
able to furnish some interesting details regarding the
mode in which he served his time,
