On the 12ai a communication was made between
the pit shaft and the trench that has been dug fronS
the pit mouth to the Dearn and Dove Canal, and the
water was allowed to flow into the workings. When
the pit is at work about fifty cubic yards of water are
removed from the low dip workings per day.
Pumping having ceased since Honday forenoon,
there will be in the lowest part of the pit about 250
cubic yards of water. It is the intention of the en-
gineers to fill up two broad gates, each 300 yards
long, and the stream of water is now running in at the
rate of 400 cubic feet per hour, so that several days
will be consumed in filling up the pit to the
height required. In the space that will be thus sub-
merged it is believed that no bodies will be found,
so that the friends of the deceased men will not have
this trouble to aggravate their already deeply wounded
feelings. When sufficient water has been run into the
pit, the engineers in charge will take steps to ascertain
the state of affairs below, and if the fire is out measures
will at once be taken to recover the bodies. It is quite
impossible to say what course will be adopted, as so
mach will depend upon the state of affairs at the time.
The temperature on Friday in the downcast shaft, at
twelve o'clock, was forty-two degrees, and in the
upcast forty-five degrees. There was a small quantity
of smoke issuing from the cupola. In the neighbour-
hood of the pit everything was quiet. The excitement
of the previous days had quite subsided, and only a
few persons in charge of the works, a few policemen,
and some fifteen or twenty spectators were to be
seen. The relatives of those entombed below appear
to have been satisfied with the explanations that
have been given of the position of affairs, and are
awaiting at their homes with what resignation they may
possess for the time when it may be possible to recover
the bodies. The men who were injured by the explo-
sion are all reported to be progressing favourably.
In addition to the list of names of those who are still
in the pit, the following have been mentioned :
Walter Lockwood, married, two children Tames
Davies, of Jump, hurrier ; Richard Watson,
married, two children, and wife pregnant; John Ellis,
of Barnley. who was described as single, was a mar-
ried man with one child. On Thursday afternoon a
meeting was held in the National schoolroom, Wore-
borough Dale, at which a number of the clergy and
gentry of the, neighbourhood were present. The Rev.
W;Banham, incumbent of St. Thomas's, Worsborough
Dale, was called to the chair. It was resolved, on the mo-
tion of S. J. Cooper, Esq., seconded by the Rev. J. New-
man, That this meeting desires to express its deep and
heartfelt sympathy with the surviving sufferers at the
late awful catastrophe at Edmond's Main Colliery, and.
with the widows, orphans, and relatives of those who
have been so suddenly deprived of life; and that, as an
expression of such sympathy, a public subscription be
immediately set on foot for the relief of such sufferers
in addition to any parochial relief that in &y be granted
by the authorities of the district.' A committee was
appointed for carrying out the above resolution. The
Barnsley Banking Company were appointed treasurers
The proprietors of the colliery have given £2OO, and
undertaken to defray the cost of the interment
of the dead. Messrs. Brown and Jeffeock, mining
engineers, have given £25. Subscriptions may
be paid to the Rev. W. Benham, or to the
treasurers. Incidents are still related of the touching
manifestations of sorrow by female relatives of the
those dead in the pit. Early on Friday a poor woman,
whose appearance clearly indicated that she was sorrow-
ing for friends below, was seen to approach the pit.
After walking for a time near the drawing shafts, she
went to the cupola, thinking she was unobserved, and
through the temporary opening that had been made in
the brick chimney that rises above the shaft, gazed into
the darkness, as though her eyes could penetrate the
darkness and see the beloved forma below. She was
accosted by. one of the neighbours—a goodhearted
-
countryman, who asked if she had lost any relative.
She replied that her father, husband, and son were all
dead in the mine. She still lingered about the shaft,
and appeared in such distress that her interrogator
feared to leave her, and after some persuasion induced
her to go away with him, but she did so with the
remark, Ah master.it is hard to part, and hard even
to leave the place.'

i'he following has been transmitted to the Glasgow
Herald by a lady in Edinburgh, distinguished for her
benevolent spirit and literary abilities :
Sir,—l had a most affecting interview yesterday with
the unfortunate sister of the notorious Mrs. M`Lachlan,
who is utterly ruined by the had fame of that wretched
culprit, and is now emigrating to Australia, having been
dismissed from the family in which she had been hither-
to a respectable servant. ! The case seemed so hard, of
visiting the sins of one sister on another, that I sub-
scribed 30s. to assist in the poor girl's outfit, but
lamented not being able to do more. I never saw any
one suffering under such intense despair—not loud,
but deep. She is to be accompanied by a sister equally
destitute, They have got a passage from the Emigration
Society; but it occurs to me that among the numerous
admirers of Mrs. M‘Lachlan in Glasgow there may
be some who would humanely extend their sympathy to
the innocent as well as to the guilty, and bestow some
pecuniary assistance on those poor outcasts, who are
driven from their respectable homes as servants into a
banishment as distressing as if they had been themselves
culprits. I had their papers carefully examined and
their story tested by a clergyman, who is convinced of
the truthfulness of their calamity. Therefore,. I now
appeal to the enthusiasm of Glasgow for generops help
to those whom no judge or jury ever condemned, and
who would desire to share in some of the interest felt in
Mrs. M`Lachlan, as they are ruined by her disgrace. I
inclose my card, and shall convey to the sufferers any
donations. They sail in a few days, banished for life
from. friends and country, to struggle in a distant land.—
Yours, 'C. S.'
The editor of the Herald will take charge of and remit
any sums whicll may be committed to his charge in
behalf of those innocent and unfortunate girls.

Mr. William. Henry Gladstone, eldest son of the Chan-
cellor of the Exchequer, took his degree at Oxford on.
Thursday, having obtained, after leavingEton, a student-
ship of Christ Church, a first class in moderation; and
for his degree,. a second in classics, and a third in law
and modern history. His father took a doubl• first as
a student of Christ Church._

The royal paddle yacht Osborne, Master Commando
George B. Bower, arrived at Portsmouth on Saturday
morning, from the Mediterranean, last from Plymouth.
The Osborne has been in attendance on his Royal
Highness the Prince of Wales and their Royal Highnesses
the Prince and Princess of Prussia during their tour 1
along the coasts of the Mediterranean. After landing
the Prince of Wales at Marseilles, the Osborne left for
England, calling at Gibraltar to take in coal and effect
temporary repairs to her broken paddle shaft. Sailing
again on the Bth inst., Lislym was reached on the 10th,
and she left again on the same day- Owing to the
damaged state of the Osborne's paddle shaft, the voyage
home has been made under half speed. Since leaving
Gibraltar heavy weather was experienced, and especially
in crossing the Bay of Biscay and at the mouth of the
Channel.

TEE REVOLUTION. IN GREECE

(From the Times Special Correspondent.)

Ancms, Pee. 2.—The politician and diplomatist at
Athens, before laying down his programme for the day,
should take a look at the old town clock of the Asty,
commonly called the Tower of the Winds,' and see
from which side the wind blows. By doing so he would
save himself a good d al of trouble and annoyance, be-
sides avoiding no end of mistakes and blunders. No
physical or political barometer is more infillible in this
windridden plain of Attica than that elegant octagon
tower in marble. Observe which of the eight emble-
matic figures in basrelief, facing the corresponding
points of the corn} ass, rules the day, and you will
know the temper of Athens for the day. Is
it the smiling figure of gentle Zephyrus, float-
ing soft..y along, ar:d scattering into the air a lapful of
flowers,' then Athens is in rosy humour, and both
diplomatist and politician may play safely with Athe-
nians. is it sultry Enrus, With stern and scowling
aspect, •announcing a hurricane; or mild Notus,
threatening to deluge Athens from his overflowing urn,
and they may venture on almost everything, for Athens
is so enervated and &moralised as to have lost all power
of resistance. T) 4rould, as is more probable at this
time of year, biuAering Dorcas, in his thick sleeved
mantle and hih laced buskins, blow his twisted cone,
then let them beware, for Athens is in a dangerous
humour, and not to be trifled with. Those sudden
*violent gusts rushing down through the gap between
Pentelicus and P. rues, and sweeping the dust of the
valley of the Cephissus, would irritate the most cold-
blooded mortil—how much more so the Athenians,
naturally rather excitable and obstinate!
Well, rarely has Boreas shown himself merrier and
madder than within these last few days, and this was
just the moment •thosen by those who had probably ne-
glected to look at the Tower of the Winds, or else dis-
regarded its w.frniaags, to oppose the general feeling of
the country in favour of Prince Alfred. The rcsult
was, that we had rather an exciting time of it, and that
the Provisional Government, yielding to the general im-
patience, as ota were informed by telegraph, issued a
decree for tie election of the Sovereign of Greece by
direct universal suffrage. Not often have the adver-
saries of a popular movement given such impetus to it
as in this instance.

The dernon-trations were tYv er. The whole country,
almost without the exception of a single town or pro-
vince, had raised its voice in favour of Prince Alfred.
High and low, town and country, civilians and military,
the clergy and the municipalities, had all joined. TRere
remained but one anxiety and one uncertainty—namely,
Will England consent to ield to the wishes or the
Greek nation? But even in this direction things
seemed to assume a brighter aspect towards the middle
of last week, when news arrived from the Greek Lega-
tion in London, according to which both Lord Pal-
merston and Earl Russell had, in their conversations
-with M. Tricoupi, poken in a manner which was
decidedly encouraging to Greek affairs and wishes.
Twen,y-four hours afterwards all was changed, ex-
cept the keen north wind. Circumstances had arisen
which seemed to give reality to the rumours- which pre-
vailed bout a combination of foreign influences with
the reactionary elements at home to work against the
popular movement in favour of Prince Alfred. The
.Aion, the Russian organ, and the Eipis, formerly the
organ of the Court, but now accused of having been
bought by the French Minister, had raised their voices
against the demonstrations, and tried to get up an
agitation for an orthodox Sovereign; and the officers
and functionaries devoted to the old regime, who had
been allowed to rerc.ain in the capital, began to show
signs of activity. In the midst of this arrived the
French steamer with Kolokotroni, the late Prime
Minister, on board.

This brought down the.storm against all those who
were known as adherents of the late dynasty. Most of
them had before received' from the Government the
order to leave' .but the order bad not been enforced.
Now the popular temper was such that the Provisional
Government thought it wise not to delay the enforcing
of the order. In this order was included Kolokotroni
and the two editors of the objectionable papers. The
first found an asylum on board the French flag ship, and
one of the latter.at the French 'mission in Patis.4a. This
VSS at once looked upon as a proof of the lurking sus-
picion that foreign influence had been the real author of
the attempts made to oppose the movement in favour of
Prince Alfred.

>On Saturday afternoon, however, a deputation
'waited on the Government, asking it to issue a decree
for the e'ection of Prince Alfred by universal suffrage,
even before the meeting of the Assembly. The Pro-
visional Government—probably less accessible to the
influence of Boreas, or, according to popular opinion,
too accessible to .other influences—began by hesitating,
and at last asked for 21 hours" to consider matters.
When the deputation returned next day, a.farther delay
was .asked till evening, and when that had expired the
deputation, instead of an knawer, was shown a telegram
Just arrived from the Greek Legation in London. Ac-
cording to this telegram, E..rl Russellhad declared that,
as Russia had withdrawn Prime Leuchtenberg, and as
both Russia and France recognized the validity of the
protocols, the acceptance of Prinee Alfred became like-
wise impossible. _

The news spread like wildfire,.and•every one seemed
headless and helpless. No. wonder. When the Athe-
nians decided to brave France and Russia, they
.had
hoped to be backed by the third protecting Power,
England..

ut could the telegrem be true? Might itnet be got
up for the occasion.? Some people thought the Govern-
ment quite capable of such things.; others recollected
the saying of M. Piscatori about the usefulness of a
mensonge de vingt-quatre heures,' and than there
seemed to be something rather suspicious .about those
unintelligible .ciphers.
_ _ _

To clear up-doubts, the British Legation was ap-
pealed to, and a hard time it was for Mr. Scarlett on
that Sunday evening as, one after another, all those who
had, or thought they had, some claim to receive in-
formation rushed in hot haste to -ascertain whether any
news confirming the telegram had reached the Legation.
But the result was, if possible, only greater perplexity.
The British Minister had received no information belrond
a telegram on the 16th, and the instruction dated the
20th, which had came out by the last mail, and neither
contained any clue to the mystery. -
Still, with the disposition which existed to catch .at
every strew, the very vagueness of• these instructions
left ascope for the most favourable interpretation. Free-
dom of election was., of course, eonstrued into acquies-
cence in the result of the election. Yet, with all this
good will at interpretation, there was no denying that
the telegram had produced a stunning effect. It was the
hardest trial which the Greeks have had as yet to stand.
It required strong faith and unusual firmness to perse-
vere. If the whole was a trap, those who laid it
deserve all credit. But again they had forgotten old
Boreas, who blew more merrily than ever during that
agitated night of Sunday, and on Monday morning
Athens awoke firmer and more decided than ever.
That one night had metamorphosed the people.
What had been yesterday a question of policy, of in-
terests, of expediency, had changed to-day into a
question of prineple and of national honour. They
understood that it was unworthy of a people who
claimed to be independent to be swayed, as they have
been hitherto, by the good pleasure or displeasure of
patrons, and that their first consideration ought always
to be their own well understood interest. This once
brought home to them, all hesitation ceased. Once the
election over it will be for England to decide whether
she thinks fit to accept the offer or not. This resolution
once taken every one was anxious to press matters and
bring them to an issue, so as to prevent all further
intrigues. Again, therefore, a deputation returned to
the Provisional Government, and after a good deal of
aliseussion, and perhaps some slight pressure, obtained
from it the promise of a decree ordering a plebiscite for
the election of the Sovereign by universal suffrage.
The proceeding was no doubt slightly revolutionary, I
but Until the Assembly meets, and a legal means is
thus given to the people to express its wishes, it is in
the nature of things that the self-same Demos which
proclaimed the Provisional Government in the Uni-
versity-square on the night of the 23rd of October
should consider itself as the representative of popular
'Wishes. If the Government yielded it was because
there could be little doubt that the small deputation
was tzul3r representing the wishes of the people, and
that, d all Greece behind it.
This happened
yesterday afternoon, and this morning
the decree
'The P made its appearance. It is as follows :
rovisional Government; taking into cousiderp,
Lion the unanimous and unmistakeable wish of the
Hellenic people to proceed at once to the choice of tht
King by direct suffrage, decrees :--
1. The Hellenic People is called upon to choose by
direct election the Ring of Greece. 2. In every Di-
marchy (Maine) a public list will be opened, in v;hich
every Greek citizen who has completed his 20th year
win write the name of the
election begins in Ring he chooses. 3. The
every commune on the third day after
the publication of the present decree. The election
lasts ten days, 4. The voting is superintended by a
Commission consisting of the Dimarch (Maire), the
eldest priest and the schoolmaster. The priests will
p
Write for those who are illiterate. Every evening a
eproces verbal'is drawn u on the lists and counter-
signed by the Commission. At the end of the voting
the lists of each commune are sent to the Eparch or
Nomarch (Prefet and Sous-Prefet), and by them to the
Ministry of the Interior. This latter will consign them
to the National Assembly, which will count up the total
number of votes each candidate has received. 'The
Voting begins each day at 9 a.m., and lasts till 4 p.m.
5. 'lips will be opened at the Consulates and Vice-
Consulates, according to Art. 2, in which every Greek
citizen abroad will write the name of the Ring whom I
he chooses. The work of superintending the voting
devolves on the respective Consuls, Vice-Consuls, or

Consular agents, assTated by two of the most prominent
members of the community. All the other regulations
of the present decre-- are applied in the same manner as
in the electons at home. 6. The Minister of the In-
terior will give special instructions for the printing of
the lists. Athens, Nov. 19 (Dec. I).'
Nothing can be simpler than this decree, and it is
generally approved. About the result I have not heard
even a doubt expressed. The general impression is that
after the manifestations all over the country in favour of
Prince Alfred, no Government which values its exis-
tence would dare to resort to any of the legerdemain of
which universal suffrage admits. Besides, the decree
is so conceived that it scarcely admits of any falsifica-
tion on a large scale. The lists are public, hence acces-
sible to any one who wishes to inspect them, and they
are to be presented to the National Assembly, which is
to ascertain the total of the votes for e,ch candidate.
But in. spite of this precautions will be taken to see the
thing fairly worked.

articles.title: BRUTAL IfURD_ER IN LIVERPOOL.
articles.text:
BRUTAL IfURD_ER IN LIVERPOOL.

At the Liverpool Assizes on the 16th, Thomas
Edwards, a butcher, was indicted for the murder of
Isabella Tongue, a woman with whom he had been
cohabiting for upwards of eleven years. The woman
was a prostitute and lived in a court off Norman-
street, Liverpool. Before she became acquainted
with Edwards, the deceased had, it ailpeared, an
intimacy with a man named Sullivan. Sullivan,
however, had been compelled to leave the country,
and only returned in November last. Then the con-
nection between him and Tongue was renewed, and
in consequence Edwards became dreadfully excited
and jealous. On the 27th November Edwards came
home ie the evening, and on finding that Tongue
had been out with Sullivan all ‘day, he became very
angry, and began to drink ale and rum. During
the evening he went out and got more drink, and
finally laid down on the sofa. Early in the morn-
ing Sullivan and the deceased returned to the
house, and Edwards angrily asked where Tongue
had been all day. The deceased made no reply, but
Sullivan said to the prisoner, 'What is that to you?
She has been out with me.' At this time Edwards
did not say any more, but sat near the fira with Sul-
livan, the deceased, and other women. The deceased
noticed that Edwards hada knife with him, and she
therefore, feeling alarmed for her life, suggested that
Sullivan and Edwards should go upstairs to bed
together, and that she and another female inmate
of the house, named Wilson, should sleep together
below. Sullivan and Edwards did go up stairs, but
the prisoner almost immediately returned below,
and (according to the deposition of the deceased)
demanded money from her, which she refused,
declaring that she would not prostitute herself for
him any longer. The prisonerthen stabbed Tongue
furiously in the neck and other parts of the body,
and she died very soon afterwards.
The evidence adduced supported the charge.
Mr. Pope, for the defence elicited that the priso-
ner was drunk, and that the deceased had an 'ill
will' to the prisoner. Upon these, points he com-
mented strongly in his defence.
The jury returned a verdict of guilty, with a
recommendation to mercy. The judge passed sen-
tence of death on the prisoner.

articles.title: _PROGRAMME OF THE NEW ITALIAN
articles.text:
_PROGRAMME OF THE NEW ITALIAN

MINISTRY.

The following is the programme of the new Italian
_Ministry as presented by M. Farini, the President of
,Council, to the Italian Parliament :
GENTLEMEN,—Since we hold from the confidence of
the King the important ,charge of the administration of
the State, it is our duty to declare that, before all, we
shall seek in the support of the Parliament, that authority
which is indispensable to establish good organisation at
home, and represent the honour and interests of Italy
abroad. The nation ,understands that the time has
come to secure the ,eonquests and the benefits of
unity, and to give an effectual impulse to internal
organisation. We propose to ourselves to respond to
that expectation of the people, by scrupulously study-
ing their wants and their interests; by accomplishing
the administrative reforms pointed out by experience,
on the bases of a wide.clecentralisation, and by giving
.an intelligent direction to the developments of .con-
stitutional liberties in every part of the organisation of
the State. That development of liberty has public
order for its first and necessary condition. If public
&an quillity were not firmly- maintained, Italy would
.feel her confidence in .her own triumph diminish, and
.would find as an obstacle in her path..the insurmount-
able opposition of the Governments and the peoples of
.Europe. The Italians, firm and assuredin the principles
of unity and national right, have proved themsell-,,s in-
capable of forgetting their deep devotedness to the
monarchy and law. To the spectacle 'of the civil
wisdom which Italy has displayed is added the
.feeling of national gratitude towards the army,
the symbol and pledge of our destinies; of the
army which, after heroically fighting the battle
of independence, gave in a painful ,conjuncture the
noblest example of self-denial and discipline, by restoring
the.autherity of violated law. On taking office, it is
scarcely necessary to declare that we hold the faith
which, lives in the soul of every Italian, the principles of
public law which constitute the nation, and the desires
which the Parliament has solemnly expressed. Unshaken
in our conviction that Italian unity will be realised, we
think that we respond to a general sentiment of dignity
in abstaining from making promises which would not be
promptly followed by effects, and we find in this same
conviction the right of declaring to Italy that she must
await the accomplishment from the gradualidevelopment
of events, and from opportunities prepared and waited for
withoutillusions as well as without mistrust.
,(Cheers from
the Centre.) The task of our regeneration commenced
and progressed by the spontaneous adhesionof all, by
the united.efforts of each individual will,.and,presented
itself to Europe as a guarantee of tranquillity and prp-
gress among civilised nations. We shall follow the
same path, taking the general condition of Europe into
account, and being watchful of upholding the influence
and entire independence of Italy. (Cheers.) It is a
great undertaking which Providence has visibly in-
trusted to our generation, by granting us favourable op-
portunities, the me,cessary qualities, and, above all, that
brave and honest King, in whose wisdom the faith of
the nation gathers fresh vigour, who has given his name
to the new-born concord of Italy, and in whom the
indissoluble destinies of Italy and the dynasty unite to
form but one.'

An English magazine has appeared at St. Peters-
burg. It is called the Nevski Magazine.
The Gazette du _Danube states that the importation of
arms into Servia through Wallachia has become so ex-
tensive that diplomatic interference has taken place,
France associating in the complaint. It is asserted that
an active conspiracy is at work, with the object of
bringing about an insurrection in the territories subject
to the Turkish sovereignty.
CrnexsTMs FARE.—It m 27 not be without interest to
state the fact that one Norwich poulterer has now
nearly ready for consumption from 8,000 to 9,000 geese.
A large portion of these will be dispatched to the metro-
polis, together with the usual liberal supplies of Nor-
folk turkeys.'
Owing to the recent derangement in the Australian
mails, the outgoing steamer will, in the usual course;
have left before the incoming one can arrive, and this,
coupled with the fact that the New Zealand advice.
(with the exception of Otago) are already a month
behind, has caused apparently a general wish that the
Government should take steps to delay, if necessary,
the next departure.
Music IN ViEraw.k..—The concert season began here
about a month ago, and some of the performances are
highly interesting for lovers of classical music. The
music of Beethoven Mendelssohn, and Mozart is always
well rendered by the orchestra of the Vienna Opera,
' and some of the symphonies of the former have recently
been pLayed in a way that is perfectly marvellous. A
I few days ago a Serenade' (a symphony in six parts)
by Johann Brahms was performed here, and the pro-
fessional world is still loud in its praises. The Emperor
has given to the Musical Society of Vienna a piece of
ground on which to build a conservatoriuni with the
nececssary concert-rooms and offices.— Vienna _Letter.
THE NEW TURKISH FRIGATES.—AdmiraI Mehemet
Pacha, sent some months ago on a mission to London in
connexion with the proposed new iron-clad frigates has
been telegraphed to return. Yaver Bey, first chamber-
lain, will, it is said, proceed to-morrow by the French
mail to replace him. We regret to learn that our recent
information as to the abandonment of the intention to
build these costly and unnecessary vessels, though
true at the time, has been falsified by a subsequent
decision. Notwithstanding the stat 3 of the Treasury
they are to be gone on with, and a first instalment
(80,000) of their cost was sent off the week before last,
a portion of the sum, we are assured, having been drawn
from the Custom-house, notwithstanding the arrange-
ment that its revenue is to be very differently employed.
—Levant Herald, Dec. 3.
THE LIBERAL CAUSE IN SOUTHAMPTON. —A meeting
of Southampton Liberals was held on the 15th inst.
to take into consideration the measures necessary , for
their protection, when it was resolved to have a meet-
ing of the while liberal party after Christmas' at which .
leaders will he chosen for the purpose of selecting
o indichtes and protecting Liberal voters in the registra-
tion court. Owing to the split in the Liberal narks that
court has recently been abandoned to the Tories, who
have struck off a number of good Liberals, and placed
on the register a number of spurious Tory voters.

articles.title: CONVICTS AT PORTLAND.
articles.text:
THE CONVICTS AT PORTLAND.

In the Times of Tuesday there appears a long account
of the mode of life at the Portland Prison, where men
under sentence of penal servitude undergo their 'hard
labour'

There are always from 1,400 to 1,600 convicts at
Portland, mostly working in gangs by themselves, but
now and then in close proximity to groups of free
labourers. You know at once when you are coming
upon the ground mostly worked by the former; on all
the steep headlands and high commanding bluffs which
are being scarped into perpendicular walls for the fort of
this Channel Gibraltar stalk the tall figures of the warders
all around. There is nothing of the listless routine of
sentry duty about these men. They carry their rifles
ready, a 4 seem all eyes and ears as they scan the ground
beneath them, like eager sportsmen looking for a
shot. Passing through two or three lines of such
vigilant 'look-outs' is rather impressing, and prepares
the visitor to expect such scenes of labour and enforced
toil among the convicts as .would induce them to run
some risk to escape. Nothing of the sort is, however, to
be seen as you turn into the Old St. Paul's quarries,
where some of the blocks rejected by Sir Christopher
Wren are still upon the ground. Here, amid a number
of old rusty cranes, on the hills overlooking the sea, a
large body of the convicts are at work in gangs of 25 or
30, each gang having its own warder, who, by the way,
has 15 hours' work to the convicts' 9 or 10. Toe
prisoners require no pointing tout, their dress, their
closely shaven aspect, their hatd, firm, ruddy, healthy
look, like pugilists in condition for a tight, and, above
all, their slow, lazy style of working, or rather moving,
which contrasts so strangely with the busy energy and
speed of the free workmen near at hand, all show them
at a glance to be 'penal servitudes' at hard labour.'
Here are men of every glade of infamy and crime, men
who were once clerks, merchants, and even commissioned
officers, down to poachers, burglars, murderers, and
that worst and most inveterate of all ruffians, who has
been inured to every form of punishment known to the
law short of hanging—the true London criminal. Some
few are employed in platelaying, some in blacksmiths'
shops, some at masons' or bricklayers' work upon the
great fortifications of the Verne; but the main bulk are
kept in the quarries. To nearly all, however, no matter
how employed, the some remark applies as to light and
slothful labours, and nearly all are alike In their
vicious and forbidding aspect—their low., narrow,
retreating foreheads, keen, restless eyes, and vin-
dictive animal features. This is not the mere effect
of prejudice on seeing them as 'convicts. The
type of the criminal head and face is well known
in Portland and its neighbourhood. They may be
recognised as a negro would be recognised in Boston.
Of all the convicts in Portland now there are not
.five per cent, whom any man judging by their mere
looks alone would 'ever think of trusting in a position
requiring the exertion of sense or the forbearance of
honesty. Some few among the number in these
quarries work in heavy chains, in most quaint dress of
gray and yellow, and gray and black. The former are
those who halve tried to break away, the latter are
ruffians who have used, or from their threats are known
to intend, violence to the warders. Both, however,
clank about with a defiant swagger as if their chains
were honourable distinctions of their strength and
esurage, in which light there is but too much reason to
believe they-are also regarded by many of their fellow-
prisoners. In 'these quarries the .men work at quarrying
and dressing blocks of stone in winter about eight and
a-half hours a day, in summer nine hours, and some-
times a little over. The work, indeed, would be hard
labour if fairly done, an. there are some few, but
very few, who really do work well and as .if
labour was a relief to them. But the great majority
take matters very easily indeed, as may be judged
when five convicts kept at their work only quarry
about as .much stone in a day as two free
labourers working for their hire. It is not suggestive
of hard,work,to see a fellow put down a heavy hammer
that he ought to be wielding dustily and stop to swing
his arms and clap his hands to keep himself warm.
When this is the hard labour' wecan see at once wily
convicts do .not dread it. When we come to know how
they are nurtured and lodged in the ,prisoniu order that
their strength may be keptup to the required standard
for this imaginary hard labour whichthey are supposed
to perform, we get a real light thrown upon the in-
difference with which penal servitude in this country is
regarded, and gain a clue to .the reason why it is that
so large a proportion of ticket-ef-leave men are, to say
the least, not unwilling to return to the so-called 'penal
servitude.' ,Perhaps while the visitor is regarding this
mockery of work it may begin to rain.; at once the
mimic toil ceases, and the convicts are marched off in
gangs to sheds erected for the (purpose, where they are
carefully sheltered from the weather, and can look out
with complacency upon the free labourer, who, having
himself and his family to keep, must stay and bear what-
ever weather Heaven sends, wet or dry, hot or cold.
The contrast ;between the condition of the two, how-
ever, by no means ends I ere. The comforts that are
denied sti misery, though proffered to crime, have been
an old theme ,of invective ever since the new convict
'system' came into operation. At no part of England,
however, is the superior condition of the convict, as
compared witinthat of the honest labourer, brought side
by side into such startling contrast as at Portland.
When twelve o'clock comes in the works at the
Verne, the free labourer, who has done more quarrying
than any two ,convicts that day, ,may be seen sitting
down to his meal of bread and cheese, sometimes with a
bit of dried fish-or a tin pot of coffee, the latter gene-
rally unsweetened. The convict leaves off work at half-
past eleven, and goes to his cell to wash, comb his hair,
:in fact, make a little toilet, before he sits down to his
very ample dinner. The prison is wide and lofty in all
the chambers and avenues, well lighted and well venti-
lated, yet kept comfortably warm, and, above all, so
scrupulously clean that it is a comfort to look at it.
While the hard-labour ' men are making their toilets
their dinners are carefully got ready, weighed out, and
served smoking hotin bright clean tins, and at 12 o'clock
each man comes forward with his gang, and receives
every one his separate allowance. Their dinner three
days a week is as follows :—One pint of ,soup properly
seasoned, thickened with barley, rice, .carrots, and
onions, and equal in nutriment to any ever placed on a
gentleman's table; 5-1 s ounces of cooked meat, free oi
lerpn; 11b, of potatoeS, and 10 ounces of rich suet pud-
ding. On three days asi -k the pudding is replaced
with six .ounces of bread, and on Sundays the meat is
xncreased to six ounces. With this little dinner in his
!in every man retires to his comfortable cell, where he
is allowed an hour to consume it at his leisure,—not
that the time is always so spent; many have, or affect
to have, suspicion as to the weights or quantities they
have got, and these fellows, some ef whom ;reface a
point of doing it for the sake of giving trouble, have to
be accompanied to the kitchen by the warders, where,
according to the rules of the prison, they are entitled to
have everything re-weighed and measured before their
eyes. All, however, do not nine in their cells—some
are portioned out in larger rooms in cosy little messes
of eight or ten. These are mostly men in the third and
fourth stage—that is, men who have completed two-
thirds or three-fourths of the time—not of the sentence
—noboay completes that—but the time at which they
are entitled to claim their ticket-of-leave. They have
extra comforts and privileges beyond dining in messes.
In addition to the dinner we have inentiened the men
in the third stage receive on Sundays two ounces' of
cheese, with three ounces of bread and half a pint of
beer after it; while the men in the fourth stage receive
the same as to bread and cheese and beer as the third,
with the addition of a trea& pudding after dinner on
Thursdays, baked mutton, in lieu of beef, on Thursdays
and Fridays, and baked beef, instead of boiled, on Sun-
days and Mondays. Here, then, we begin by giving
our convicts a daily dinner such as for nutriment,
quality, and quantity few labouring men can afford on
Sundays, and we gradually raise the sale of luxuries
till they dine at last on soup, baked beef, bread and
cheese, and beer, and pudding. Yet the public, who
don't know these things, wonder why penal servitude is
not dreaded, and why, above all others, ticket-of-leave
men who have undergone this piinishment ' should,
after their spell of liberty in the slums of great cities,
show such an accountable desire to return to it again.
. After describing some of the incidents of the convicts'
life—their privilege of making complaints to the
governor, and of obtaining small favours, such 'as
exchanging their gruel for tea, if preferred,' and of
writing letters to their friends, the writer describes the
convicts' breakfast :--

Their breakia-sion Suncay and three days a week is
a pint of tea and 12 ounces of bread; on the other three
days a pint of cocoa and the same quantity of bread;
and in this meal only is there no difference made, men
in all stages of their captivity faring alike. After
breakfast there is chapel, and at seven in summer, and
half-past seven in winter, there is the usual muster and
walk to the quarries, when there is the usual hard
labour' we have described till half-past eleven, when
they return to wait for dinner, as before. When we add
that every prisoner has half a day's schooling every
week, and that on this half day he takes a bath and has
his hair cut; that on Saturday afternoon all work ends
at 4.30; that on Sundays, after service, the prisoners
may walk about the yard, or sit in their cells and read,
we have told all the terrors of 'penal servitude' and
hard labour ' oit the public works.

THE SOUTHERN MAIN DRAINAGE.--The first stone
in connexion with the outfall in Erith marshes has just
been laid, and the tunnel sewer between Plumstead and
Greenwich is now completed. A curious discovery has
been made during the construction of the works in the
marshes, Nti here some thousands of,yew trees eight to
fifteen feet below the level have been exhumed, pert ctly
sound, embedded in layers of leaves and peat, and
supposed to ha some hundred years old

articles.text:
11017 HISTORY IS WRITTEN IN

Mr. Foublanque in his Napoleon and l'echeli '
translates the examination paper of a Chinese candidate
in a competitive examination who had been set to write
a history of the recent war. It begins as follows In
the fifth moon of the 10th year of the reign of Hien Fung,
the wisest and greatest Emperor that the world has yet
known, if we except the Lord who now reigns, and who
Is to all his predecessors, as the sun is to a paper lantern,
it was determined by the Emperor, whose heart was big,
and who loved his people, to drive out of his dominions,
which means from off the face of the world, all foreign
devils and barbarians, who, by cunning devices and
falsehood, had gained admission into the land. Now,
these foreign devils and barbarians became afraid, and
they prepared a humble petition, praying to be allowed
to send deputies to offer tribute and submission to the
Ruler of the Universe. When the Lord of Ten Thousand
Years heard of this audacious request, his anger was
aroused, and, he ordered that when these foreigners came
they should be slain. It is true, and all men should
know, that far away across a sea which the stupid bar-
barians call the Red, because its waters are blue, there
are some islands inhabited by savages who are called
English, French, American, and other -.le names. These
lands are remote, and very poor, so much so that, although
under the Imperial sceptre the Ruler of the Work had
taken pity on them, and allowed their people to dwell in
peace and piggishness. Great was the goodness and the
wisdom of the Emperor Bien Fung ! But these foreign
devili have wicked hearts, and they came in many ships
and with many soldiers' and tried to cre,te fear among
the people; and three of their great men—the greatest
no greater than a second-class white-button mandarin—
presumed to approach the shores of the Empire, even unto
the mouth of the Peih.o, and demanded permission to
throw themselves at the foot of the celestial throne. The
names of these men were Lau-Ghin, an Englishman,
Bar-Gin, a Frenchman, and Yanki-Wad, an American,
They took with them Jay-Ho, an English sea-mandarin,
with many ships -; and they said to him, We weuld go
to Pekin • but, see 1 there are braves on the banks, and
they will kill us!' And Jay-Ho said (Ho was a fool!).
'Come with me, and fear not, for I will drive them away!'
And Glo and Ghin said, Be it se but wae was more
cunning, and he surrendered himself to our braves, who
carried him to Pekin in a wooden cage, and there im-
prisoned him. And Jay-Ho brought 743 ships, each
carrying 2,317 soldiers, and 419 guns, and he attempted
to enter the river; whereupon 100 braves were sent to
attack him, and they burned all the ships, and slew all
the barbarians, only nine of whom escaped; and among
these were Glo and (Thin.'

articles.title: TURKISH EXHIBITION.
articles.text:
TURKISH EXHIBITION.

The ;following announcement has been forwarded-to
-us from the Turkish Embassy :
'‘ A National Exhibiti*n is to opened at Constanti-
nople on the Ist Ramazan (20th February, 1863), for
three months. Although reserved exclusively for the
products of the so'l and industry- of the country,
nevertheless agricult ral and industrial machines and
implements, for pm+ 'cal use, from foreign ananufac-
tories wkll be ad, _tted. Manufacturers wishing
to exhibit such articles will enjoy the benefit
of a remission of the Customs' duties. It is
well understood that the admission of foreign pro-
ducts will be limited to this sole category, -and that a
-manufacturer cannot send more than one article of the

The articles abovementioned which, after having been

of the ImperialkGovernment than the exemption from
• customs' duties.'

articles.text:
BREACH OF PROMYSE CASE.

In the Court ‘of Exchequer, Dublin, ma ,Friday, the
assessor sat,for:the purpose of assessing the damages in
a case of breath of promise of marriage. The plaintiff,.
Miss Isabella E. Rattle, was the daughter of a ravect-
able solicitor now • deceased, and was a young lady of
great personal attractions, accomplished, and well
educated. In :February, 1362, she became a governess
in the family of Captain and Mrs. Graham, Maryville,
near Cashel, .where she became acquainted with the
defendant, Robert Graham, a brother of Capt. Graham's,
and at that time living at Dundrum, county of Tipperary,
• where he had charge of a dispensary district. Ile fre-
quently dined with the family of ,Captain Graham, and
soon paid such marked attention to the governess as to
attract the notice of the family. Love letters followed,
ending in a proposalof marriage in the end of August,
1862, the defendant coming to ,Dublin in the beginning
I of September, and settling the preliminaries of marriage
'with the mother and biother of the plaintiff. The day
I was fixed for the marriage, and plaintiff gave up her
situation, but shortly after defendant broke off the en-
gagement, as the plaintiff alleged, at the instance of his
family, that he might pay his addresses to another young
lady. The promise and the breach of it were not denied,
,and the only question was the amount of .the damage,
.and to assist in settling it the love corrPspondenee on
,both sides was put .in. The letters of the defendant
were ardent, and filled withverses expressing the warmest
feelings, though not of a very high order of poetry. En
one of them, to the lady's brother, after the marriage I
had been decided ,on, he says he considered her to be a,
young lady of high intellectual attainments and' subli-
mity of disposition and feelings.' Miss Ruttle also
•wrote something in the poetical vein, concluding one of I
her effusions thus.:—

'Source of joy And woe,—feiler of stern fate,
Lord of high and low,—woman calls thee fate;
Fierceness owns thy spell—vulture, thou, and dove,

Language cannot tell half thy pow', oh love!'
The defendant attempted to make out, in mitigation
of damages, that the advances had been made by Miss
Ruttle, who took advantage of her position in Captain
Graham's family to 'entangle a mere boy in a match;
but it was replied that the boy was 24 years of age,
and made the first advances to the young lady, who
was 2L— . . The 'damages were assessed at
£250.

SHANGRA; Oct. 25.—Two ,expeditions have been sent
from Ningpo against the rebels, And were successful.
Randing was captured by the allied forces on the 23rd
inst., and Finagoha (?), the rebel stronghold, was carried
by assault by the Imperialists on the 24th inst. The
llahomedans in Shensi have been routed, and peace is
now restored in that province. The Duke of Lancaster
has been totally wrecked off Formosa. The captain and
crew were saved. An extensive business is being trans-
acted in cotton. Ten thousand (? tons of shipping)
have been chartered for the transport of the raw mate-
rial from Ilongkong to Europe. Intelligence from
Japan states that the Tycoon has declared his inability
to punish the perpetrators of the late murder, and has
applied to the British Government for assistance. The
cholera has carried off a quarter of a million of the in-
habitants of Jedde.

NOVEMBER 6.—The Taepings are moving on Kanding,
and are expected to attempt its recapture. It is rumoured
that they are also marching to attack Sankow. An Im-
perial force is advancing for the protection of this city.
The news from Japan is unsatisfactory. The position
of foreigners was precarious. The meeting alleged to
have been 'recently held by the Daimios did not take
place. A bloodless revolution is reported to be in pro-
gress, having, among other objects, the destruction of
Jeddo. The whole country is in a most unsettled state.
Tea lower. Silk firm. Settlements in fortnight, 2,000
bales. Export to date, 49,500 bales.

HOW GENERAL WCOOK LOST HIS STARS.—A
correspondent of the Cincinnati C9invorcial says
'General Bragg exposed a fact in his official report of
the battle of Chaplin-hill which General M'Cook had
omitted to mention. The General was looking rather
shabbily here in the way of broadcloth, and was moved
to explain his seediness, which he confessed he would
not have done if Bragg had not blabbed. A night after
, the battle of Chaplin-hill had closed, one of Gilbert's
borrowed brigades was withdrawn from M'Cook's front
without his knowledge. The mystery was never ex-
plained, but that is foreign. His ambulance, contain-
ing his personal baggage, meantime, had been ordered
from the rear to his quarters, and the ambulance driver
drove through the gap left by the vagrant brigade and
halted inside of the rebel lines. The corps of head-
quarters servants who accompanied the train were gob-
bled up at the same time, but some of them escaped.
Thus General M'Cook lost his elegant new passants with
double stars, which friends had sent to him, with all of
his wearing apparel, except the threadbare and battle-
worn suit in which he fought. His servant ludicrously
descrLes the absurd scenes in the rebel camp, when the
thin-legged and spare-ribbed rebels attempted to en-
velop themselves in M'Cook's enormous drawers and
undershirts. They would hold about four rebels
apiece and three weeks' rations for padding. The
General never can get even unless he captures Hum-
phrey Marshall;

E KING or I:SMAIIIC—A dispatch from Copen-
hagen announces that the King of Denmark is rather
seriously ill. This sovereign is only fifty-four years
of age, and his death would be a serious loss for the
country, which he governs in a liberal spirit. He has
no children, and his heir-presumptive is the future
father, in-law of the Prince of Wales—Priece Christian,
of the House of Schleswig-Holstein Glucksburg. The
rights
.of that prince were established by the law of
succession of the 31st July, 1853, and. guaranteed by a
rotocol ,igned at London by the principal Powcr.T.

LONDON 1N THE FUTURE.

In seven years from this date there will be greater
changes effected in the configuration of IWemoropolis
than have been wrought during any fifty .years since
the Great Fire. We shall miss that ceaseleds and un-
broken string of omnibuses flying to Paddington, and
in which the London Conveyance Company set an ex-
ample to the London General in losing money by horse-
flesh. The Underground Railway will be working its
hundred or more trains a day, and Paddington will be•
come a civic suburb. By that time there will be two noble
bridges at Blackfriars in place of the pt eseq dilapidated
structure. The London and Chatham will attach
the villages of the south and south-east, as the Metro
politan will those of the north, and, in relieving- the
traffic,' add to it many new items. The embankment of the
Thames will give us a choice between the dangers of
Ludgate hill and Fleet-street, and some other dangers
of which we at present know nothing; but the choice
is needed, and so long as the main traffic east and west
is shut up to a highway not wide enough for the main
street of a village, we must go on working for outlets.
Then, with the number of bridges doubled, there will
be the farther relief of the main thoroughfares of all
the traffic bound for southern districts, and for which
there will be accommodation to cross the river at almost
any point where a crossing would be desirable. More
road, more markets, more bridges surely these are
advantages worth having, even at the sacrifice of many
ancient landmarks. We cannot cling to an old doorway,
or sigh over the impending fate of a brick wall that
once sheltered a great wit or a great soldier, or a great
rascal, while we are hemmed in by a crowd of people
who have lost their temper because they have lost their
way, and who simply wish to get to their destinations
by the shortest possible routes, and without having to
fight for it at every step they take, at the risk of losing
their time and breaking their necks.

Amongst the patents of invention, published recently
in the Canada Gazette, were a self adjusting and self
fastening clothes wringer; a self acting security gate;
a spring power boot crimper: a singing school mechani-
cal modulator; and an economical clothes dryer.
The Sleek, the Independance Beige, and the Courier
have so offended the ecclesiastical authorities ,of the
Grand Duchy •of Luxembourg, that the chief of the
clergy has placed an interdict upon them. The writers
in the Courier (a local paper) are declared to be excluded
from the Catholic church until' they make public recan-
tation; while those who subscribe to the paper are told
that the sacrament of penitence will not be valid to
them as loßg as they are subscribers.
The Royal Dublin Society met on the 13th inst. to
hear a lecture from Professor Gamgee on disease and
mortality among cattle. When he had concluded, Mr.
Ganley, salesmaster, made an extraordinary statement.
He said that, unless some means were devised to give
some compensation to the farmer for diseased cattle, it
was impossible to prevent him from selling them, or the
butcher from killing and selling them. Unless some
society were formed to have diseased meat paid for, it
would be killed and eaten. There was no use in mine-
ingthe matter, every one of the salesmen sold diseased
cattle. The farmer could not otherwise pay his rent.
The disease is so prevalent that he could not live were
he to submit his cattle to destruction. Professor Gamgee
said he would have gone 1,500 miles to hear this con-
fession, and he agreed with Mr. Ganley that some plan
-should be adopted for paying the farmer for diseased
-cattle.

SELLING INDIAN CIIILDREN.—The Alta CaVol-Ilia
says August Hess, —ho has returned to this city
from a pro4pecting tour through the lower part of Lake
county informs us that he saw a number of men driving
Indian children before them to sell in the Napa, Solano,
Yolo, and other countries of the Sacramento basin. In
one instance he saw two Men driving nine children;
in another, two men with four children; in another,
one man with two girls, one of them about 14 years of
age, apparently. The age of these children varies
from six to 15 yens. Rumour says that about 100
children have been taken through Lake county this
summer for sale. They do not follow the main roads,
but usually take by-paths Rumour says, further, that
the hunters catch. them in Mendocini and Humboldtt

counties, after killing their parents. If the children try
'to escape, and are likely to succeed, they shoot them.'
PROPOSED DINNER TO LORD PALMERSTON AT EDIN-
EURGH.—A meeting of the conveners of the liberal
committee was held on the 15th inst. in the Waterloo
Hotel, Edinburgh, to consider the desirability of invit-
ing Lord Palmerston to a public dinner during his
approaching visit to Scotland. Sir William Gibson
Craig was called to the chair, and the following resolu-
tions were unanimously and cordially agreed to :
'That in the prospect of Lord Palmerston paying an
early visit to Scotland in connection with his office of
Lord Rector of the University of Glasgow, it is desirable
that public expression should be given to the admiration
so generally entertained of his lordship's liberal policy
and valuable services as a statesman' and of the vigi-
lance and success with which, in the true interests of
peace, he has promoted the safety and maintained the
honour of the country. That Lord Palmerston be
respectfully solicited to accept a public entertainment
in the city of Edinburgh on as early a day as may be
consistent with his lordship's convenience.' A third
resolution appointed a committee to make the neces-
sary arrangements in the event of Lord Palmerston's
acceptance.
THE PRINCESS OF PRUSSIA AT ROME.-011 the Satur-
day before their departure from Rome, the Cresvn Prince
and Princess of Prussia, at half-past 8 in the morning,
went to the Ghetto to witness a Jewish service in the
principal synagogue. On the morning of the following;
day the Prince and Princess, with their suite were pre-
sent at pontifical mass in the Sistine Chapel, in the
afternoon`, accompanied by Mr. Odo Russell and Mr.
Pentland, attended divine service at the English Protes-
tant Church, where they heard a sermon by the Rev.
Mr. Woodward. Their Nye' Highnesses received
,Cardinal Antonelli and Monsignore Giraud at dinner in
the evening. On the Monday the Prince went to pay a
quiet farewell visit to the King of Naples at the Farnese
Paliuse. His Majesty was seated at dinner with so little
appearance of regal eclat, that some delay intervened
before he could get ready and repair to the drawing-room
to receive the Prince. Not seeing his Royal Highness
there, nor finding him make his appearance for some
time afterwards, the King sent to know where he was,
when he learnt that the Prince, after hearing that the
King was at dinner, had contented himself with leaving
a P.P.C. The counterpart of this little incident took
place later in the evening at the Caffarelli Palace. Din-
ner was just over, and tbeir Royal Highnesses were in
the drawing-room with their guests, Mr. Adeane, M. P.,
Lady Elizabeth Adeane, and Mr. Odo Russell, when a
chamberlain announced to the prince that the King of
Naples had come. A few words passed in an under tone,
the chamberlain vanished, the door of the drawing-room
was reclosed, and the royal visitor returned to the Far-
nese Palace. This was all that the guests saw, but
whether the King was sent away with a not at home,'
or whether he had a momentary interview with the Prince,
or whether he originally intended only to leave a civil
message at the Caffarelli Palace, are questions on which
the gossip-mongers of Rome are still divided.
SINGULAR SUPERSTMON.—A correspondent (says the
Glasgow Herald) transmits the following account of a
superstitious ceremony which took place the other dayat
Neilston :—The jolly blacksmith there is in possess,on
of a fine young she ass, which, with her frolics, has
caused great amusement amongst the boys of the town,
while some calculating old gentlemen wondered what
could be the use of such an animal. But its usefulness
was made apparent in a very queer manner the other
day, by the appearance of a deceet young Irish woman
with a child in her arms about five months old, with the
request that she might be permitted to pass her child
three times under the ass's belly. Of course her request
was granted. Now, you must know that the ceremony
was not to cure, but to prevent the child taking the
Looping cough. The cuddle was immediately removed
from the stable, and solemnly led out to the yard.
Meantime the woman had procured a handful of oat-
meal, to be given to the cuddie while the child was
being passed and repassed under its belly. But care
had to be taken lest the cuddie should eat all the meal,
as three piles were to be kept to be put into the child's
mouth after the ceremony. All things being in readiness,
the rite was about to be performed, when it was sud-
denly interrupted with such a roar of laughter from the
two young fellows who were assisting that well nigh
frightened both cuddie and child out of their senses.
But, all being got quiet again, the child was safely
passed under the animal's belly three times, and the
'piles' of meal duly put into the child's mouth, to the
complete satisfaction of the mother, who said that the
child would never take the hooping-cough while it
lived, an' I'm very much obliged to yez an' there's
another chil' cornin' up in the evenin' to yez, to be
treated in the same way.'
We have heard,' says the Journal du Havre, 'that
a company is now being formed. in Paris for the purpose
of transforming the garden of the Palais Royal into a
winter garden like the immense greenhouses annexed
to the palaces of the wealthier Russian nobles. The
company proposes to bear the whole expense of making
the garden a place of recreation u.nequalied in the
world. It would be devoted to concerts, games of all
kinds, artistic exhibitions, &c. In May, every year,
the glass roof would be removed, and the garden
opened to the public as usual.'
NATRICIDE.—A shocking case of matricide has occurred
at Warta nhill, near Dumfries. A stocking-maker,
named Thomas Cathrae, who resided with his wife and
his widowed mother, occasioned a family quarrel by hie
devotion to drink. Though in a state of intoxication,
he endeavoured to leave his workshop for further indul-
gence at the public-house. The mother and wife
interfered to prevent his going away from his premises,
and in the scuffle that ensu d the son struck his mother
a blow on the head which in a few minutes caused her
death. The murderer is in custody.

'SPARROW MURDER.—A country paper of this week
has the following announcement Crawley Sparrow
Club.—The annual dinner took place at the George Inn
on Wednesday last. The first prize was awarded to
Mr. J. Redford, Worth, for having destroyed within the
year 1,467. Mr. Heaysman took the second, with 1,448
destroyed. Mr. Stone third, with 982 affixed. Total
destroyed, 11,944. Old birds, 8,663; young ditto, 722;
eggs, 2,ss9."—Times.
Who killed Cock sparrow?
I,' said three men of Crawley,
With my club in ray mawley,
I killed Cock-sparrow!'
Who saw him die?
I,' said Caterpillar,
And I blessed sparrow-killer,
As I saw him die.'

Who'll dance On his grave?
'l,' said Mr. Slug,
With Green fly and Red-bug,
We'll dance on his grave.'

Who'll weep for his loss?
'l,' said young Wheat-shoot,
Fruit, and Flower-bud and root,
We'll veep for his loss.'

OUR OFFENCE TO THE YANKEES.
While wrath distorts thy visage lank and haggard,
Why grin at me, and glare with evil eye?
Why, in the strain of a malignant blackguard,
Jonathan threaten and revile me—why.?
Why so vindictive is your roaring flood
Of foul abuse ? What. have I done, that makes
You keep declaring that you:11 have my blood,
More venomous in spite than maddened snakes?
Not I your landmarks imve removed, nor when
- You were hard pressed in battle for the right,
A quarrel for a few enlisted men
Did I pick with you, and impede your fight.
Ah ! those are wrongs by which one might be driven
To menace, rail, and vow revenge like you.
Such, injuries are not to be forgiven
To those who suffer them by those who do.

'REMEMBER THE G'ROTTER!'
A CHRISTMAS CAROL.
Remember, remember, the first of November,
Slippery, sludgy, and fog;—
For I sees good reason why this glummy season
Should keep us in pocket and tog.'
Hurrah! 4
Then a squeeze and a shake for Sir George's sake!
A squeeze of the gorge for the friends of Sir George!
Hip, Hip, Hurrah!

Remember, remember, the last of November,—
Old Bailey and sentences long,—
If we drops upon Bramwell, it's queer but he'll clam
well;
He gave it our pals hot and strong.
Then Hurrah!
For a twist and a wrench for the cock of the bench!
A jolly good shake for Judge Bramwell's sake!
Hurrah!

All hail to November !—But welcome December,
For we'll 'put the hug on' yer yet;
So the shiners are swagg'd, we don't care if we're
lagg'd,
A ticket-of-leave we shall get.
Hurrah!
Then a twist and a hug for the Londoner's lug!
A jolly good squeeze for the Cockney's wheeze
Hurrah!
Choruss.
A cord, a cord,

For Beggar and Lord,
A trusty steel to poke him;.
An Indian Claw,'
To fraetmie his jaw,
And a jolly good squeeze to choke him!

FRENCH AND ENGLISH BUILDING.
Another street of palace-domes
Is added to the outward splendour
Of Paris, rivalling old Rome's
For which Rome freedom did surrender.
Alas, how London lags behind!
Cry some, our humble structures scorning;
But here a man may speak his mind,
And Punch tells truth without a warning.

True, Paris is the finest place
In Europe and the world, to look at;
At none folk plays with truer grace
None do they better dance and cook at.
in most fine arts they much excel;
No finery than their's is finer:
But we in greater freedom dwell,
Though our magnificence is minor.
While France in building leads the way,
Behold, by general resolution,
What homage Greece unites to pay
The fabric of our Constitution.
That edifice, which praise has won
From such an unexpected quarter,
We Britons would exchange for none
The proudest pile of stone and mortar.

Wity's a conjuring trick like the rejection of a suitor?
Because it's sleight of hand.
THOUGHT ON TRANSPORTATION.—As we don't hang
our criminal rubbish at home, we had better shoot it
abroad.

OUR COMPLIMENT FROM GREECE.—Thitannia presents
her compliments to France and Russia, and begs them
to observe that Honesty is the best Foreign Policy.
DIED OF OVERWORK—A SEWING MACHINE.—This
Sewing Machine was alive, and died because it could
not compete with other sewing machines that didn't
require feeding, nor clothing, and could live rent free.
In other words, this sewing machine was a poor Shirt..
maker.

'SWEET SOUNDS.'—MdIIe. Patti is giving, with the
greatest success, a series of performances at Paris. A
celebrated Critic says, 'Her singing is full of so much
lightness and sweetness, that the series promises to be
quite a vocal Patti-serie.
GREAT THEATRICAL SENEATION.---(A Prophecy.)—
The French version of the Battle of Waterloo' is
produced at Drury Lane, and meets with the greatest
success. We need not say it is brought out as a bur-
lesque, and is received throughout with shouts of
laughter. The'denouement,' in which the French win
the battle, is pronounced to be one of the greatest bibs
of fun since the days of Mother Goose.'
THE LIQUIDATION THAT IS WANTED. MORE. de
Lesseps is said to have expressed his great delight at
seeing the waters of the Mediterranean flow into one
of the tributary canals that are to cut through the
Isthmus of Suez. We have no doubt that the great
engineer overflowed with joy on the happy occasion,
but we fancy what would give him grt ater pleasure
than anything else would be to see the subscriptions
flow in. But the question is, where is the Bank 'hat
they are to come from?
THE BIGHT MAN IN 'THE RIGHT PLACE.—We 800 that
our old Baron Munchausen, who has long been lying
unknown, is about to be translated into French. We
beg to recommend as the very best editor of the work,
Monsieur Thiers. In fact, if it were published as a
continuation of his Histoire du Consulat et de l'Empire,'
we are convinced thit most of its subscribers would not
be able to tell the difference.

A FRIEND IN NEED.—In one of the hospitals at
Alexandria we saw a young fellow near an open window
lustily singing, I'm a bold soldier boy.' 'And what is
the matter with you P" Blind, Sir, blind as a bat.'
Poor Joe Parsons was in front at Antietam Creek, and a
ball passed directly through his eyes, across his face,
destroying his sight for ever. But he was as happy as a
lark. It might ha' been worse, yer see.' 'I was hit,'
he said, and it knocked me down. hay there all night,
and the next day the fight was renewed. I could stand
the pain, yer see, but the balls was flying all round, and
I wanted to get away. I couldn't see nothin', though.
At last I heard a feller groanin' beyond me. " Hello!"
says I, "Hello, yours( lf," says he. "Who be Yin'?"
says I—" a Rebel ?' "You're a Yankee," says he. "So
I am," says I. "What's the matter with your' "My
leg's smashed," sayshe. " Can't yer walk ?" "No." "Can
yer see F" "Yes," "Well," saya,"you'rea—Rebel,
but will you do me a little favour "I will," says
he, "ef I ken." Then I says, "Well, ole butternut, I
can't see nothin'. My eyes is knocked out, but I ken
walk. Come over yere. Let's git out o' this. You
pint the way, an' tote yer off the field on my bank."
"Bully for you," says he. And so we managed to git
together. We shook hands on it. I took a wink outer
his canteen, and he got on to my shoulders. I did the
walkin' for both, an he did the navigatin'. An' of he
didn't malze me carry hira straight into a rebel Colonel's
a mile away, I'm a liar! Hows'ever, the Colonel
came up, an' says he, " Whar d'yer come from Who
be yet r I told him. He said I was done for, and
couldn't do no more shoot'n ; an' he sent me over to our
lines. So I came down here with the wounded boys,
where we're doin' pretty well, all things considered.'
'But you will never see the light again, my poor fellow.'
'That's so,' he answered, glibly, but I can't help it,
you notice. I did my dooty ; got shot pop in the eye_
an' that's my misfort'n not my fault—as the old man
said of his blind hoes. hut—" I'm a bold soldier boy."'
—.Philadelphia .Enquirer.

- -

be formed for the purpose of co lecting Subscriptions
for the Distressed Operatives in the North, and that
Societies be requested either to levy their Members or
raise voluntary Subscriptions, in order that the Com-
mittee may be enabled to supplement the grants now
being made by the existing committees."

Subscriptions miy be sent in money, post-office
orders, or postage stamps to Mr. GEORGE POTTER,

and Cinderella, or The Little Glass Slipper." The
Story will be orally and musically told by George

PARIS Permanent Universal Exln-
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.

For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success in stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast nnmber of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establishment thare of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious buildimT, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhir.ited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111, and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is open, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, with liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties, or to sell them or, the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.

The whole of tke capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
oourse of construction) will be opened early in the sum
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has already been taken up.
Admission will be gratuitous on at least ' five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a Generdl Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rates for general observance; and agencies will be esta,
blished in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be els isified, so
that those of the same nature from different conntri s,
being placed in juxta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually In advance)
Will be charged, the space being tak n for six years.
The first rate (.£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
The second rate (£1 per squax e m-tre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.
Drawings of the Building can be seen at the principal
Railway Stations and Exchahges in London arm the
country; in the Refreshment rooms of the present
London Exhibition, and at the Oakes of Messrs. J.
STUDDY LE IGII &CG., 27. Leadeuhall-street, London.

whom forms of agreement and fall information may be
obtained.

THE Rev. G. C. (" Boatswain ")
SMITH, now in his 81st year, has become greatly
enfeebled, and is in straightened circumstances, lie
needs an attendant, but cannot pay one. Mr. Smith has
been labouring as a Christian Minister about fifty-eight
years. It will be remembered that he commenced
Destitute Sailors' Asylums and the first Sailors' Home,
from whence sprang all the other &Hors' Homes. He
gave great blows to the crimping system, revived open-
air preaching, and commenced and carried on for many
years all the efforts for the religious instruction of
sailors. Besides which he originated the first Temper-
ance Society in Britain, and established the London
Mission (1814) and Sailors' Orphan and Magdalen
Homes, and commenced the efforts for the religions
instruction of soldiers. For all this Mr. Smith has
passed unrewarded by his countrymen. Now that he is
aged and poor, a friend pleads that public gratitude and
sympathy might be manifested.
